questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Which of the following diagrams shows a unit circle in the coordinate plane with a central angle of $-{290}^{∘}$ in the standard position?
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that:

- A unit circle has a radius of $1$ and is centered at the origin in the coordinate plane.

- An angle in the standard position has its initial side on the positive $x$-axis, a vertex that lies at the origin.

- It rotates such that a positive angle is measured counter-clockwise, and a negative angle is measured clockwise.

Therefore, the correct diagram is as follows:

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Which of the following diagrams shows the unit circle in the coordinate plane with a central angle of $-\frac{\pi }{4}$ in the standard position?
questions.worked_solution:
To help us to visualize the angle, we first convert the measure of the angle into degrees. 

To convert the measure of an angle in radians to an equivalent measure in degrees, we multiply the measure in radians by $\frac{{180}^{∘}}{\pi }.$ This gives

$$
(-\frac{\pi }{4})\cdot (\frac{{180}^{∘}}{\pi })=-{45}^{∘}.
$$

Therefore,  $-\frac{\pi }{4}$ is equivalent to $-{45}^{∘}.$

Then, recall that:

- A unit circle has a radius of $1$ and is centered at the origin in the coordinate plane.

- An angle in the standard position has its initial side on the positive $x$-axis and its vertex is at the origin.

- A positive angle has a rotation that is measured counter-clockwise, and a negative angle is measured clockwise.

Therefore, the correct diagram is as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14222483/assets/a3106bc6788215147adfed66ac038523a73191a9b0182f35089bd1d7b2f87787.png)

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Recall that, in the coordinate plane, an angle $\theta$ in the standard position has its vertex at the origin, its initial side lies along the positive $x$-axis, and it rotates such that a positive angle is measured counter-clockwise.

Since a positive angle is always measured counter-clockwise, this means that a negative angle is measured *clockwise*.

For example, we can represent the angles $\theta = -45^\circ, -135^\circ, -225^\circ,$ and $-315^\circ$ as central angles of the unit circle (in the standard way) as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14222483/assets/0b33ba078eecacd9f8d40622fb21be5ec710a22b6e69458006c5d9422441285a.png)

tutorials.problem:
Sometimes, we wish to represent negative angles in the coordinate plane without reference to the unit circle.

As with positive angles, the convention for representing negative angles is the same as without the unit circle.

For example, we can represent the angles $\theta = -45^\circ, -135^\circ, -225^\circ,$ and $-315^\circ$ in the coordinate plane in the standard way as follows:

To convert the measure of an angle in radians to an equivalent measure in degrees, we multiply the measure in radians by $\frac{{180}^{∘}}{\pi }.$ This gives

$$
-(\frac{17\pi }{9})\cdot (\frac{{180}^{∘}}{\pi })=-{340}^{∘}.
$$

So, the angle $-\frac{17\pi }{9}$ is equivalent to $-{340}^{∘}.$ 

Now, we recall that:

- An angle in the standard position has its initial side on the positive $x$-axis, and a vertex that lies at the origin.

- It rotates such that a positive angle is measured counter-clockwise, and a negative angle is measured clockwise.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: A cat’s position relative to a fixed origin $O$ is given by the function $x(t)=3{t}^{2}+t$ meters, where $t$ is the time in hours. Find the average position of the cat between $2$ and $4$ hours.
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the average value of the position on $[{t}_{1},{t}_{2}],$ we use the average value formula

$$
{x}_{\text{avg}}=\frac{1}{{t}_{2}-{t}_{1}}\,{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{4-2}\,{\int }_{2}^{4}(3{t}^{2}+t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{({t}^{3}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2})|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[({4}^{3}+\frac{{4}^{2}}{2})-({2}^{3}+\frac{{2}^{2}}{2})] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[(64+8)-(8+2)] \\  & =31.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the average position is $31\,\text{m}.$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
A robotic rover moves in a straight line with velocity 
$v(t)=3{t}^{2}-t,$ where $t$ is measured in seconds and $v$ is measured in meters per second. 

Find the average acceleration ${a}_{\text{avg}}$ of the rover over the time interval $t\in [0,2].$ Do not round your answer.

${a}_{\text{avg}}=$ 
{{field-1}}
${\text{m/s}}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
The average acceleration is the average rate of change of the velocity, so

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{v(b)-v(a)}{b-a} \\  & =\frac{v(2)-v(0)}{2-0} \\  & =\frac{[3(2)^{2}-2]-[3(0)^{2}-0]}{2} \\  & =\frac{(12-2)-0}{2} \\  & =\frac{10}{2} \\  & =5\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the average acceleration is $5\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
A small rover moves along a straight track with velocity 
$v(t)=\sqrt{t}+2,$ where $t$ is measured in seconds and $v$ is measured in meters per second.

Find the average velocity ${v}_{\text{avg}}$ on the interval $[1,4].$ Do not round your answer.

${v}_{\text{avg}}=$ 
{{field-1}}
$\text{m/s}$
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the average value of the velocity on $[{t}_{1},{t}_{2}],$ we use the average value formula

$$
{v}_{\text{avg}}=\frac{1}{{t}_{2}-{t}_{1}}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}v(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{4-1}{\int }_{1}^{4}(\sqrt{t}+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{(\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}+2t)|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(\frac{2}{3}\cdot 8+8)-(\frac{2}{3}\cdot 1+2)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(\frac{16}{3}+8)-(\frac{2}{3}+2)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\frac{40}{3}-\frac{8}{3}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{32}{3}) \\  & =\frac{32}{9}\,\text{m/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the average velocity is $\frac{32}{9}\,\text{m/s}.$

To calculate the average value of the position on $[{t}_{1},{t}_{2}],$ we use the average value formula

$$

$$

$$

Question 1

A cat’s position relative to a fixed origin O is given by the function x(t)=3t2+t meters, where t is the time in hours. Find the average position of the cat between 2 and 4 hours.

a
32m
b
16m
c
31m
d
632m
e
312m
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To calculate the average value of the position on [t1,t2], we use the average value formula xavg=1t2−t1∫t1t2x(t)dt.

So, we get

xavg=14−2∫24(3t2+t)dt=12(t3+t22)|24=12[(43+422)−(23+222)]=12[(64+8)−(8+2)]=31.

Therefore, the average position is 31m.

Question 2
?

A train is moving north-east with velocity v(t)=6t2+8t+100km/h, where t is the time in hours. Find the average velocity of the train on the interval t∈[1,4].

a
166km/h
b
158km/h
c
162km/h
d
160km/h
e
164km/h
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To calculate the average value of the velocity on [t1,t2], we use the average value formula vavg=1t2−t1∫t1t2v(t)dt.

So, we get

vavg=14−1∫14(6t2+8t+100)dt=13(2t3+4t2+100t)|14=13((2(4)3+4(4)2+100(4))−(2(1)3+4(1)2+100(1)))=13((128+64+400)−(2+4+100))=162.

Therefore, the average velocity is 162km/h.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
A robotic rover moves in a straight line with velocity 
$v(t)=3{t}^{2}-t,$ where $t$ is measured in seconds and $v$ is measured in meters per second. 

Find the average acceleration ${a}_{\text{avg}}$ of the rover over the time interval $t\in [0,2].$ Do not round your answer.

${a}_{\text{avg}}=$ 
{{field-1}}
${\text{m/s}}^{2}$
question.worked_solution:
The average acceleration is the average rate of change of the velocity, so

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{v(b)-v(a)}{b-a} \\  & =\frac{v(2)-v(0)}{2-0} \\  & =\frac{[3(2)^{2}-2]-[3(0)^{2}-0]}{2} \\  & =\frac{(12-2)-0}{2} \\  & =\frac{10}{2} \\  & =5\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the average acceleration is $5\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
A small rover moves along a straight track with velocity 
$v(t)=\sqrt{t}+2,$ where $t$ is measured in seconds and $v$ is measured in meters per second.

Find the average velocity ${v}_{\text{avg}}$ on the interval $[1,4].$ Do not round your answer.

${v}_{\text{avg}}=$ 
{{field-1}}
$\text{m/s}$
question.worked_solution:
To calculate the average value of the velocity on $[{t}_{1},{t}_{2}],$ we use the average value formula

$$
{v}_{\text{avg}}=\frac{1}{{t}_{2}-{t}_{1}}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}v(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{4-1}{\int }_{1}^{4}(\sqrt{t}+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{(\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}+2t)|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(\frac{2}{3}\cdot 8+8)-(\frac{2}{3}\cdot 1+2)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(\frac{16}{3}+8)-(\frac{2}{3}+2)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\frac{40}{3}-\frac{8}{3}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{32}{3}) \\  & =\frac{32}{9}\,\text{m/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the average velocity is $\frac{32}{9}\,\text{m/s}.$

feedback.problem:
A particle’s acceleration in ${\text{m/s}}^{2}$ is given by the function $a(t)=\sqrt{t},$ where $t$ is the time in seconds.  

Find the average acceleration ${a}_{\text{avg}}$ of the particle on the interval $[1,4].$ Do not round your answer.

${a}_{\text{avg}}=$ 
{{field-1}}
${\text{m/s}}^{2}$
feedback.worked_solution:
To calculate the average value of the acceleration on $[{t}_{1},{t}_{2}],$ we use the average value formula

$$
{a}_{\text{avg}}=\frac{1}{{t}_{2}-{t}_{1}}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}a(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{4-1}{\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{(\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2})|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(\frac{2}{3}\cdot 8)-(\frac{2}{3}\cdot 1)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{16}{3}-\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{14}{3}) \\  & =\frac{14}{9}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the average acceleration is $\frac{14}{9}\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Determine the real roots of the cubic equation $10{y}^{3}-y=2{y}^{3}+y.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(y)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}10{y}^{3}-y & =2{y}^{3}+y \\ 8{y}^{3}-y & =y \\ 8{y}^{3}-2y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $2y.$ We can factor out the $2y$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}8{y}^{3}-2y & =0 \\ 2y(4{y}^{2}-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $4{y}^{2}-1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2y(4{y}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ 2y(2y+1)(2y-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $y=0,$ $z=-\frac{1}{2},$ and $y=\frac{1}{2}.$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Solve for $x$ where $4{x}^{3}+3x=3{x}^{3}-4x.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(x)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{3}+3x & =3{x}^{3}-4x \\ {x}^{3}+3x & =-4x \\ {x}^{3}+7x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $x.$ We can factor out the $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}+7x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}+7) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${x}^{2}+7=0$ has no real solutions, we cannot factor the expression ${x}^{2}+7$  further.

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the only solution is $x=0.$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Find the roots of the polynomial $p(t)=6{t}^{6}+15{t}^{5}+6{t}^{4}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the roots of the polynomial, we must solve the equation $p(t)=0,$ that is

$$
6{t}^{6}+15{t}^{5}+6{t}^{4}=0.
$$

First, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $3{t}^{4}.$ We can factor out the $3{t}^{4}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{4}(2{t}^{2}+5t+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $2{t}^{2}+5t+2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{4}(2{t}^{2}+5t+2) & =0 \\ 3{t}^{4}(2t+1)(t+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $t=0,$ $t=-\frac{1}{2},$ and $t=-2.$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(y)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}10{y}^{3}-y & =2{y}^{3}+y \\ 8{y}^{3}-y & =y \\ 8{y}^{3}-2y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $2y.$ We can factor out the $2y$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}8{y}^{3}-2y & =0 \\ 2y(4{y}^{2}-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $4{y}^{2}-1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2y(4{y}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ 2y(2y+1)(2y-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $y=0,$ $z=-\frac{1}{2},$ and $y=\frac{1}{2}.$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Determine the real roots of the cubic equation 10y3−y=2y3+y.

a
y=−12,0,12
b
y=0,1,12
c
y=−12,0,1
d
y=−12,0,13
e
y=−2,0,1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form Pn(y)=0. To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes 0: 10y3−y=2y3+y8y3−y=y8y3−2y=0

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of 2y. We can factor out the 2y as follows: 8y3−2y=02y(4y2−1)=0

Now, we factor the expression 4y2−1 as follows: 2y(4y2−1)=02y(2y+1)(2y−1)=0

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are y=0, z=−12, and y=12.

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(x)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{3}+3x & =3{x}^{3}-4x \\ {x}^{3}+3x & =-4x \\ {x}^{3}+7x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $x.$ We can factor out the $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}+7x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}+7) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${x}^{2}+7=0$ has no real solutions, we cannot factor the expression ${x}^{2}+7$  further.

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the only solution is $x=0.$

Question 2
?

Solve for x where 4x3+3x=3x3−4x.

a
x=0
b
x=0,5
c
x=0,3,5
d
x=−1,0,5
e
x=−1,0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form Pn(x)=0. To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes 0: 4x3+3x=3x3−4xx3+3x=−4xx3+7x=0

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of x. We can factor out the x as follows: x3+7x=0x(x2+7)=0

Since x2+7=0 has no real solutions, we cannot factor the expression x2+7 further.

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the only solution is x=0.

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To find the roots of the polynomial, we must solve the equation $p(t)=0,$ that is

$$
6{t}^{6}+15{t}^{5}+6{t}^{4}=0.
$$

First, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $3{t}^{4}.$ We can factor out the $3{t}^{4}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{4}(2{t}^{2}+5t+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $2{t}^{2}+5t+2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{4}(2{t}^{2}+5t+2) & =0 \\ 3{t}^{4}(2t+1)(t+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $t=0,$ $t=-\frac{1}{2},$ and $t=-2.$

Find the roots of the polynomial p(t)=6t6+15t5+6t4.

a
t=−4,−1,0
b
t=−6,−32,0
c
t=−2,−1,1
d
t=−2,−12,0
e
t=−2,0,1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the roots of the polynomial, we must solve the equation p(t)=0, that is 6t6+15t5+6t4=0.

First, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of 3t4. We can factor out the 3t4 as follows: 3t4(2t2+5t+2)=0

Now, we factor the expression 2t2+5t+2 as follows: 3t4(2t2+5t+2)=03t4(2t+1)(t+2)=0

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are t=0, t=−12, and t=−2.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Determine the real roots of the cubic equation $10{y}^{3}-y=2{y}^{3}+y.$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(y)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}10{y}^{3}-y & =2{y}^{3}+y \\ 8{y}^{3}-y & =y \\ 8{y}^{3}-2y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $2y.$ We can factor out the $2y$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}8{y}^{3}-2y & =0 \\ 2y(4{y}^{2}-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $4{y}^{2}-1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2y(4{y}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ 2y(2y+1)(2y-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $y=0,$ $z=-\frac{1}{2},$ and $y=\frac{1}{2}.$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Determine the real roots of the cubic equation 10y3−y=2y3+y.

a
y=−12,0,12
b
y=0,1,12
c
y=−12,0,1
d
y=−12,0,13
e
y=−2,0,1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form Pn(y)=0. To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes 0: 10y3−y=2y3+y8y3−y=y8y3−2y=0

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of 2y. We can factor out the 2y as follows: 8y3−2y=02y(4y2−1)=0

Now, we factor the expression 4y2−1 as follows: 2y(4y2−1)=02y(2y+1)(2y−1)=0

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are y=0, z=−12, and y=12.

question.html:
Question 1
?

Determine the real roots of the cubic equation 10y3−y=2y3+y.

a
y=−12,0,12
b
y=0,1,12
c
y=−12,0,1
d
y=−12,0,13
e
y=−2,0,1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form Pn(y)=0. To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes 0: 10y3−y=2y3+y8y3−y=y8y3−2y=0

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of 2y. We can factor out the 2y as follows: 8y3−2y=02y(4y2−1)=0

Now, we factor the expression 4y2−1 as follows: 2y(4y2−1)=02y(2y+1)(2y−1)=0

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are y=0, z=−12, and y=12.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem: Determine the real roots of the cubic equation $10{y}^{3}-y=2{y}^{3}+y.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(y)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}10{y}^{3}-y & =2{y}^{3}+y \\ 8{y}^{3}-y & =y \\ 8{y}^{3}-2y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $2y.$ We can factor out the $2y$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}8{y}^{3}-2y & =0 \\ 2y(4{y}^{2}-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $4{y}^{2}-1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2y(4{y}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ 2y(2y+1)(2y-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $y=0,$ $z=-\frac{1}{2},$ and $y=\frac{1}{2}.$

question.problem: Solve for $x$ where $4{x}^{3}+3x=3{x}^{3}-4x.$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form ${P}_{n}(x)=0.$ To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes $0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{3}+3x & =3{x}^{3}-4x \\ {x}^{3}+3x & =-4x \\ {x}^{3}+7x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $x.$ We can factor out the $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}+7x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}+7) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${x}^{2}+7=0$ has no real solutions, we cannot factor the expression ${x}^{2}+7$  further.

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the only solution is $x=0.$

?

Solve for x where 4x3+3x=3x3−4x.

a
x=0
b
x=0,5
c
x=0,3,5
d
x=−1,0,5
e
x=−1,0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's rewrite the polynomial equation in the form Pn(x)=0. To do this, we subtract all the terms from the right-hand side so that the right-hand side becomes 0: 4x3+3x=3x3−4xx3+3x=−4xx3+7x=0

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of x. We can factor out the x as follows: x3+7x=0x(x2+7)=0

Since x2+7=0 has no real solutions, we cannot factor the expression x2+7 further.

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the only solution is x=0.

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $x.$ We can factor out the $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}+7x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}+7) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${x}^{2}+7=0$ has no real solutions, we cannot factor the expression ${x}^{2}+7$  further.

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the only solution is $x=0.$

question.problem: Find the roots of the polynomial $p(t)=6{t}^{6}+15{t}^{5}+6{t}^{4}.$
question.worked_solution:
To find the roots of the polynomial, we must solve the equation $p(t)=0,$ that is

$$
6{t}^{6}+15{t}^{5}+6{t}^{4}=0.
$$

First, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $3{t}^{4}.$ We can factor out the $3{t}^{4}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{4}(2{t}^{2}+5t+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $2{t}^{2}+5t+2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{4}(2{t}^{2}+5t+2) & =0 \\ 3{t}^{4}(2t+1)(t+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $t=0,$ $t=-\frac{1}{2},$ and $t=-2.$

Question 3

Find the roots of the polynomial p(t)=6t6+15t5+6t4.

a
t=−4,−1,0
b
t=−6,−32,0
c
t=−2,−1,1
d
t=−2,−12,0
e
t=−2,0,1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the roots of the polynomial, we must solve the equation p(t)=0, that is 6t6+15t5+6t4=0.

First, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of 3t4. We can factor out the 3t4 as follows: 3t4(2t2+5t+2)=0

Now, we factor the expression 2t2+5t+2 as follows: 3t4(2t2+5t+2)=03t4(2t+1)(t+2)=0

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are t=0, t=−12, and t=−2.

Question 3
?

Find the roots of the polynomial p(t)=6t6+15t5+6t4.

a
t=−4,−1,0
b
t=−6,−32,0
c
t=−2,−1,1
d
t=−2,−12,0
e
t=−2,0,1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the roots of the polynomial, we must solve the equation p(t)=0, that is 6t6+15t5+6t4=0.

First, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of 3t4. We can factor out the 3t4 as follows: 3t4(2t2+5t+2)=0

Now, we factor the expression 2t2+5t+2 as follows: 3t4(2t2+5t+2)=03t4(2t+1)(t+2)=0

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are t=0, t=−12, and t=−2.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}5\sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 \\ -4 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}14 & 16 & -22 \\ -22 & 16 & 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{72}[\begin{aligned}7 & 8 & -11 \\ -11 & 8 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Ur=[−132−124320−13212],Σr=[6004],Vr=[12−121212] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, find the pseudoinverse A+.

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

U=[12−121212],Σ=[25000],V=[110−310310110] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of A, find the pseudoinverse A+.

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{10} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{10}\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -6 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].

Therefore, we have

$$

$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}14 & 16 & -22 \\ -22 & 16 & 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{72}[\begin{aligned}7 & 8 & -11 \\ -11 & 8 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}14 & 16 & -22 \\ -22 & 16 & 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{72}[\begin{aligned}7 & 8 & -11 \\ -11 & 8 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
question.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -6 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Ur=[00110−310310110],Σr=[2100010],Vr=[1001] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, find the pseudoinverse A+.

a
120[0130−62]
b
120[1030−26]
c
120[0130−62]
d
120[03102−6]
e
120[3102−60]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VrΣr+UrT,

where Σr+ is the pseudoinverse of Σr.

First, notice that

Σr+=1210[1002],UrT=110[0130−31].

Therefore, we have

A+=VrΣr+UrT=[1001]⋅1210[1002]⋅110[0130−31]=120[1001]⋅[1002]⋅[0130−31]=120[1002]⋅[0130−31]=120[0130−62].

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Ur=[12−12],Σr=[25],Vr=[110310] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, find the pseudoinverse A+.

a
120[3322]
b
130[2323]
c
120[1−13−3]
d
110[1122]
e
110[1−13−3]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VrΣr+UrT,

where Σr+ is the pseudoinverse of Σr.

First, notice that

Vr=110[13],Σr+=125[1],UrT=12[1−1].

Therefore, we have

A+=VrΣr+UrT=110[13]⋅125[1]⋅12[1−1]=120[13]⋅[1]⋅[1−1]=120[13]⋅[1−1]=120[1−13−3].

Using A^{+}=V_r\operatorname{diag}(1/6,1/4)U_r^{T} gives (1/72)[7,8,-11;-11,8,7], option c. This agrees with my earlier answer, the submitted response graded Correct, and Math Academy's worked solution.

Using A^{+}=V\Sigma^{+}U^{T}, the nonzero singular component gives A^{+}=(1/20)[1,1;3,3], option e. This agrees with my earlier answer and Math Academy's worked solution. The recorded submission was option a, which is mathematically different, so its Incorrect grade is consistent.

Since V_r=I, A^{+}=\Sigma_r^{-1}U_r^{T}. Scaling the rows of U_r^{T} by 1/(2\sqrt{10}) and 1/\sqrt{10}) gives (1/20)[0,1,3;0,-6,2], option a. This agrees with my earlier answer, the submitted response graded Correct, and Math Academy's worked solution.

Using A^{+}=V_r\Sigma_r^{-1}U_r^{T}, the scalar factor is 1/(2\sqrt{5}\sqrt{10}\sqrt{2})=1/20 and the outer product is [1,-1;3,-3]. Thus option c is correct, agreeing with my earlier answer, the submitted response graded Correct, and Math Academy's worked solution.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}5\sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
question.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 \\ -4 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

U=[−12121212],Σ=[52000],V=[−35454535] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of A, find the pseudoinverse A+.

a
150[−443−3]
b
150[−344−3]
c
150[3−3−44]
d
125[−344−3]
e
125[3−3−44]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VΣ+UT,

where Σ+ is the pseudoinverse of Σ.

First, notice that

V=15[−3443],Σ+=152[1000],UT=12[−1111].

Therefore, we have

A+=VΣ+UT=15[−3443]⋅152[1000]⋅12[−1111]=150[−3443]⋅[1000]⋅[−1111]=150[−3040]⋅[−1111]=150[3−3−44].

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 \\ -4 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}5\sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$

U=[−12121212],Σ=[52000],V=[−35454535] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of A, find the pseudoinverse A+.

a

c
150[3−3−44]
d
125[−344−3]
e
125[3−3−44]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VΣ+UT,

where Σ+ is the pseudoinverse of Σ.

First, notice that

V=15[−3443],Σ+=152[1000],UT=12[−1111].

Therefore, we have

A+=VΣ+UT=15[−3443]⋅152[1000]⋅12[−1111]=150[−3443]⋅[1000]⋅[−1111]=150[−3040]⋅[−1111]=150[3−3−44].

solution.reasoning: The pseudoinverse is A^{+}=V\Sigma^{+}U^{T}, where \Sigma^{+}=\operatorname{diag}(1/(5\sqrt{2}),0). Thus A^{+}=\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}-3/5\\4/5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1/\sqrt{2}&1/\sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{50}\begin{bmatrix}3&-3\\-4&4\end{bmatrix}, which is option c. No Math Academy answer-key or grading evidence was supplied.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}5\sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 \\ -4 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
question.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}14 & 16 & -22 \\ -22 & 16 & 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{72}[\begin{aligned}7 & 8 & -11 \\ -11 & 8 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}14 & 16 & -22 \\ -22 & 16 & 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{72}[\begin{aligned}7 & 8 & -11 \\ -11 & 8 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}14 & 16 & -22 \\ -22 & 16 & 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{72}[\begin{aligned}7 & 8 & -11 \\ -11 & 8 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Ur=[−132−124320−13212],Σr=[6004],Vr=[12−121212] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, find the pseudoinverse A+.

a
172[−118778−11]

c
172[78−11−1187]

1144[56−13−1365]

Correct
EXPLANATION

If A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VrΣr+UrT,

where Σr+ is the pseudoinverse of Σr.

First, notice that

Vr=12[1−111],Σr+=124[4006],UrT=132[−14−1−303].

Therefore, we have

A+=VrΣr+UrT=12[1−111]⋅124[4006]⋅132[−14−1−303]=1144[1−111]⋅[4006]⋅[−14−1−303]=1144[4−646]⋅[−14−1−303]=1144[1416−22−221614]=172[78−11−1187].

solution.reasoning: For a reduced SVD, A^{+}=V_r\Sigma_r^{-1}U_r^{T}, with \Sigma_r^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(1/6,1/4). Multiplication gives first row (-1/36+1/8,4/36,-1/36-1/8)=(7,8,-11)/72 and second row (-1/36-1/8,4/36,-1/36+1/8)=(-11,8,7)/72. Therefore option c is mathematically correct. Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}14 & 16 & -22 \\ -22 & 16 & 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{72}[\begin{aligned}7 & 8 & -11 \\ -11 & 8 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
question.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

U=[12−121212],Σ=[25000],V=[110−310310110] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of A, find the pseudoinverse A+.

a
15[1236]
b
120[−11−33]
c
110[1155]
d
110[1−13−3]
e
120[1133]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VΣ+UT,

where Σ+ is the pseudoinverse of Σ.

First, notice that

V=110[1−331],Σ+=125[1000],UT=12[11−11].

Therefore, we have

A+=VΣ+UT=110[1−331]⋅125[1000]⋅12[11−11]=120[1−331]⋅[1000]⋅[11−11]=120[1030]⋅[11−11]=120[1133].

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$

Question 3
?

U=[12−121212],Σ=[25000],V=[110−310310110] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of A, find the pseudoinverse A+.

a
15[1236]
b
120[−11−33]
c
110[1155]
d
110[1−13−3]
e
120[1133]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VΣ+UT,

where Σ+ is the pseudoinverse of Σ.

First, notice that

V=110[1−331],Σ+=125[1000],UT=12[11−11].

Therefore, we have

A+=VΣ+UT=110[1−331]⋅125[1000]⋅12[11−11]=120[1−331]⋅[1000]⋅[11−11]=120[1030]⋅[11−11]=120[1133].

solution.reasoning: The pseudoinverse is A^{+}=V\Sigma^{+}U^{T}, where \Sigma^{+}=\operatorname{diag}(1/(2\sqrt{5}),0). Thus A^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1/\sqrt{10}\\3/\sqrt{10}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1/\sqrt{2}&1/\sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{20}\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\3&3\end{bmatrix}, matching option e. No Math Academy answer-key or grading evidence was supplied.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{10} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{10}\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
question.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -6 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -6 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Ur=[00110−310310110],Σr=[2100010],Vr=[1001] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, find the pseudoinverse A+.

a
120[0130−62]
b
120[1030−26]
c
120[0130−62]
d
120[03102−6]
e
120[3102−60]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VrΣr+UrT,

where Σr+ is the pseudoinverse of Σr.

First, notice that

Σr+=1210[1002],UrT=110[0130−31].

Therefore, we have

A+=VrΣr+UrT=[1001]⋅1210[1002]⋅110[0130−31]=120[1001]⋅[1002]⋅[0130−31]=120[1002]⋅[0130−31]=120[0130−62].

solution.reasoning: For a reduced SVD, A^{+}=V_r\Sigma_r^{-1}U_r^{T}. Since V_r=I, scale the first row of U_r^{T} by 1/(2\sqrt{10}) and the second by 1/\sqrt{10}. This gives rows (0,1/20,3/20) and (0,-3/10,1/10), matching option a. No Math Academy answer-key or grading evidence was supplied.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem:
$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{10} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{10}\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -6 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Ur=[00110−310310110],Σr=[2100010],Vr=[1001] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, find the pseudoinverse A+.

a
120[0130−62]
b
120[1030−26]
c
120[0130−62]
d
120[03102−6]
e
120[3102−60]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VrΣr+UrT,

where Σr+ is the pseudoinverse of Σr.

First, notice that

Σr+=1210[1002],UrT=110[0130−31].

Therefore, we have

A+=VrΣr+UrT=[1001]⋅1210[1002]⋅110[0130−31]=120[1001]⋅[1002]⋅[0130−31]=120[1002]⋅[0130−31]=120[0130−62].

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
question.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Ur=[12−12],Σr=[25],Vr=[110310] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, find the pseudoinverse A+.

a
120[3322]
b
130[2323]
c
120[1−13−3]
d
110[1122]
e
110[1−13−3]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VrΣr+UrT,

where Σr+ is the pseudoinverse of Σr.

First, notice that

Vr=110[13],Σr+=125[1],UrT=12[1−1].

Therefore, we have

A+=VrΣr+UrT=110[13]⋅125[1]⋅12[1−1]=120[13]⋅[1]⋅[1−1]=120[13]⋅[1−1]=120[1−13−3].

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Ur=[12−12],Σr=[25],Vr=[110310] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, find the pseudoinverse A+.

a
120[3322]
b
130[2323]
c
120[1−13−3]
d
110[1122]
e
110[1−13−3]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VrΣr+UrT,

where Σr+ is the pseudoinverse of Σr.

First, notice that

Vr=110[13],Σr+=125[1],UrT=12[1−1].

Therefore, we have

A+=VrΣr+UrT=110[13]⋅125[1]⋅12[1−1]=120[13]⋅[1]⋅[1−1]=120[13]⋅[1−1]=120[1−13−3].

solution.reasoning: For a reduced SVD, A^{+}=V_r\Sigma_r^{-1}U_r^{T}. The outer product has coefficient 1/(2\sqrt{5}\sqrt{10}\sqrt{2})=1/20, giving A^{+}=\frac{1}{20}\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\3&-3\end{bmatrix}. This matches option c. No Math Academy answer-key or grading evidence was supplied.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem:
$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{20}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(x+y)^{2}\,i+{e}^{x-y}\,j$ and $C$ is the line segment traversed from the point $A(-2,1)$ to the point $B(1,-1)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(-2+3t)\,i+(1-2t)\,j.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=-2\,i+j$ and $b=i-j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(-2\,i+j)+t[(i-j)-(-2\,i+j)] \\  & =(-2\,i+j)+t(3\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(-2+3t)\,i+(1-2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-2+3t,\,y=1-2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(x+y)^{2}\,i+{e}^{x-y}\,j \\  & =(-2+3t+1-2t)^{2}\,i+{e}^{-2+3t-(1-2t)}\,j \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\,i+{e}^{5t-3}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2+3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)j \\  & =3\,i-2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((t-1)^{2}\,i+{e}^{5t-2}\,j)\cdot (3\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\cdot 3+{e}^{5t-3}\cdot (-2) \\  & =3(t-1)^{2}-2{e}^{5t-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3(t-1)^{2}-2{e}^{5t-3}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)={e}^{y}\,i+{e}^{x}\,j$ and $C$ is the line segment traversed from the point $A(2,0)$ to the point $B(4,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=2\,i$ and $b=4\,i+2\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(2\,i)+t[(4\,i+2\,j)-(2\,i)] \\  & =(2\,i)+t(2\,i+2\,j) \\  & =(2t+2)\,i+2t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2t+2\,y=2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{y}\,i+{e}^{x}\,j \\  & ={e}^{2t}\,i+{e}^{2t+2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+2)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)j \\  & =2\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{2t}\,i+{e}^{2t+2}\,j)\cdot (2\,i+2\,j) \\  & ={e}^{2t}\cdot 2+{e}^{2t+2}\cdot 2 \\  & =2{e}^{2t}(1+{e}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{e}^{2t}(1+{e}^{2})\,dt \\  & =(1+{e}^{2}){e}^{2t}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1+{e}^{2})({e}^{2}-1) \\  & ={e}^{4}-1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=2{x}^{7}\,i+{5}^{x+y}\,j$ and $C$ is the line segment traversed from the point $A(2,3)$ to the point $B(5,4)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(2+3t)\,i+(3+t)\,j.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=2\,i+3\,j$ and $b=5\,i+4\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(2\,i+3\,j)+t[(5\,i+4\,j)-(2\,i+3\,j)] \\  & =(2\,i+3\,j)+t(3\,i+j) \\  & =(2+3t)\,i+(3+t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2+3t,\,y=3+t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2{x}^{7}\,i+{5}^{x+y}\,j \\  & =2(2+3t)^{7}\,i+{5}^{2+3t+3+t}\,j \\  & =2(2+3t)^{7}\,i+{5}^{5+4t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2+3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3+t)j \\  & =3\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2(2+3t)^{7}\,i+{5}^{5+4t}\,j)\cdot (3\,i+j) \\  & =2(2+3t)^{7}\cdot 3+{5}^{5+4t}\cdot 1 \\  & =6(2+3t)^{7}+{5}^{5+4t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6(2+3t)^{7}+{5}^{5+4t}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\,i+\sqrt{xy}\,j$ and $C$ is the line segment traversed from the point $A(1,1)$ to the point $B(4,3)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(1+3t)\,i+(1+2t)\,j.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=i+j$ and $b=4\,i+3\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(i+j)+t[(4\,i+3\,j)-(i+j)] \\  & =(i+j)+t(3i+2\,j) \\  & =(1+3t)\,i+(1+2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=1+3t,\,y=1+2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\,i+\sqrt{xy}\,j \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+3t+1+2t)\,i+\sqrt{(1+3t)(1+2t)}\,j \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)\,i+\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+2t)j \\  & =3\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)\,i+\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}\,j)\cdot (3\,i+2\,j) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)\cdot 3+\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}\cdot 2 \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)+2\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)+2\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$
