questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)={e}^{x}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j$ and $C$ is the line segment traversed from the point $A(3,2)$ to the point $B(1,5)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(3-2t)\,i+(2+3t)\,j.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=3\,i+2\,j$ and $b=i+5\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(3\,i+2\,j)+t[(i+5\,j)-(3\,i+2\,j)] \\  & =(3\,i+2\,j)+t(-2\,i+3\,j) \\  & =(3-2t)\,i+(2+3t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3-2t,\,y=2+3t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{x}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j \\  & ={e}^{3-2t}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+3t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3-2t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2+3t)j \\  & =-2\,i+3\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{3-2t}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+3t)\,j)\cdot (-2\,i+3\,j) \\  & ={e}^{3-2t}\cdot (-2)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+3t)\cdot 3 \\  & =-2{e}^{3-2t}+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+3t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-2{e}^{3-2t}+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+3t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j$ and $C$ is the curve $y=2{x}^{2}-1$ traversed from the point $A(1,1)$ to the point $B(2,7)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=t\,i+(2{t}^{2}-1)\,j.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. This is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =t\,i+(2{t}^{2}-1)\,j,\,1\le t\le 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=2{t}^{2}-1.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}-1)j \\  & =i+4t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1)\,j)\cdot (i+4t\,j) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1)\cdot 4t \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{1}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i+2y\,j$ and $C$ is the curve $\operatorname{ln}⁡y-x=0$ traversed from the point $A(0,1)$ to the point $B(1,e).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Making $x$ the subject of the equation, we have

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡y-x=0\,⟹\,x=\operatorname{ln}⁡y.
$$

So, the parametrization of the curve is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+t\,j,\,1\le t\le e.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,y=t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+2y\,j \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+2t\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{t}\,i+j) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+2t\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{t}+2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{1}^{e}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{t}+2t)\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡t}{2}+{t}^{2}]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =(\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡e}{2}+{e}^{2})-(0+1) \\  & ={e}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i+y\,j$ and $C$ is the curve $y=3{x}^{2}+1$ traversed from the point $A(0,1)$ to the point $B(1,4).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Since $y$ is the subject of the equation, a parametrization is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =t\,i+(3{t}^{2}+1)\,j,\,0\le t\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=3{t}^{2}+1.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =t\,i+(3{t}^{2}+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}+1)j \\  & =i+6t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+(3{t}^{2}+1)\,j)\cdot (i+6t\,j) \\  & =t\cdot 1+(3{t}^{2}+1)\cdot 6t \\  & =t+18{t}^{3}+6t \\  & =7t+18{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(7t+18{t}^{3})\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{7{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{9{t}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{7(1)^{2}}{2}+\frac{9(1)^{4}}{2})-0 \\  & =\frac{16}{2} \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j$ and $C$ is the curve ${y}^{3}=x+3$ traversed from the point $A(-3,0)$ to the point $B(5,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Making $x$ the subject of the equation, we have

$$
{y}^{3}=x+3\,⟹\,x={y}^{3}-3.
$$

So, the parametrization of the curve is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =({t}^{3}-3)\,i+t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{3}-3,\,y=t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j \\  & =({t}^{3}-3)\,i+{t}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(({t}^{3}-3))i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =3{t}^{2}i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(({t}^{3}-3)\,i+{t}^{2}\,j)\cdot (3{t}^{2}\,i+j) \\  & =({t}^{3}-3)\cdot 3{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =3{t}^{5}-9{t}^{2}+{t}^{2} \\  & =3{t}^{5}-8{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3{t}^{5}-8{t}^{2})\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{6}}{2}-\frac{8{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{{2}^{6}}{2}-\frac{8(2)^{3}}{3})-0 \\  & =32-\frac{64}{3} \\  & =\frac{32}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=2y\,i+{x}^{2}\,j$ and $C$ is the curve $\sqrt{y}=x+3$ traversed from the point $A(-3,0)$ to the point $B(-1,4)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(\sqrt{t}-3)\,i+t\,j.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. This is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =(\sqrt{t}-3)\,i+t\,j,\,0\le t\le 4.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\sqrt{t}-3,\,y=t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2t\,i+(\sqrt{t}-3)^{2}\,j \\  & =2t\,i+(t-6\sqrt{t}+9)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t}-3)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2t\,i+(t-6\sqrt{t}+9)\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,i+j) \\  & =2t\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+t-6\sqrt{t}+9 \\  & =\sqrt{t}+t-6\sqrt{t}+9 \\  & =t-5\sqrt{t}+9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{4}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(t-5\sqrt{t}+9)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14222363/assets/00ff3216e6876673a388eb3eaa0e7d02e268f5e679593ebd9fe01e2840099e1b.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i+xy\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of a circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(0,2)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+xy\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14222363/assets/f7bacafcbe893c0d21ea45a916190a49aa3a3532834cff4704f707c100bf8e6a.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=3y\,i+2x\,j$ and $C$ is the the arc of the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $3$ respectively, traversed anticlockwise from $A(0,3)$ to $B(-1,0)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to find the parametrization of an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $3$ respectively. It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =3y\,i+2x\,j \\  & =9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-9{sin}^{2}⁡t+6{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =6{cos}^{2}⁡t-9{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(6{cos}^{2}⁡t-9{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of a circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point $(0,3)$ to the point $(-3,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+9{sin}^{2}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+9{sin}^{2}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+27{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =9\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }9\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & =9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & =9{[{sin}^{3}⁡t-\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡t}{2}]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =9[0-(1-\frac{1}{2})] \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14222363/assets/c5e026312ab8a2ccfc61a37246c954b56550316661f158743cc2c46411a97f53.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(y-x)\,i-x\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}=2$  traversed counterclockwise from the point $(\sqrt{2},0)$ to the point $(0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Notice that we can write its equation as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, our curve is a part-ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $\sqrt{2}$ and $1$ respectively. This curve can be parameterized as

$$
r(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(y-x)\,i-x\,j \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\sqrt{2}({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}\,dt \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}t]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}]-[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)-0] \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}]-[-\frac{1}{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =1-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14222363/assets/4807f92defb4202359a32ca046073cd138db396a0975164e42b96126ac0cc591.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)={e}^{x}\,i+{e}^{-2y}\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(0,1)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{x}\,i+{e}^{-2y}\,j \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Line Integrals Over Line Segments
canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf F(x, y) =(1-y)^2\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}$ and $C$ is the line segment traversed from the point $A(0, 2)$ to the point $B(1,0).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$\mathbf{a} = 2\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{i}.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =2j+t[i-2j] \\  & =t\,i+(2-2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t = 1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = t, \qquad
	y = 2-2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(1-y)^{2}\,i+x\,j \\  & =(1-(2-2t))^{2}\,i+t\,j \\  & =(2t-1)^{2}\,i+t\,j \\  & =(4{t}^{2}-4t+1)\,i+t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-2t)j \\  & =i-2j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((4{t}^{2}-4t+1)\,i+t\,j)\cdot (i-2j) \\  & =(4{t}^{2}-4t+1)\cdot (1)+(t)\cdot (-2) \\  & =4{t}^{2}-6t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{2}-6t+1\,dt \\  & =(\frac{4}{3}{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}+t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{4}{3}-3+1)-0 \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Line Integrals Over Line Segments

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Line Integrals Over Cartesian Curves
canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf F(x, y) = y\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}$ and $C$ is the curve $y^3 = x-5$ traversed from the point $A(5,0)$ to the point $B(6,1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Making $x$ the subject of the equation, we have

$$
y^3 = x-5
\qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad
x = y^3 + 5.
$$

So, we can parametrize the curve using

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =({t}^{3}+5)\,i+t\,j,\,0\le t\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = t^3+5, \qquad
y = t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,j \\  & =t\,i+({t}^{3}+5)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+5)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =3{t}^{2}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+({t}^{3}+5)\,j)\cdot (3{t}^{2}\,i+j) \\  & =t\cdot 3{t}^{2}+({t}^{3}+5)\cdot 1 \\  & =3{t}^{3}+{t}^{3}+5 \\  & =4{t}^{3}+5.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{3}+5\,dt \\  & ={[{t}^{4}+5t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =1+5-0 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Line Integrals Over Cartesian Curves

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Line Integrals Over Circles and Ellipses
canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf F(x, y) = y\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}$ and $C$ is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The notation $\displaystyle\oint$ is used to remind us that we're dealing with a line integral over a *closed* curve.

We will use the formula

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} + \sin{t}\,\mathbf{j},
\qquad 0 \leq t \lt 2\pi.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = \cos{t}, \qquad
y = \sin{t}.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,j=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-(1-{cos}^{2}⁡t)+{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡t-1 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The line integral of a vector-valued function $\mathbf F$ along a piecewise smooth curve $C$ is denoted

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r .
$$

This integral represents the total work done by $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle from an initial point $A$ to a terminal point $B$ along the curve.

If the curve can be parameterized by the function $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ then we can calculate the line integral using the following formula:

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r= \int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t)\,\textrm dt
$$

Often, the trickiest part is finding a parameterization for $C.$ In this lesson, we'll consider several different cases

observed_steps.name: Example: Line Integrals Over Line Segments
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$\mathbf{a} = 2\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{i}.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =2j+t[i-2j] \\  & =t\,i+(2-2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t = 1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = t, \qquad
	y = 2-2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(1-y)^{2}\,i+x\,j \\  & =(1-(2-2t))^{2}\,i+t\,j \\  & =(2t-1)^{2}\,i+t\,j \\  & =(4{t}^{2}-4t+1)\,i+t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-2t)j \\  & =i-2j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((4{t}^{2}-4t+1)\,i+t\,j)\cdot (i-2j) \\  & =(4{t}^{2}-4t+1)\cdot (1)+(t)\cdot (-2) \\  & =4{t}^{2}-6t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{2}-6t+1\,dt \\  & =(\frac{4}{3}{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}+t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{4}{3}-3+1)-0 \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Line Integrals Over Line Segments
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=-2\,i+j$ and $b=i-j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(-2\,i+j)+t[(i-j)-(-2\,i+j)] \\  & =(-2\,i+j)+t(3\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(-2+3t)\,i+(1-2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-2+3t,\,y=1-2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(x+y)^{2}\,i+{e}^{x-y}\,j \\  & =(-2+3t+1-2t)^{2}\,i+{e}^{-2+3t-(1-2t)}\,j \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\,i+{e}^{5t-3}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2+3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)j \\  & =3\,i-2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((t-1)^{2}\,i+{e}^{5t-2}\,j)\cdot (3\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\cdot 3+{e}^{5t-3}\cdot (-2) \\  & =3(t-1)^{2}-2{e}^{5t-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3(t-1)^{2}-2{e}^{5t-3}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫CF⋅dr, where F(x,y)=(x+y)2i+ex−yj and C is the line segment traversed from the point A(−2,1) to the point B(1,−1)?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=(−2+3t)i+(1−2t)j.

a
∫01(t−1)2+e5t−3dt
b
∫013t2−2etdt
c
∫013(t−1)2−2e5t−3dt
d
∫012(t−3)2−3e5t−1dt
e
∫01(t−3)2+et−1dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to parameterize the line segment. The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are a=−2i+j and b=i−j. So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

r(t)=a+t(b−a)=(−2i+j)+t[(i−j)−(−2i+j)]=(−2i+j)+t(3i−2j)=(−2+3t)i+(1−2t)j,

where t varies from t=0 (at the point A) to t=1 (at the point B). Thus, along the curve C, we have x=−2+3t,y=1−2t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=(x+y)2i+ex−yj=(−2+3t+1−2t)2i+e−2+3t−(1−2t)j=(t−1)2i+e5t−3j.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(−2+3t)i+ddt(1−2t)j=3i−2j.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=((t−1)2i+e5t−2j)⋅(3i−2j)=(t−1)2⋅3+e5t−3⋅(−2)=3(t−1)2−2e5t−3.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫CF⋅dr=∫01F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫013(t−1)2−2e5t−3dt.

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Line Integrals Over Line Segments
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=2\,i$ and $b=4\,i+2\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(2\,i)+t[(4\,i+2\,j)-(2\,i)] \\  & =(2\,i)+t(2\,i+2\,j) \\  & =(2t+2)\,i+2t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2t+2\,y=2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{y}\,i+{e}^{x}\,j \\  & ={e}^{2t}\,i+{e}^{2t+2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+2)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)j \\  & =2\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{2t}\,i+{e}^{2t+2}\,j)\cdot (2\,i+2\,j) \\  & ={e}^{2t}\cdot 2+{e}^{2t+2}\cdot 2 \\  & =2{e}^{2t}(1+{e}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{e}^{2t}(1+{e}^{2})\,dt \\  & =(1+{e}^{2}){e}^{2t}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1+{e}^{2})({e}^{2}-1) \\  & ={e}^{4}-1\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=2\,i+3\,j$ and $b=5\,i+4\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(2\,i+3\,j)+t[(5\,i+4\,j)-(2\,i+3\,j)] \\  & =(2\,i+3\,j)+t(3\,i+j) \\  & =(2+3t)\,i+(3+t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2+3t,\,y=3+t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2{x}^{7}\,i+{5}^{x+y}\,j \\  & =2(2+3t)^{7}\,i+{5}^{2+3t+3+t}\,j \\  & =2(2+3t)^{7}\,i+{5}^{5+4t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2+3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3+t)j \\  & =3\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2(2+3t)^{7}\,i+{5}^{5+4t}\,j)\cdot (3\,i+j) \\  & =2(2+3t)^{7}\cdot 3+{5}^{5+4t}\cdot 1 \\  & =6(2+3t)^{7}+{5}^{5+4t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6(2+3t)^{7}+{5}^{5+4t}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2(2+3t)^{7}\,i+{5}^{5+4t}\,j)\cdot (3\,i+j) \\  & =2(2+3t)^{7}\cdot 3+{5}^{5+4t}\cdot 1 \\  & =6(2+3t)^{7}+{5}^{5+4t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6(2+3t)^{7}+{5}^{5+4t}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫CF⋅dr, where F(x,y)=2x7i+5x+yj and C is the line segment traversed from the point A(2,3) to the point B(5,4)?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=(2+3t)i+(3+t)j.

a
∫01(2+3t)7+55+4tdt
b
∫013(2+3t)7+4⋅55+4tdt
c
∫014(5+4t)7+3⋅52+3tdt
d
∫016(3t)7+54tdt
e
∫016(2+3t)7+55+4tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to parameterize the line segment. The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are a=2i+3j and b=5i+4j. So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

r(t)=a+t(b−a)=(2i+3j)+t[(5i+4j)−(2i+3j)]=(2i+3j)+t(3i+j)=(2+3t)i+(3+t)j,

where t varies from t=0 (at the point A) to t=1 (at the point B). Thus, along the curve C, we have x=2+3t,y=3+t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=2x7i+5x+yj=2(2+3t)7i+52+3t+3+tj=2(2+3t)7i+55+4tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(2+3t)i+ddt(3+t)j=3i+j.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(2(2+3t)7i+55+4tj)⋅(3i+j)=2(2+3t)7⋅3+55+4t⋅1=6(2+3t)7+55+4t.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫CF⋅dr=∫01F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫016(2+3t)7+55+4tdt.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Line Integrals Over Line Segments
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=i+j$ and $b=4\,i+3\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(i+j)+t[(4\,i+3\,j)-(i+j)] \\  & =(i+j)+t(3i+2\,j) \\  & =(1+3t)\,i+(1+2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=1+3t,\,y=1+2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\,i+\sqrt{xy}\,j \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+3t+1+2t)\,i+\sqrt{(1+3t)(1+2t)}\,j \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)\,i+\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+2t)j \\  & =3\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)\,i+\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}\,j)\cdot (3\,i+2\,j) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)\cdot 3+\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}\cdot 2 \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)+2\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)+2\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\,i+\sqrt{xy}\,j$ and $C$ is the line segment traversed from the point $A(1,1)$ to the point $B(4,3)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(1+3t)\,i+(1+2t)\,j.$*
question.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=i+j$ and $b=4\,i+3\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(i+j)+t[(4\,i+3\,j)-(i+j)] \\  & =(i+j)+t(3i+2\,j) \\  & =(1+3t)\,i+(1+2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=1+3t,\,y=1+2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\,i+\sqrt{xy}\,j \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+3t+1+2t)\,i+\sqrt{(1+3t)(1+2t)}\,j \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)\,i+\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+2t)j \\  & =3\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)\,i+\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}\,j)\cdot (3\,i+2\,j) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)\cdot 3+\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}\cdot 2 \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)+2\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+5t)+2\sqrt{1+5t+6{t}^{2}}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫CF⋅dr, where F(x,y)=ln⁡(x+y)i+xyj and C is the line segment traversed from the point A(1,1) to the point B(4,3)?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=(1+3t)i+(1+2t)j.

a
∫015ln⁡(5t)+66tdt
b
∫01ln⁡(2+5t)+1+5t+6t2dt
c
∫015ln⁡(2+5t)+61+5t+6t2dt
d
∫013ln⁡(2+5t)+21+5t+6t2dt
e
∫012ln⁡(5t)+36tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to parameterize the line segment. The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are a=i+j and b=4i+3j. So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

r(t)=a+t(b−a)=(i+j)+t[(4i+3j)−(i+j)]=(i+j)+t(3i+2j)=(1+3t)i+(1+2t)j,

where t varies from t=0 (at the point A) to t=1 (at the point B). Thus, along the curve C, we have x=1+3t,y=1+2t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=ln⁡(x+y)i+xyj=ln⁡(1+3t+1+2t)i+(1+3t)(1+2t)j=ln⁡(2+5t)i+1+5t+6t2j.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(1+3t)i+ddt(1+2t)j=3i+2j.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(ln⁡(2+5t)i+1+5t+6t2j)⋅(3i+2j)=ln⁡(2+5t)⋅3+1+5t+6t2⋅2=3ln⁡(2+5t)+21+5t+6t2.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫CF⋅dr=∫01F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫013ln⁡(2+5t)+21+5t+6t2dt.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=3\,i+2\,j$ and $b=i+5\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(3\,i+2\,j)+t[(i+5\,j)-(3\,i+2\,j)] \\  & =(3\,i+2\,j)+t(-2\,i+3\,j) \\  & =(3-2t)\,i+(2+3t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3-2t,\,y=2+3t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{x}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j \\  & ={e}^{3-2t}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+3t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3-2t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2+3t)j \\  & =-2\,i+3\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{3-2t}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+3t)\,j)\cdot (-2\,i+3\,j) \\  & ={e}^{3-2t}\cdot (-2)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+3t)\cdot 3 \\  & =-2{e}^{3-2t}+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+3t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-2{e}^{3-2t}+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+3t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫CF⋅dr, where F(x,y)=exi+ln⁡yj and C is the line segment traversed from the point A(3,2) to the point B(1,5)?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=(3−2t)i+(2+3t)j.

a
∫01e−2t+ln⁡(3t)dt
b
∫01e2+3t+ln⁡(3−2t)dt
c
∫013e2+3t−2ln⁡(3−2t)dt
d
∫01−2e3−2t+3ln⁡(2+3t)dt
e
∫01e3−2t+ln⁡(2+3t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to parameterize the line segment. The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are a=3i+2j and b=i+5j. So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

r(t)=a+t(b−a)=(3i+2j)+t[(i+5j)−(3i+2j)]=(3i+2j)+t(−2i+3j)=(3−2t)i+(2+3t)j,

where t varies from t=0 (at the point A) to t=1 (at the point B). Thus, along the curve C, we have x=3−2t,y=2+3t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=exi+ln⁡yj=e3−2ti+ln⁡(2+3t)j.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(3−2t)i+ddt(2+3t)j=−2i+3j.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(e3−2ti+ln⁡(2+3t)j)⋅(−2i+3j)=e3−2t⋅(−2)+ln⁡(2+3t)⋅3=−2e3−2t+3ln⁡(2+3t).

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫CF⋅dr=∫01F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫01−2e3−2t+3ln⁡(2+3t)dt.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Line Integrals Over Line Segments
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Making $x$ the subject of the equation, we have

$$
y^3 = x-5
\qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad
x = y^3 + 5.
$$

So, we can parametrize the curve using

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =({t}^{3}+5)\,i+t\,j,\,0\le t\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = t^3+5, \qquad
y = t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,j \\  & =t\,i+({t}^{3}+5)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+5)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =3{t}^{2}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+({t}^{3}+5)\,j)\cdot (3{t}^{2}\,i+j) \\  & =t\cdot 3{t}^{2}+({t}^{3}+5)\cdot 1 \\  & =3{t}^{3}+{t}^{3}+5 \\  & =4{t}^{3}+5.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{3}+5\,dt \\  & ={[{t}^{4}+5t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =1+5-0 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Example: Line Integrals Over Cartesian Curves
question.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf F(x, y) = y\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}$ and $C$ is the curve $y^3 = x-5$ traversed from the point $A(5,0)$ to the point $B(6,1).$
question.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Making $x$ the subject of the equation, we have

$$
y^3 = x-5
\qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad
x = y^3 + 5.
$$

So, we can parametrize the curve using

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =({t}^{3}+5)\,i+t\,j,\,0\le t\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = t^3+5, \qquad
y = t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,j \\  & =t\,i+({t}^{3}+5)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+5)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =3{t}^{2}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+({t}^{3}+5)\,j)\cdot (3{t}^{2}\,i+j) \\  & =t\cdot 3{t}^{2}+({t}^{3}+5)\cdot 1 \\  & =3{t}^{3}+{t}^{3}+5 \\  & =4{t}^{3}+5.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{3}+5\,dt \\  & ={[{t}^{4}+5t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =1+5-0 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 6
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Line Integrals Over Cartesian Curves
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. This is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =t\,i+(2{t}^{2}-1)\,j,\,1\le t\le 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=2{t}^{2}-1.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}-1)j \\  & =i+4t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1)\,j)\cdot (i+4t\,j) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1)\cdot 4t \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{1}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j$ and $C$ is the curve $y=2{x}^{2}-1$ traversed from the point $A(1,1)$ to the point $B(2,7)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=t\,i+(2{t}^{2}-1)\,j.$*
question.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. This is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =t\,i+(2{t}^{2}-1)\,j,\,1\le t\le 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=2{t}^{2}-1.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}-1)j \\  & =i+4t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1)\,j)\cdot (i+4t\,j) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1)\cdot 4t \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{1}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF⋅dr, where F(x,y)=cos⁡xi+sin⁡yj and C is the curve y=2x2−1 traversed from the point A(1,1) to the point B(2,7)?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=ti+(2t2−1)j.

a
∫12sin⁡t+4tsin⁡(t2−1)dt
b
∫12sin⁡t+4tsin⁡(t2)dt
c
∫01sin⁡t+4tcos⁡(t2)dt
d
∫01cos⁡t+4tsin⁡(2t2−1)dt
e
∫12cos⁡t+4tsin⁡(2t2−1)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to parameterize the curve. This is given by

r(t)=ti+(2t2−1)j,1≤t≤2.

Thus, along the curve C, we have x=t,y=2t2−1.

As a result,

F(r(t))=cos⁡xi+sin⁡yj=cos⁡ti+sin⁡(2t2−1)j.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(t)i+ddt(2t2−1)j=i+4tj.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(cos⁡ti+sin⁡(2t2−1)j)⋅(i+4tj)=cos⁡t⋅1+sin⁡(2t2−1)⋅4t=cos⁡t+4tsin⁡(2t2−1).

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫CF⋅dr=∫12F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫12cos⁡t+4tsin⁡(2t2−1)dt.
question.knowledge_point: Line Integrals Over Cartesian Curves

observed_steps.name: Question 7
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Line Integrals Over Cartesian Curves
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Making $x$ the subject of the equation, we have

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡y-x=0\,⟹\,x=\operatorname{ln}⁡y.
$$

So, the parametrization of the curve is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+t\,j,\,1\le t\le e.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,y=t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+2y\,j \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+2t\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{t}\,i+j) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+2t\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{t}+2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{1}^{e}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{t}+2t)\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡t}{2}+{t}^{2}]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =(\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡e}{2}+{e}^{2})-(0+1) \\  & ={e}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 7
?

Evaluate ∫CF⋅dr, where F(x,y)=xi+2yj and C is the curve ln⁡y−x=0 traversed from the point A(0,1) to the point B(1,e).

a
e−12
b
e−12
c
e2+12
d
e+12
e
e2−12
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Making x the subject of the equation, we have

ln⁡y−x=0⟹x=ln⁡y.

So, the parametrization of the curve is given by

r(t)=ln⁡ti+tj,1≤t≤e.

Thus, along the curve C, we have x=ln⁡t,y=t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=xi+2yj=ln⁡ti+2tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(ln⁡t)i+ddt(t)j=1ti+j.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(ln⁡ti+2tj)⋅(1ti+j)=ln⁡t⋅1t+2t⋅1=ln⁡tt+2t.

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

∫CF⋅dr=∫1eF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫1e(ln⁡tt+2t)dt=[ln2⁡t2+t2]1e=(ln2⁡e2+e2)−(0+1)=e2−12

observed_steps.name: Question 8
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Line Integrals Over Cartesian Curves
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Since $y$ is the subject of the equation, a parametrization is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =t\,i+(3{t}^{2}+1)\,j,\,0\le t\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=3{t}^{2}+1.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =t\,i+(3{t}^{2}+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}+1)j \\  & =i+6t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+(3{t}^{2}+1)\,j)\cdot (i+6t\,j) \\  & =t\cdot 1+(3{t}^{2}+1)\cdot 6t \\  & =t+18{t}^{3}+6t \\  & =7t+18{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(7t+18{t}^{3})\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{7{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{9{t}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{7(1)^{2}}{2}+\frac{9(1)^{4}}{2})-0 \\  & =\frac{16}{2} \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 9
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Line Integrals Over Cartesian Curves
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Making $x$ the subject of the equation, we have

$$
{y}^{3}=x+3\,⟹\,x={y}^{3}-3.
$$

So, the parametrization of the curve is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =({t}^{3}-3)\,i+t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{3}-3,\,y=t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j \\  & =({t}^{3}-3)\,i+{t}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(({t}^{3}-3))i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =3{t}^{2}i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(({t}^{3}-3)\,i+{t}^{2}\,j)\cdot (3{t}^{2}\,i+j) \\  & =({t}^{3}-3)\cdot 3{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =3{t}^{5}-9{t}^{2}+{t}^{2} \\  & =3{t}^{5}-8{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3{t}^{5}-8{t}^{2})\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{6}}{2}-\frac{8{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{{2}^{6}}{2}-\frac{8(2)^{3}}{3})-0 \\  & =32-\frac{64}{3} \\  & =\frac{32}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Making x the subject of the equation, we have

y3=x+3⟹x=y3−3.

So, the parametrization of the curve is given by

r(t)=(t3−3)i+tj,0≤t≤2.

Thus, along the curve C, we have x=t3−3,y=t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=xi+y2j=(t3−3)i+t2j.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt((t3−3))i+ddt(t)j=3t2i+j.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. This is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =(\sqrt{t}-3)\,i+t\,j,\,0\le t\le 4.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\sqrt{t}-3,\,y=t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2t\,i+(\sqrt{t}-3)^{2}\,j \\  & =2t\,i+(t-6\sqrt{t}+9)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t}-3)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2t\,i+(t-6\sqrt{t}+9)\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,i+j) \\  & =2t\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+t-6\sqrt{t}+9 \\  & =\sqrt{t}+t-6\sqrt{t}+9 \\  & =t-5\sqrt{t}+9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{4}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(t-5\sqrt{t}+9)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF⋅dr, where F(x,y)=2yi+x2j and C is the curve y=x+3 traversed from the point A(−3,0) to the point B(−1,4)?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=(t−3)i+tj.

a
 ∫04(t−5t+9)dt
b
 ∫04(t−t+9)dt
c
 ∫04(t+6t+9)dt
d
 ∫04(t−4t+3)dt
e
 ∫04(t+5t+3)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to parameterize the curve. This is given by

r(t)=(t−3)i+tj,0≤t≤4.

Thus, along the curve C, we have x=t−3,y=t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=2ti+(t−3)2j=2ti+(t−6t+9)j.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(t−3)i+ddt(t)j=12ti+j.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(2ti+(t−6t+9)j)⋅(12ti+j)=2t⋅12t+t−6t+9=t+t−6t+9=t−5t+9.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫CF⋅dr=∫04F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫04(t−5t+9)dt.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Line Integrals Over Cartesian Curves
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The notation $\displaystyle\oint$ is used to remind us that we're dealing with a line integral over a *closed* curve.

We will use the formula

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} + \sin{t}\,\mathbf{j},
\qquad 0 \leq t \lt 2\pi.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = \cos{t}, \qquad
y = \sin{t}.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,j=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-(1-{cos}^{2}⁡t)+{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡t-1 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Example: Line Integrals Over Circles and Ellipses
question.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf F(x, y) = y\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}$ and $C$ is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction.
question.worked_solution:
The notation $\displaystyle\oint$ is used to remind us that we're dealing with a line integral over a *closed* curve.

We will use the formula

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} + \sin{t}\,\mathbf{j},
\qquad 0 \leq t \lt 2\pi.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = \cos{t}, \qquad
y = \sin{t}.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,j=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-(1-{cos}^{2}⁡t)+{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡t-1 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Line Integrals Over Circles and Ellipses
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+xy\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt.\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 11
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫CF⋅dr, where F(x,y)=xi+xyj and C is the arc of a circle of radius 2 centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point (2,0) to the point (0,2)?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=2cos⁡ti+2sin⁡tj.

a
∫0π/2(4sin⁡tcos2⁡t−2cos⁡t)dt
b
∫0π/2(4sin⁡tcos2⁡t−2sin⁡tcos⁡t)dt
c
∫0π(8sin⁡tcos2⁡t−4sin⁡t)dt
d
∫0π/2(8sin⁡tcos2⁡t−4sin⁡tcos⁡t)dt
e
∫π3π/2(8sin⁡tcos2⁡t+4sin2⁡tcos⁡t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius 2 centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as

r(t)=2cos⁡ti+2sin⁡tj,0≤t≤π2.

So, along the curve C, we have x=2cos⁡t,y=2sin⁡t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=xi+xyj=2cos⁡ti+2cos⁡t⋅2sin⁡tj=2cos⁡ti+4cos⁡tsin⁡tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(2cos⁡t)i+ddt(2sin⁡t)j=−2sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(2cos⁡ti+4cos⁡tsin⁡tj)⋅(−2sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj)=2cos⁡t⋅(−2sin⁡t)+4cos⁡tsin⁡t⋅2cos⁡t=−4sin⁡tcos⁡t+8sin⁡tcos2⁡t.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫CF⋅dr=∫0π/2F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫0π/2(8sin⁡tcos2⁡t−4sin⁡tcos⁡t)dt.
question.knowledge_point: Line Integrals Over Circles and Ellipses

observed_steps.name: Question 12
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Line Integrals Over Circles and Ellipses
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to find the parametrization of an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $3$ respectively. It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =3y\,i+2x\,j \\  & =9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-9{sin}^{2}⁡t+6{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =6{cos}^{2}⁡t-9{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(6{cos}^{2}⁡t-9{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 12
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF(r)⋅dr, where F(x,y)=3yi+2xj and C is the the arc of the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes 1 and 3 respectively, traversed anticlockwise from A(0,3) to B(−1,0)?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj.

a
∫0π(cos2⁡t−3sin2⁡t)dt
b
∫π/2π(3cos2⁡t+6sin2⁡t)dt
c
∫0π/2(6cos⁡t+9sin2⁡t)dt
d
∫π/2π(6cos2⁡t−9sin2⁡t)dt
e
∫π/2π(6cos2⁡t+3sin⁡t)dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to find the parametrization of an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes 1 and 3 respectively. It can be parametrized as

r(t)=cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj,π2≤t≤π.

So, along the curve C, we have x=cos⁡t,y=3sin⁡t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=3yi+2xj=9sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(cos⁡t)i+ddt(3sin⁡t)j=−sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(9sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj)⋅(−sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj)=−9sin2⁡t+6cos2⁡t=6cos2⁡t−9sin2⁡t.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫CF(r)⋅dr=∫π/2πF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫π/2π(6cos2⁡t−9sin2⁡t)dt.
question.knowledge_point: Line Integrals Over Circles and Ellipses

observed_steps.name: Question 13
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Line Integrals Over Circles and Ellipses
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+9{sin}^{2}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+9{sin}^{2}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+27{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =9\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }9\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & =9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & =9{[{sin}^{3}⁡t-\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡t}{2}]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =9[0-(1-\frac{1}{2})] \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }9\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & =9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & =9{[{sin}^{3}⁡t-\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡t}{2}]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =9[0-(1-\frac{1}{2})] \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate ∫CF(r)⋅dr, where F(x,y)=xi+y2j and C is the arc of a circle of radius 3 centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point (0,3) to the point (−3,0).

EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius 3 centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as

r(t)=3cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj,π2≤t≤π.

So, along the curve C, we have x=3cos⁡t,y=3sin⁡t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=xi+y2j=3cos⁡ti+9sin2⁡tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(3cos⁡t)i+ddt(3sin⁡t)j=−3sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(3cos⁡ti+9sin2⁡tj)⋅(−3sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj)=−9cos⁡tsin⁡t+27sin2⁡tcos⁡t=9cos⁡t(3sin2⁡t−sin⁡t).

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

∫CF(r)⋅dr=∫π/2πF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫π/2π9cos⁡t(3sin2⁡t−sin⁡t)dt=9∫π/2πcos⁡t(3sin2⁡t−sin⁡t)dt=9[sin3⁡t−sin2⁡t2]π/2π=9[0−(1−12)]=−92

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Notice that we can write its equation as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, our curve is a part-ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $\sqrt{2}$ and $1$ respectively. This curve can be parameterized as

$$
r(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(y-x)\,i-x\,j \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\sqrt{2}({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}\,dt \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}t]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}]-[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)-0] \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}]-[-\frac{1}{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =1-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{x}\,i+{e}^{-2y}\,j \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫CF⋅dr, where F(x,y)=exi+e−2yj and C is the arc of a circle of radius 1 centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point (1,0) to the point (0,1)?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=cos⁡ti+sin⁡tj.

a
∫0π/2cos⁡tecos⁡t+sin⁡te−2sin⁡tdt
b
∫0π/2cos⁡t+sin⁡tdt
c
∫0π/2ecos⁡t+e−2sin⁡tdt
d
∫0π/2cos⁡t−sin⁡tdt
e
∫0π/2−sin⁡tecos⁡t+cos⁡te−2sin⁡tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius 1 centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as

r(t)=cos⁡ti+sin⁡tj,0≤t≤π2.

So, along the curve C, we have x=cos⁡t,y=sin⁡t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=exi+e−2yj=ecos⁡ti+e−2sin⁡tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(cos⁡t)i+ddt(sin⁡t)j=−sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(ecos⁡ti+e−2sin⁡tj)⋅(−sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj)=ecos⁡t⋅(−sin⁡t)+e−2sin⁡t⋅cos⁡t=−sin⁡tecos⁡t+cos⁡te−2sin⁡t.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫CF⋅dr=∫0π/2F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫0π/2−sin⁡tecos⁡t+cos⁡te−2sin⁡tdt.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(x+y)^{2}\,i+{e}^{x-y}\,j$ and $C$ is the line segment traversed from the point $A(-2,1)$ to the point $B(1,-1)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(-2+3t)\,i+(1-2t)\,j.$*
question.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=-2\,i+j$ and $b=i-j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(-2\,i+j)+t[(i-j)-(-2\,i+j)] \\  & =(-2\,i+j)+t(3\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(-2+3t)\,i+(1-2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-2+3t,\,y=1-2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(x+y)^{2}\,i+{e}^{x-y}\,j \\  & =(-2+3t+1-2t)^{2}\,i+{e}^{-2+3t-(1-2t)}\,j \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\,i+{e}^{5t-3}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2+3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)j \\  & =3\,i-2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((t-1)^{2}\,i+{e}^{5t-2}\,j)\cdot (3\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\cdot 3+{e}^{5t-3}\cdot (-2) \\  & =3(t-1)^{2}-2{e}^{5t-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3(t-1)^{2}-2{e}^{5t-3}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫CF⋅dr, where F(x,y)=(x+y)2i+ex−yj and C is the line segment traversed from the point A(−2,1) to the point B(1,−1)?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=(−2+3t)i+(1−2t)j.

a
∫01(t−1)2+e5t−3dt
b
∫013t2−2etdt
c
∫013(t−1)2−2e5t−3dt
d
∫012(t−3)2−3e5t−1dt
e
∫01(t−3)2+et−1dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to parameterize the line segment. The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are a=−2i+j and b=i−j. So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

r(t)=a+t(b−a)=(−2i+j)+t[(i−j)−(−2i+j)]=(−2i+j)+t(3i−2j)=(−2+3t)i+(1−2t)j,

where t varies from t=0 (at the point A) to t=1 (at the point B). Thus, along the curve C, we have x=−2+3t,y=1−2t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=(x+y)2i+ex−yj=(−2+3t+1−2t)2i+e−2+3t−(1−2t)j=(t−1)2i+e5t−3j.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(−2+3t)i+ddt(1−2t)j=3i−2j.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=((t−1)2i+e5t−2j)⋅(3i−2j)=(t−1)2⋅3+e5t−3⋅(−2)=3(t−1)2−2e5t−3.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫CF⋅dr=∫01F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫013(t−1)2−2e5t−3dt.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Line Integrals Over Line Segments
last_observation.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=-2\,i+j$ and $b=i-j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(-2\,i+j)+t[(i-j)-(-2\,i+j)] \\  & =(-2\,i+j)+t(3\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(-2+3t)\,i+(1-2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-2+3t,\,y=1-2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(x+y)^{2}\,i+{e}^{x-y}\,j \\  & =(-2+3t+1-2t)^{2}\,i+{e}^{-2+3t-(1-2t)}\,j \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\,i+{e}^{5t-3}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2+3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)j \\  & =3\,i-2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((t-1)^{2}\,i+{e}^{5t-2}\,j)\cdot (3\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\cdot 3+{e}^{5t-3}\cdot (-2) \\  & =3(t-1)^{2}-2{e}^{5t-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3(t-1)^{2}-2{e}^{5t-3}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
