question.name: Question 12
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14222363/assets/f7bacafcbe893c0d21ea45a916190a49aa3a3532834cff4704f707c100bf8e6a.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=3y\,i+2x\,j$ and $C$ is the the arc of the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $3$ respectively, traversed anticlockwise from $A(0,3)$ to $B(-1,0)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*
question.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to find the parametrization of an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $3$ respectively. It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =3y\,i+2x\,j \\  & =9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-9{sin}^{2}⁡t+6{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =6{cos}^{2}⁡t-9{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(6{cos}^{2}⁡t-9{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 12
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF(r)⋅dr, where F(x,y)=3yi+2xj and C is the the arc of the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes 1 and 3 respectively, traversed anticlockwise from A(0,3) to B(−1,0)?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj.

a
∫0π(cos2⁡t−3sin2⁡t)dt
b
∫π/2π(3cos2⁡t+6sin2⁡t)dt
c
∫0π/2(6cos⁡t+9sin2⁡t)dt
d
∫π/2π(6cos2⁡t−9sin2⁡t)dt
e
∫π/2π(6cos2⁡t+3sin⁡t)dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to find the parametrization of an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes 1 and 3 respectively. It can be parametrized as

r(t)=cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj,π2≤t≤π.

So, along the curve C, we have x=cos⁡t,y=3sin⁡t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=3yi+2xj=9sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(cos⁡t)i+ddt(3sin⁡t)j=−sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(9sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj)⋅(−sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj)=−9sin2⁡t+6cos2⁡t=6cos2⁡t−9sin2⁡t.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫CF(r)⋅dr=∫π/2πF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫π/2π(6cos2⁡t−9sin2⁡t)dt.

last_observation.name: Question 12
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Line Integrals Over Circles and Ellipses
last_observation.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to find the parametrization of an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $3$ respectively. It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =3y\,i+2x\,j \\  & =9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-9{sin}^{2}⁡t+6{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =6{cos}^{2}⁡t-9{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(6{cos}^{2}⁡t-9{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*

$$

question.html:
Question 12
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF(r)⋅dr, where F(x,y)=3yi+2xj and C is the the arc of the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes 1 and 3 respectively, traversed anticlockwise from A(0,3) to B(−1,0)?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj.

a
∫0π(cos2⁡t−3sin2⁡t)dt
b
∫π/2π(3cos2⁡t+6sin2⁡t)dt
c
∫0π/2(6cos⁡t+9sin2⁡t)dt
d
∫π/2π(6cos2⁡t−9sin2⁡t)dt
e
∫π/2π(6cos2⁡t+3sin⁡t)dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to find the parametrization of an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes 1 and 3 respectively. It can be parametrized as

r(t)=cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj,π2≤t≤π.

So, along the curve C, we have x=cos⁡t,y=3sin⁡t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=3yi+2xj=9sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(cos⁡t)i+ddt(3sin⁡t)j=−sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(9sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj)⋅(−sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj)=−9sin2⁡t+6cos2⁡t=6cos2⁡t−9sin2⁡t.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫CF(r)⋅dr=∫π/2πF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫π/2π(6cos2⁡t−9sin2⁡t)dt.
question.knowledge_point: Line Integrals Over Circles and Ellipses

solution.reasoning: The anticlockwise arc corresponds to π/2≤t≤π. With r(t)=(cos t,3sin t), we have r'(t)=(-sin t,3cos t) and F(r(t))=(9sin t,2cos t). Their dot product is 6cos²t−9sin²t, giving option d. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked example concerns a different problem.

feedback.name: Question 12
feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14222363/assets/f7bacafcbe893c0d21ea45a916190a49aa3a3532834cff4704f707c100bf8e6a.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=3y\,i+2x\,j$ and $C$ is the the arc of the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $3$ respectively, traversed anticlockwise from $A(0,3)$ to $B(-1,0)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to find the parametrization of an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $3$ respectively. It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =3y\,i+2x\,j \\  & =9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-9{sin}^{2}⁡t+6{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =6{cos}^{2}⁡t-9{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(6{cos}^{2}⁡t-9{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.html:
Question 12
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫CF(r)⋅dr, where F(x,y)=3yi+2xj and C is the the arc of the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes 1 and 3 respectively, traversed anticlockwise from A(0,3) to B(−1,0)?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj.

a
∫0π(cos2⁡t−3sin2⁡t)dt
b
∫π/2π(3cos2⁡t+6sin2⁡t)dt
c
∫0π/2(6cos⁡t+9sin2⁡t)dt
d
∫π/2π(6cos2⁡t−9sin2⁡t)dt
e
∫π/2π(6cos2⁡t+3sin⁡t)dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to find the parametrization of an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes 1 and 3 respectively. It can be parametrized as

r(t)=cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj,π2≤t≤π.

So, along the curve C, we have x=cos⁡t,y=3sin⁡t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=3yi+2xj=9sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(cos⁡t)i+ddt(3sin⁡t)j=−sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(9sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj)⋅(−sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj)=−9sin2⁡t+6cos2⁡t=6cos2⁡t−9sin2⁡t.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫CF(r)⋅dr=∫π/2πF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫π/2π(6cos2⁡t−9sin2⁡t)dt.

question.name: Question 13
question.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of a circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point $(0,3)$ to the point $(-3,0).$
question.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+9{sin}^{2}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$

Question 13
?

Evaluate ∫CF(r)⋅dr, where F(x,y)=xi+y2j and C is the arc of a circle of radius 3 centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point (0,3) to the point (−3,0).

a
72
b
−74
c
−92
d
−94
e
52
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius 3 centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as

r(t)=3cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj,π2≤t≤π.

So, along the curve C, we have x=3cos⁡t,y=3sin⁡t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=xi+y2j=3cos⁡ti+9sin2⁡tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(3cos⁡t)i+ddt(3sin⁡t)j=−3sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(3cos⁡ti+9sin2⁡tj)⋅(−3sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj)=−9cos⁡tsin⁡t+27sin2⁡tcos⁡t=9cos⁡t(3sin2⁡t−sin⁡t).

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

∫CF(r)⋅dr=∫π/2πF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫π/2π9cos⁡t(3sin2⁡t−sin⁡t)dt=9∫π/2πcos⁡t(3sin2⁡t−sin⁡t)dt=9[sin3⁡t−sin2⁡t2]π/2π=9[0−(1−12)]=−92

question.html:
Question 13
?

Evaluate ∫CF(r)⋅dr, where F(x,y)=xi+y2j and C is the arc of a circle of radius 3 centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point (0,3) to the point (−3,0).

a
72
b
−74
c
−92
d
−94
e
52
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius 3 centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as

r(t)=3cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj,π2≤t≤π.

So, along the curve C, we have x=3cos⁡t,y=3sin⁡t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=xi+y2j=3cos⁡ti+9sin2⁡tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(3cos⁡t)i+ddt(3sin⁡t)j=−3sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(3cos⁡ti+9sin2⁡tj)⋅(−3sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj)=−9cos⁡tsin⁡t+27sin2⁡tcos⁡t=9cos⁡t(3sin2⁡t−sin⁡t).

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

∫CF(r)⋅dr=∫π/2πF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫π/2π9cos⁡t(3sin2⁡t−sin⁡t)dt=9∫π/2πcos⁡t(3sin2⁡t−sin⁡t)dt=9[sin3⁡t−sin2⁡t2]π/2π=9[0−(1−12)]=−92

feedback.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of a circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point $(0,3)$ to the point $(-3,0).$
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+9{sin}^{2}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+9{sin}^{2}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+27{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =9\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }9\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & =9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & =9{[{sin}^{3}⁡t-\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡t}{2}]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =9[0-(1-\frac{1}{2})] \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 14
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14222363/assets/c5e026312ab8a2ccfc61a37246c954b56550316661f158743cc2c46411a97f53.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(y-x)\,i-x\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}=2$  traversed counterclockwise from the point $(\sqrt{2},0)$ to the point $(0,1).$
question.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Notice that we can write its equation as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, our curve is a part-ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $\sqrt{2}$ and $1$ respectively. This curve can be parameterized as

$$
r(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(y-x)\,i-x\,j \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\sqrt{2}({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}\,dt \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}t]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}]-[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)-0] \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}]-[-\frac{1}{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =1-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

Evaluate ∫CF(r)⋅dr, where F(x,y)=(y−x)i−xj and C is the arc of the ellipse x2+2y2=2 traversed counterclockwise from the point (2,0) to the point (0,1).

a
12−π22
b
12+π2
c
1−π2
d
1−π22
e
12−π2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Notice that we can write its equation as

x22+y2=1.

So, our curve is a part-ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes 2 and 1 respectively. This curve can be parameterized as

r(t)=2cos⁡ti+sin⁡tj,0≤t≤π2.

So, along the curve C, we have x=2cos⁡t,y=sin⁡t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=(y−x)i−xj=(sin⁡t−2cos⁡t)i−2cos⁡tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(2cos⁡t)i+ddt(sin⁡t)j=−2sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=((sin⁡t−2cos⁡t)i−2cos⁡tj)⋅(−2sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj)=(sin⁡t−2cos⁡t)⋅(−2sin⁡t)−2cos⁡t⋅cos⁡t=2sin⁡tcos⁡t−2(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=sin⁡2t−2.

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

∫CF(r)⋅dr=∫0π/2F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫0π/2sin⁡2t−2dt=[−12cos⁡2t−2t]0π/2=[−12cos⁡π−π22]−[−12cos⁡(0)−0]=[12−π22]−[−12]=12−π22+12=1−π22

last_observation.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Notice that we can write its equation as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, our curve is a part-ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $\sqrt{2}$ and $1$ respectively. This curve can be parameterized as

$$
r(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(y-x)\,i-x\,j \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\sqrt{2}({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}\,dt \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}t]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}]-[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)-0] \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}]-[-\frac{1}{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =1-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Notice that we can write its equation as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, our curve is a part-ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $\sqrt{2}$ and $1$ respectively. This curve can be parameterized as

$$
r(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(y-x)\,i-x\,j \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\sqrt{2}({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}\,dt \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}t]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}]-[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)-0] \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}]-[-\frac{1}{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =1-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate ∫CF(r)⋅dr, where F(x,y)=(y−x)i−xj and C is the arc of the ellipse x2+2y2=2 traversed counterclockwise from the point (2,0) to the point (0,1).

a

EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Notice that we can write its equation as

x22+y2=1.

So, our curve is a part-ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes 2 and 1 respectively. This curve can be parameterized as

r(t)=2cos⁡ti+sin⁡tj,0≤t≤π2.

So, along the curve C, we have x=2cos⁡t,y=sin⁡t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=(y−x)i−xj=(sin⁡t−2cos⁡t)i−2cos⁡tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(2cos⁡t)i+ddt(sin⁡t)j=−2sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=((sin⁡t−2cos⁡t)i−2cos⁡tj)⋅(−2sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj)=(sin⁡t−2cos⁡t)⋅(−2sin⁡t)−2cos⁡t⋅cos⁡t=2sin⁡tcos⁡t−2(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=sin⁡2t−2.

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

∫CF(r)⋅dr=∫0π/2F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫0π/2sin⁡2t−2dt=[−12cos⁡2t−2t]0π/2=[−12cos⁡π−π22]−[−12cos⁡(0)−0]=[12−π22]−[−12]=12−π22+12=1−π22

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(y-x)\,i-x\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}=2$  traversed counterclockwise from the point $(\sqrt{2},0)$ to the point $(0,1).$
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Notice that we can write its equation as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, our curve is a part-ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $\sqrt{2}$ and $1$ respectively. This curve can be parameterized as

$$
r(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(y-x)\,i-x\,j \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\sqrt{2}({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}\,dt \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-\sqrt{2}t]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}]-[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)-0] \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}]-[-\frac{1}{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =1-\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

a

EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Notice that we can write its equation as

x22+y2=1.

So, our curve is a part-ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes 2 and 1 respectively. This curve can be parameterized as

r(t)=2cos⁡ti+sin⁡tj,0≤t≤π2.

So, along the curve C, we have x=2cos⁡t,y=sin⁡t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=(y−x)i−xj=(sin⁡t−2cos⁡t)i−2cos⁡tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(2cos⁡t)i+ddt(sin⁡t)j=−2sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=((sin⁡t−2cos⁡t)i−2cos⁡tj)⋅(−2sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj)=(sin⁡t−2cos⁡t)⋅(−2sin⁡t)−2cos⁡t⋅cos⁡t=2sin⁡tcos⁡t−2(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=sin⁡2t−2.

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

∫CF(r)⋅dr=∫0π/2F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫0π/2sin⁡2t−2dt=[−12cos⁡2t−2t]0π/2=[−12cos⁡π−π22]−[−12cos⁡(0)−0]=[12−π22]−[−12]=12−π22+12=1−π22

question.name: Question 15
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14222363/assets/4807f92defb4202359a32ca046073cd138db396a0975164e42b96126ac0cc591.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)={e}^{x}\,i+{e}^{-2y}\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(0,1)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*
question.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{x}\,i+{e}^{-2y}\,j \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫CF⋅dr, where F(x,y)=exi+e−2yj and C is the arc of a circle of radius 1 centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point (1,0) to the point (0,1)?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=cos⁡ti+sin⁡tj.

a
∫0π/2cos⁡tecos⁡t+sin⁡te−2sin⁡tdt
b
∫0π/2cos⁡t+sin⁡tdt
c
∫0π/2ecos⁡t+e−2sin⁡tdt
d
∫0π/2cos⁡t−sin⁡tdt
e
∫0π/2−sin⁡tecos⁡t+cos⁡te−2sin⁡tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius 1 centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as

r(t)=cos⁡ti+sin⁡tj,0≤t≤π2.

So, along the curve C, we have x=cos⁡t,y=sin⁡t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=exi+e−2yj=ecos⁡ti+e−2sin⁡tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(cos⁡t)i+ddt(sin⁡t)j=−sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(ecos⁡ti+e−2sin⁡tj)⋅(−sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj)=ecos⁡t⋅(−sin⁡t)+e−2sin⁡t⋅cos⁡t=−sin⁡tecos⁡t+cos⁡te−2sin⁡t.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫CF⋅dr=∫0π/2F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫0π/2−sin⁡tecos⁡t+cos⁡te−2sin⁡tdt.

last_observation.name: Question 15
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Line Integrals Over Circles and Ellipses
last_observation.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{x}\,i+{e}^{-2y}\,j \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫CF⋅dr, where F(x,y)=exi+e−2yj and C is the arc of a circle of radius 1 centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point (1,0) to the point (0,1)?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=cos⁡ti+sin⁡tj.

a
∫0π/2cos⁡tecos⁡t+sin⁡te−2sin⁡tdt
b
∫0π/2cos⁡t+sin⁡tdt
c
∫0π/2ecos⁡t+e−2sin⁡tdt
d
∫0π/2cos⁡t−sin⁡tdt
e
∫0π/2−sin⁡tecos⁡t+cos⁡te−2sin⁡tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius 1 centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as

r(t)=cos⁡ti+sin⁡tj,0≤t≤π2.

So, along the curve C, we have x=cos⁡t,y=sin⁡t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=exi+e−2yj=ecos⁡ti+e−2sin⁡tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(cos⁡t)i+ddt(sin⁡t)j=−sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(ecos⁡ti+e−2sin⁡tj)⋅(−sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj)=ecos⁡t⋅(−sin⁡t)+e−2sin⁡t⋅cos⁡t=−sin⁡tecos⁡t+cos⁡te−2sin⁡t.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫CF⋅dr=∫0π/2F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫0π/2−sin⁡tecos⁡t+cos⁡te−2sin⁡tdt.
question.knowledge_point: Line Integrals Over Circles and Ellipses

solution.reasoning: For r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t), the specified arc has 0≤t≤\pi/2 and r'(t)=(-\sin t,\cos t). Hence F(r(t))·r'(t)=-\sin t e^{\cos t}+\cos t e^{-2\sin t}, matching option e. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked example concerns a different problem.

feedback.name: Question 15
feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14222363/assets/4807f92defb4202359a32ca046073cd138db396a0975164e42b96126ac0cc591.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)={e}^{x}\,i+{e}^{-2y}\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(0,1)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{x}\,i+{e}^{-2y}\,j \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,dt.\end{aligned}

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=cos⁡ti+sin⁡tj.

a
∫0π/2cos⁡tecos⁡t+sin⁡te−2sin⁡tdt
b
∫0π/2cos⁡t+sin⁡tdt
c
∫0π/2ecos⁡t+e−2sin⁡tdt
d
∫0π/2cos⁡t−sin⁡tdt
e
∫0π/2−sin⁡tecos⁡t+cos⁡te−2sin⁡tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius 1 centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as

r(t)=cos⁡ti+sin⁡tj,0≤t≤π2.

So, along the curve C, we have x=cos⁡t,y=sin⁡t.

As a result,

F(r(t))=exi+e−2yj=ecos⁡ti+e−2sin⁡tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(cos⁡t)i+ddt(sin⁡t)j=−sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(ecos⁡ti+e−2sin⁡tj)⋅(−sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj)=ecos⁡t⋅(−sin⁡t)+e−2sin⁡t⋅cos⁡t=−sin⁡tecos⁡t+cos⁡te−2sin⁡t.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫CF⋅dr=∫0π/2F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫0π/2−sin⁡tecos⁡t+cos⁡te−2sin⁡tdt.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for $y=-4+2{x}^{7}-12{x}^{2}+{x}^{5/4}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we apply the addition, constant multiple, and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4+2{x}^{7}-12{x}^{2}+{x}^{5/4}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{7})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(12{x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5/4}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4)+2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{7})-12\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5/4}) \\  & =0+2\cdot 7{x}^{(7-1)}-12\cdot 2{x}^{(2-1)}+\frac{5}{4}\cdot {x}^{(\frac{5}{4}-1)} \\  & =14{x}^{6}-24x+\frac{5}{4}{x}^{1/4} \\  & =14{x}^{6}-24x+\frac{5\sqrt[4]{x}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for $y=2{x}^{7}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}+2x-2.$
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we apply the addition, constant multiple, and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{7}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}+2x-2) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{7})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{7})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-2})+2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2) \\  & =2\cdot 7{x}^{(7-1)}+(-2){x}^{(-2-1)}+2\cdot 1-0 \\  & =14{x}^{6}-2{x}^{-3}+2 \\  & =14{x}^{6}-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}+2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.raw_html:
2.Differentiating a Sum of Functions With Constant Factors?

Calculate dydx for y=2x7+1x2+2x−2.

questions.name: Question 3
questions.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is the sum of three power functions. So, we apply the sum rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{8}-{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{8})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-2}) \\  & =8{x}^{(8-1)}-3{x}^{(3-1)}+(-2){x}^{-2-1} \\  & =8{x}^{7}-3{x}^{2}-2{x}^{-3} \\  & =8{x}^{7}-3{x}^{2}-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Find ${f}^{′}(x)$ for  $f(x)={x}^{2}+\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is the sum of three power functions. So, we apply the sum rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-1}) \\  & =2{x}^{(2-1)}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{1/2-1}-(-1){x}^{(-1-1)} \\  & =2x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2}+{x}^{-2} \\  & =2x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: If $y=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{{x}^{3}}},$ find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first rewrite the function as

$$
y=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}=\frac{1}{3}{x}^{-3/2}.
$$

Then, we apply the constant multiple and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{3}{x}^{-3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (-\frac{3}{2}){x}^{(-\frac{3}{2}-1)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-5/2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{5}}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Negative Power Function Using the Constant Multiple Rule
questions.raw_html:
5.Differentiating a Negative Power Function Using the Constant Multiple Rule?

If y=13x3, find dydx.

H
Wed, Oct 14th @ 7:45 PM|Elapsed: 0:15Correct

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Here, we apply the addition, constant multiple, and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4+2{x}^{7}-12{x}^{2}+{x}^{5/4}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{7})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(12{x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5/4}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4)+2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{7})-12\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5/4}) \\  & =0+2\cdot 7{x}^{(7-1)}-12\cdot 2{x}^{(2-1)}+\frac{5}{4}\cdot {x}^{(\frac{5}{4}-1)} \\  & =14{x}^{6}-24x+\frac{5}{4}{x}^{1/4} \\  & =14{x}^{6}-24x+\frac{5\sqrt[4]{x}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Calculate dydx for y=−4+2x7−12x2+x5/4.

a
14x6−24x+5x44
b
14x6+22x−5x144
c
14x6+24x+5x−144
d
2x6−24x+54x3
e
14x6−12x2+5x124
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Here, we apply the addition, constant multiple, and power rules:

dydx=ddx(−4+2x7−12x2+x5/4)=ddx(−4)+ddx(2x7)−ddx(12x2)+ddx(x5/4)=ddx(−4)+2⋅ddx(x7)−12⋅ddx(x2)+ddx(x5/4)=0+2⋅7x(7−1)−12⋅2x(2−1)+54⋅x(54−1)=14x6−24x+54x1/4=14x6−24x+5x44

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Here, we apply the addition, constant multiple, and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{7}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}+2x-2) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{7})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{7})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-2})+2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2) \\  & =2\cdot 7{x}^{(7-1)}+(-2){x}^{(-2-1)}+2\cdot 1-0 \\  & =14{x}^{6}-2{x}^{-3}+2 \\  & =14{x}^{6}-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}+2\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate dydx for y=2x7+1x2+2x−2.

a
7x6−2x3+2
b
14x6−2x3+2
c
14x6−2x3−2
d
14x6−2x3
e
14x6+2x3+2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Here, we apply the addition, constant multiple, and power rules:

dydx=ddx(2x7+1x2+2x−2)=ddx(2x7)+ddx(x−2)+ddx(2x)−ddx(2)=2⋅ddx(x7)+ddx(x−2)+2⋅ddx(x)−ddx(2)=2⋅7x(7−1)+(−2)x(−2−1)+2⋅1−0=14x6−2x−3+2=14x6−2x3+2

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is the sum of three power functions. So, we apply the sum rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{8}-{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{8})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-2}) \\  & =8{x}^{(8-1)}-3{x}^{(3-1)}+(-2){x}^{-2-1} \\  & =8{x}^{7}-3{x}^{2}-2{x}^{-3} \\  & =8{x}^{7}-3{x}^{2}-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Find f′(x) for f(x)=x8−x3+1x2.

a
8x7−2x2−2x3
b
8x7−3x2+2x3
c
8x7−3x2−2x3
d
7x7−3x2−2x3
e
8x7−3x2−3x3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The function f(x) is the sum of three power functions. So, we apply the sum rule, and we get

f′(x)=ddx(x8−x3+1x2)=ddx(x8)−ddx(x3)+ddx(x−2)=8x(8−1)−3x(3−1)+(−2)x−2−1=8x7−3x2−2x−3=8x7−3x2−2x3.

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is the sum of three power functions. So, we apply the sum rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-1}) \\  & =2{x}^{(2-1)}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{1/2-1}-(-1){x}^{(-1-1)} \\  & =2x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2}+{x}^{-2} \\  & =2x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Find ${f}^{′}(x)$ for  $f(x)={x}^{2}+\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{x}.$
question.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is the sum of three power functions. So, we apply the sum rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-1}) \\  & =2{x}^{(2-1)}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{1/2-1}-(-1){x}^{(-1-1)} \\  & =2x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2}+{x}^{-2} \\  & =2x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Find f′(x) for f(x)=x2+x−1x.

a
2x−12x+1x2
b
2x+1x−1x2
c
2x+12x+1x2
d
2x+1x+1x2
e
2x+12x−1x2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function f(x) is the sum of three power functions. So, we apply the sum rule, and we get

f′(x)=ddx(x2+x−1x)=ddx(x2)+ddx(x1/2)−ddx(x−1)=2x(2−1)+12x1/2−1−(−1)x(−1−1)=2x+12x−1/2+x−2=2x+12x+1x2.

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We first rewrite the function as

$$
y=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}=\frac{1}{3}{x}^{-3/2}.
$$

Then, we apply the constant multiple and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{3}{x}^{-3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (-\frac{3}{2}){x}^{(-\frac{3}{2}-1)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-5/2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{5}}}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: If $y=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{{x}^{3}}},$ find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$
question.worked_solution:
We first rewrite the function as

$$
y=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}=\frac{1}{3}{x}^{-3/2}.
$$

Then, we apply the constant multiple and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{3}{x}^{-3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (-\frac{3}{2}){x}^{(-\frac{3}{2}-1)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-5/2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{5}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

If y=13x3, find dydx.

a
13x5
b
1x3
c
−12x5
d
−13x
e
12x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We first rewrite the function as y=13x3=13x−3/2.

Then, we apply the constant multiple and power rules:

dydx=ddx(13x−3/2)=13⋅ddx(x−3/2)=13⋅(−32)x(−32−1)=−12x−5/2=−12x5

The power rule gives f′(x)=8x^7-3x^2-2/x^3 for x ≠ 0, confirming the earlier answer c and Math Academy’s worked solution. The recorded submission was option a, with -2x^2 instead of -3x^2, so its Incorrect grade is consistent with the mathematics.

The power rule gives f′(x)=2x+(1/2)x^{-1/2}+x^{-2}=2x+1/(2\sqrt{x})+1/x^2 for x>0. This confirms the earlier option c answer. Math Academy graded that exact submission Correct, and its worked solution states the same derivative.

For x>0, y=(1/3)x^{-3/2}, so the power rule gives dy/dx=-(1/2)x^{-5/2}=-1/(2\sqrt{x^5}). This confirms the earlier option c answer. Math Academy graded that exact submission Correct, and its worked solution states the same derivative.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for $y=-4+2{x}^{7}-12{x}^{2}+{x}^{5/4}.$
question.worked_solution:
Here, we apply the addition, constant multiple, and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4+2{x}^{7}-12{x}^{2}+{x}^{5/4}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{7})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(12{x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5/4}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4)+2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{7})-12\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5/4}) \\  & =0+2\cdot 7{x}^{(7-1)}-12\cdot 2{x}^{(2-1)}+\frac{5}{4}\cdot {x}^{(\frac{5}{4}-1)} \\  & =14{x}^{6}-24x+\frac{5}{4}{x}^{1/4} \\  & =14{x}^{6}-24x+\frac{5\sqrt[4]{x}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Calculate dydx for y=−4+2x7−12x2+x5/4.

a
14x6−24x+5x44
b
14x6+22x−5x144
c
14x6+24x+5x−144
d
2x6−24x+54x3
e
14x6−12x2+5x124
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Here, we apply the addition, constant multiple, and power rules:

dydx=ddx(−4+2x7−12x2+x5/4)=ddx(−4)+ddx(2x7)−ddx(12x2)+ddx(x5/4)=ddx(−4)+2⋅ddx(x7)−12⋅ddx(x2)+ddx(x5/4)=0+2⋅7x(7−1)−12⋅2x(2−1)+54⋅x(54−1)=14x6−24x+54x1/4=14x6−24x+5x44

last_observation.worked_solution:
Here, we apply the addition, constant multiple, and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4+2{x}^{7}-12{x}^{2}+{x}^{5/4}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{7})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(12{x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5/4}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4)+2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{7})-12\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5/4}) \\  & =0+2\cdot 7{x}^{(7-1)}-12\cdot 2{x}^{(2-1)}+\frac{5}{4}\cdot {x}^{(\frac{5}{4}-1)} \\  & =14{x}^{6}-24x+\frac{5}{4}{x}^{1/4} \\  & =14{x}^{6}-24x+\frac{5\sqrt[4]{x}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate dydx for y=−4+2x7−12x2+x5/4.

a

c

EXPLANATION

dydx=ddx(−4+2x7−12x2+x5/4)=ddx(−4)+ddx(2x7)−ddx(12x2)+ddx(x5/4)=ddx(−4)+2⋅ddx(x7)−12⋅ddx(x2)+ddx(x5/4)=0+2⋅7x(7−1)−12⋅2x(2−1)+54⋅x(54−1)=14x6−24x+54x1/4=14x6−24x+5x44

feedback.problem: Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for $y=-4+2{x}^{7}-12{x}^{2}+{x}^{5/4}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Here, we apply the addition, constant multiple, and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4+2{x}^{7}-12{x}^{2}+{x}^{5/4}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{7})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(12{x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5/4}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4)+2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{7})-12\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5/4}) \\  & =0+2\cdot 7{x}^{(7-1)}-12\cdot 2{x}^{(2-1)}+\frac{5}{4}\cdot {x}^{(\frac{5}{4}-1)} \\  & =14{x}^{6}-24x+\frac{5}{4}{x}^{1/4} \\  & =14{x}^{6}-24x+\frac{5\sqrt[4]{x}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{7}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}+2x-2) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{7})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{7})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-2})+2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2) \\  & =2\cdot 7{x}^{(7-1)}+(-2){x}^{(-2-1)}+2\cdot 1-0 \\  & =14{x}^{6}-2{x}^{-3}+2 \\  & =14{x}^{6}-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}+2\end{aligned}

Question 2
?

Calculate dydx for y=2x7+1x2+2x−2.

a
7x6−2x3+2
b
14x6−2x3+2
c
14x6−2x3−2
d
14x6−2x3
e
14x6+2x3+2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Here, we apply the addition, constant multiple, and power rules:

dydx=ddx(2x7+1x2+2x−2)=ddx(2x7)+ddx(x−2)+ddx(2x)−ddx(2)=2⋅ddx(x7)+ddx(x−2)+2⋅ddx(x)−ddx(2)=2⋅7x(7−1)+(−2)x(−2−1)+2⋅1−0=14x6−2x−3+2=14x6−2x3+2

Question 2
?

Calculate dydx for y=2x7+1x2+2x−2.

a
7x6−2x3+2
b
14x6−2x3+2
c
14x6−2x3−2
d
14x6−2x3
e
14x6+2x3+2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Here, we apply the addition, constant multiple, and power rules:

dydx=ddx(2x7+1x2+2x−2)=ddx(2x7)+ddx(x−2)+ddx(2x)−ddx(2)=2⋅ddx(x7)+ddx(x−2)+2⋅ddx(x)−ddx(2)=2⋅7x(7−1)+(−2)x(−2−1)+2⋅1−0=14x6−2x−3+2=14x6−2x3+2

question.name: Question 3
question.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is the sum of three power functions. So, we apply the sum rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{8}-{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{8})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-2}) \\  & =8{x}^{(8-1)}-3{x}^{(3-1)}+(-2){x}^{-2-1} \\  & =8{x}^{7}-3{x}^{2}-2{x}^{-3} \\  & =8{x}^{7}-3{x}^{2}-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Find f′(x) for f(x)=x8−x3+1x2.

a
8x7−2x2−2x3
b
8x7−3x2+2x3
c
8x7−3x2−2x3
d
7x7−3x2−2x3
e
8x7−3x2−3x3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The function f(x) is the sum of three power functions. So, we apply the sum rule, and we get

f′(x)=ddx(x8−x3+1x2)=ddx(x8)−ddx(x3)+ddx(x−2)=8x(8−1)−3x(3−1)+(−2)x−2−1=8x7−3x2−2x−3=8x7−3x2−2x3.

last_observation.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is the sum of three power functions. So, we apply the sum rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{8}-{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{8})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-2}) \\  & =8{x}^{(8-1)}-3{x}^{(3-1)}+(-2){x}^{-2-1} \\  & =8{x}^{7}-3{x}^{2}-2{x}^{-3} \\  & =8{x}^{7}-3{x}^{2}-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Find f′(x) for f(x)=x8−x3+1x2.

a
8x7−2x2−2x3
b
8x7−3x2+2x3
c
8x7−3x2−2x3
d
7x7−3x2−2x3
e
8x7−3x2−3x3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The function f(x) is the sum of three power functions. So, we apply the sum rule, and we get

f′(x)=ddx(x8−x3+1x2)=ddx(x8)−ddx(x3)+ddx(x−2)=8x(8−1)−3x(3−1)+(−2)x−2−1=8x7−3x2−2x−3=8x7−3x2−2x3.

decision.exposure_note: KP association unavailable; use the base accuracy without pooling unknown skills

solution.reasoning: Rewrite 1/x^2 as x^{-2}. The power rule gives f′(x) = 8x^7 - 3x^2 - 2x^{-3}, matching option c for x ≠ 0. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is the sum of three power functions. So, we apply the sum rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{8}-{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{8})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-2}) \\  & =8{x}^{(8-1)}-3{x}^{(3-1)}+(-2){x}^{-2-1} \\  & =8{x}^{7}-3{x}^{2}-2{x}^{-3} \\  & =8{x}^{7}-3{x}^{2}-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Find ${f}^{′}(x)$ for  $f(x)={x}^{2}+\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{x}.$
question.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is the sum of three power functions. So, we apply the sum rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-1}) \\  & =2{x}^{(2-1)}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{1/2-1}-(-1){x}^{(-1-1)} \\  & =2x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2}+{x}^{-2} \\  & =2x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Find f′(x) for f(x)=x2+x−1x.

a
2x−12x+1x2
b
2x+1x−1x2
c
2x+12x+1x2
d
2x+1x+1x2
e
2x+12x−1x2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function f(x) is the sum of three power functions. So, we apply the sum rule, and we get

f′(x)=ddx(x2+x−1x)=ddx(x2)+ddx(x1/2)−ddx(x−1)=2x(2−1)+12x1/2−1−(−1)x(−1−1)=2x+12x−1/2+x−2=2x+12x+1x2.

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is the sum of three power functions. So, we apply the sum rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-1}) \\  & =2{x}^{(2-1)}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{1/2-1}-(-1){x}^{(-1-1)} \\  & =2x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2}+{x}^{-2} \\  & =2x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Find ${f}^{′}(x)$ for  $f(x)={x}^{2}+\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{x}.$
question.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-1}) \\  & =2{x}^{(2-1)}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{1/2-1}-(-1){x}^{(-1-1)} \\  & =2x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2}+{x}^{-2} \\  & =2x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find f′(x) for f(x)=x2+x−1x.

a
2x−12x+1x2
b
2x+1x−1x2
c
2x+12x+1x2
d
2x+1x+1x2

2x+12x−1x2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function f(x) is the sum of three power functions. So, we apply the sum rule, and we get

f′(x)=ddx(x2+x−1x)=ddx(x2)+ddx(x1/2)−ddx(x−1)=2x(2−1)+12x1/2−1−(−1)x(−1−1)=2x+12x−1/2+x−2=2x+12x+1x2.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem: Find ${f}^{′}(x)$ for  $f(x)={x}^{2}+\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{x}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is the sum of three power functions. So, we apply the sum rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-1}) \\  & =2{x}^{(2-1)}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{1/2-1}-(-1){x}^{(-1-1)} \\  & =2x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2}+{x}^{-2} \\  & =2x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: If $y=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{{x}^{3}}},$ find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$
question.worked_solution:
We first rewrite the function as

$$
y=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}=\frac{1}{3}{x}^{-3/2}.
$$

Then, we apply the constant multiple and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{3}{x}^{-3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (-\frac{3}{2}){x}^{(-\frac{3}{2}-1)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-5/2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{5}}}\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 5
?

If y=13x3, find dydx.

a
13x5
b
1x3
c
−12x5
d
−13x
e
12x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We first rewrite the function as y=13x3=13x−3/2.

Then, we apply the constant multiple and power rules:

dydx=ddx(13x−3/2)=13⋅ddx(x−3/2)=13⋅(−32)x(−32−1)=−12x−5/2=−12x5

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{3}{x}^{-3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (-\frac{3}{2}){x}^{(-\frac{3}{2}-1)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-5/2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{5}}}\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 5
?

If y=13x3, find dydx.

a
13x5
b
1x3
c
−12x5
d
−13x
e
12x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We first rewrite the function as y=13x3=13x−3/2.

Then, we apply the constant multiple and power rules:

dydx=ddx(13x−3/2)=13⋅ddx(x−3/2)=13⋅(−32)x(−32−1)=−12x−5/2=−12x5

solution.reasoning: For x>0, y=(1/3)x^{-3/2}. The power rule gives dy/dx=(1/3)(-3/2)x^{-5/2}=-1/(2\sqrt{x^5}), matching option c. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem: If $y=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{{x}^{3}}},$ find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
We first rewrite the function as

$$
y=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}=\frac{1}{3}{x}^{-3/2}.
$$

Then, we apply the constant multiple and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{3}{x}^{-3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (-\frac{3}{2}){x}^{(-\frac{3}{2}-1)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-5/2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{5}}}\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
We can reflect an object in any line. Consider the diagram below. The two polygons are the mirror images of each other in the line $l.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14222660/assets/1e4dfb2939916df5d5018320819f14fcec261a1e77c171b551e9868a8c3bebc8.png)

If we want to reflect the quadrilateral $ABCD$ below in the line $l,$ we can reflect each vertex separately and then draw the segments between the resulting corresponding vertices.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14222660/assets/a47c41b41ecae2bc4c281e1b90c843ae68fa907a0d2ff49c48454fd80e2977c7.png)

Let's start by reflecting the point $A.$ To do this, we need to plot a new point $A'$ on the opposite side of $l$ at an equal distance away from $l$ as the original point $A.$

The original point $A$ is $4$ units to the left of $l,$ so we need to plot the new point $A'$ at a distance of $4$ units to the right of $l.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14222660/assets/33bb82c9d0f20df13f46060b9aec21e8c4d1231766926c47b7718bf58e1c5e32.png)

Now let's reflect other vertices of the quadrilateral in the same way:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14222660/assets/00ec763ccce462effa024486a6ff09a98b549c61179de18bb850470e835a7627.png)

Finally, we draw segments between the reflected vertices.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14222660/assets/7ffd0cfa45051d8376c46528370b34222a1ebb226987e7530d5081d69942bbde.png)

judgments.reasoning: The two perpendicular reflections give (x,y) → (-x,-y), a 180° rotation about the intersection. This places the diamond two units left and two units below the intersection, with the triangle on its left, matching option e. The earlier answer agrees with both Math Academy's Correct grade for the submitted option e and its final worked-solution diagram.

answers.ma_evidence: The submitted selection was option e, and the captured feedback grade was Correct.

judgments.reasoning: The perpendicular reflections map (x,y) to (-x,-y), rotating the figure 180° about the lines' intersection. The resulting position and orientation match option a. This confirms the earlier answer and agrees with Math Academy's Correct grade for the submitted option a and its final solution diagram.

answers.ma_evidence: The submitted selection was option a, and the captured feedback grade was Correct.

judgments.reasoning: Reflection across y=x swaps coordinates, mapping every vertex of T to T′; for example, (-1,4) maps to (4,-1). The earlier answer y=x, option a, agrees with the captured Correct grade and Math Academy's stated solution.

answers.ma_evidence: Therefore, the equation of the line of reflection is $y=x,$ as shown below.

judgments.reasoning: The reflection line lies halfway between corresponding heights: (3+(-1))/2=1 and (6+(-4))/2=1. Thus y=1, option d, is correct. The earlier answer agrees with both the captured Correct grade and Math Academy's worked solution.

answers.ma_evidence: Therefore, the line of reflection is $y=1,$ as shown below.

judgments.reasoning: Math Academy's worked diagram correctly reflects the polygon across l: corresponding vertices remain at the same height and equal horizontal distances on opposite sides of the line. Math Academy's stated line x=1/2 is correct. Corresponding vertices have equal heights, and their x-coordinates average to 1/2; for example, the bottom vertices have x-coordinates 5/2 and -3/2. question.html:
Question 3
?

The polygon T is mapped to the polygon T′ under the action of a reflection. What is the equation of the line of reflection?

a
y=x
b
y=−x
c
y=x+1
d
y=0
e
x=0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The line of reflection is the perpendicular bisector of the segments joining each point to its image.

Therefore, the equation of the line of reflection is y=x, as shown below.
question.knowledge_point: Identifying the Line of Reflection

solution.reasoning: Reflection across y=x swaps coordinates: (x,y) maps to (y,x). This sends T's vertices (-4,1), (-1,1), (-1,4), (-2.5,3), and (-4,4) to the displayed vertices of T′. Thus option a is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

question.html:
Question 4
?

The polygon P is mapped to the polygon P′ under the action of a reflection. What is the equation of the line of reflection?

a
y=32
b
y=0
c
y=2
d
y=1
e
y=12
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The line of reflection is the perpendicular bisector of the segments joining each point to its image.

Therefore, the line of reflection is y=1, as shown below.
question.knowledge_point: Identifying the Line of Reflection

solution.reasoning: The horizontal reflection line bisects corresponding heights: (6+(-4))/2=1 and (3+(-1))/2=1. Thus the line is y=1, option d. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Find the formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence if the first term is $-1$ and the second term is $-3.$
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence (in function notation) is

$$
f(n)=f(1)+(n-1)d.
$$

We are given the first term $f(1)=-1.$ Also, the common difference of the sequence can be found as

$$
d=-3-(-1)=-2.
$$

So, we substitute into the formula and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n) & =f(1)+(n-1)d \\  & =-1+(n-1)(-2) \\  & =-1-2n+2 \\  & =1-2n\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is $f(n)=1-2n.$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Find the formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence if the first term is $-5$ and the common difference is $-1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence (in function notation) is

$$
f(n)=f(1)+(n-1)d.
$$

We are told that the first term is $f(1)=-5$ and the common difference is $d=-1.$ So, we substitute into the formula and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n) & =f(1)+(n-1)d \\  & =-5+(n-1)(-1) \\  & =-5-n+1 \\  & =-4-n\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the formula for the $n$th term is $f(n)=-4-n.$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Find the $25$th term of the following arithmetic sequence. 

$$
4,\,8,\,12,\,16,\,…
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d.
$$

First, we will write the formula for the $n$th term of this sequence. From the first few terms

$$
4,\,8,\,12,\,16,\,…,
$$

we see that the first term is ${a}_{1}=4$ and the common difference is 

$$
d=8-4=4.
$$

So, we substitute into the formula and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =4+(n-1)(4) \\  & =4+4n-4 \\  & =4n\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use our formula to find the $25$th term. All we have to do is substitute $n=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =4n \\ {a}_{25} & =4(25) \\  & =100\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $25$th term of the sequence is ${a}_{25}=100.$

Question 1
?

Find the formula for the nth term of an arithmetic sequence if the first term is −1 and the second term is −3.

a
f(n)=−1+2n
b
f(n)=−1−2n
c
f(n)=1−2n
d
f(n)=2n
e
f(n)=1+2n
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The formula for the nth term of an arithmetic sequence (in function notation) is

f(n)=f(1)+(n−1)d.

We are given the first term f(1)=−1. Also, the common difference of the sequence can be found as d=−3−(−1)=−2.

So, we substitute into the formula and simplify:

f(n)=f(1)+(n−1)d=−1+(n−1)(−2)=−1−2n+2=1−2n

Therefore, the formula for the nth term is f(n)=1−2n.

Question 2
?

Find the formula for the nth term of an arithmetic sequence if the first term is −5 and the common difference is −1.

a
f(n)=−4+n
b
f(n)=−4−n
c
f(n)=−5+n
d
f(n)=−1−5n
e
f(n)=−5−n
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The formula for the nth term of an arithmetic sequence (in function notation) is

f(n)=f(1)+(n−1)d.

We are told that the first term is f(1)=−5 and the common difference is d=−1. So, we substitute into the formula and simplify:

f(n)=f(1)+(n−1)d=−5+(n−1)(−1)=−5−n+1=−4−n

Therefore, the formula for the nth term is f(n)=−4−n.

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d.
$$

First, we will write the formula for the $n$th term of this sequence. From the first few terms

$$
4,\,8,\,12,\,16,\,…,
$$

we see that the first term is ${a}_{1}=4$ and the common difference is 

$$
d=8-4=4.
$$

So, we substitute into the formula and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =4+(n-1)(4) \\  & =4+4n-4 \\  & =4n\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use our formula to find the $25$th term. All we have to do is substitute $n=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =4n \\ {a}_{25} & =4(25) \\  & =100\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $25$th term of the sequence is ${a}_{25}=100.$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Find the formula for the nth term of an arithmetic sequence if the first term is −1 and the second term is −3.

a
f(n)=−1+2n
b
f(n)=−1−2n
c
f(n)=1−2n
d
f(n)=2n
e
f(n)=1+2n
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The formula for the nth term of an arithmetic sequence (in function notation) is

f(n)=f(1)+(n−1)d.

We are given the first term f(1)=−1. Also, the common difference of the sequence can be found as d=−3−(−1)=−2.

So, we substitute into the formula and simplify:

f(n)=f(1)+(n−1)d=−1+(n−1)(−2)=−1−2n+2=1−2n

Therefore, the formula for the nth term is f(n)=1−2n.

Question 1
?

Find the formula for the nth term of an arithmetic sequence if the first term is −1 and the second term is −3.

a
f(n)=−1+2n
b
f(n)=−1−2n
c
f(n)=1−2n
d
f(n)=2n
e
f(n)=1+2n
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The formula for the nth term of an arithmetic sequence (in function notation) is

f(n)=f(1)+(n−1)d.

We are given the first term f(1)=−1. Also, the common difference of the sequence can be found as d=−3−(−1)=−2.

So, we substitute into the formula and simplify:

f(n)=f(1)+(n−1)d=−1+(n−1)(−2)=−1−2n+2=1−2n

Therefore, the formula for the nth term is f(n)=1−2n.

Question 2
?

Find the formula for the nth term of an arithmetic sequence if the first term is −5 and the common difference is −1.

a
f(n)=−4+n
b
f(n)=−4−n
c
f(n)=−5+n
d
f(n)=−1−5n
e
f(n)=−5−n
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The formula for the nth term of an arithmetic sequence (in function notation) is

f(n)=f(1)+(n−1)d.

We are told that the first term is f(1)=−5 and the common difference is d=−1. So, we substitute into the formula and simplify:

f(n)=f(1)+(n−1)d=−5+(n−1)(−1)=−5−n+1=−4−n

Therefore, the formula for the nth term is f(n)=−4−n.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Find the $25$th term of the following arithmetic sequence. 

$$
4,\,8,\,12,\,16,\,…
$$
question.worked_solution:
The formula for the $n$th term of an arithmetic sequence is

$$
{a}_{n}={a}_{1}+(n-1)d.
$$

First, we will write the formula for the $n$th term of this sequence. From the first few terms

$$
4,\,8,\,12,\,16,\,…,
$$

we see that the first term is ${a}_{1}=4$ and the common difference is 

$$
d=8-4=4.
$$

So, we substitute into the formula and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =4+(n-1)(4) \\  & =4+4n-4 \\  & =4n\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use our formula to find the $25$th term. All we have to do is substitute $n=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =4n \\ {a}_{25} & =4(25) \\  & =100\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $25$th term of the sequence is ${a}_{25}=100.$

feedback.html:
Question 3
?

Find the 25th term of the following arithmetic sequence. 4,8,12,16,…

a
104
b
100
c
96
d
98
e
92
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The formula for the nth term of an arithmetic sequence is

an=a1+(n−1)d.

First, we will write the formula for the nth term of this sequence. From the first few terms

4,8,12,16,…,

we see that the first term is a1=4 and the common difference is

d=8−4=4.

So, we substitute into the formula and simplify:

an=a1+(n−1)d=4+(n−1)(4)=4+4n−4=4n

Now, we can use our formula to find the 25th term. All we have to do is substitute n=25:

an=4na25=4(25)=100

Therefore, the 25th term of the sequence is a25=100.

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222477/assets/8934e5b6135b97b845dad9a6b87056d2c228fd2424d3a72141df694d46ccf7c0.png)

Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the parabola shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(0,0),$ and passes through the point $(-6,12).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola  that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x=2pt,\,y=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Since the parabola passes through $(-6,12),$ we can substitute $x=-6$ and $y=12$ into the standard parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-6=2pt \\ 12=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 & =2pt \\ -3 & =pt \\ t & =-\frac{3}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =p{(-\frac{3}{p})}^{2} \\ 12 & =p\cdot \frac{9}{{p}^{2}} \\ 12 & =\frac{9}{p} \\ p & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x=2(\frac{3}{4})t,\,y=(\frac{3}{4}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x=\frac{3}{2}t,\,y=\frac{3}{4}{t}^{2}.
$$

\{\begin{aligned}6=2pt \\ 3=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222477/assets/23fa9b0f268e953cf9a2b770c3a3cb83c64fa0217a55e3a5313c81bf6933fc0a.png)

Determine a set of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ that generate the above parabola. Express your answer in the form $x=2pt,y=p{t}^{2},$ where $p$ is a constant.

$x=$
{{field-1}},
$\,y=$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(0,0),$ and passes through the point $(1,2).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola  that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x=2pt,\,y=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Since the parabola passes through $(1,2),$ we can substitute $x=1$ and $y=2$ into the standard parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}1=2pt \\ 2=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =2pt \\ \frac{1}{2} & =pt \\ t & =\frac{1}{2p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =p{(\frac{1}{2p})}^{2} \\ 2 & =p\cdot \frac{1}{4{p}^{2}} \\ 2 & =\frac{1}{4p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x=2(\frac{1}{8})t,\,y=(\frac{1}{8}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x=\frac{1}{4}t,\,y=\frac{1}{8}{t}^{2}.
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Determine a set of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ that generate a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ and which passes through the point $(-8,8).$ Express your answer in the form $x=2pt,y=p{t}^{2},$ where $p$ is a constant.

$x=$
{{field-1}},
$\,y=$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical parabola  that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x=2pt,\,y=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Since the parabola passes through $(-8,8),$ we can substitute $x=-8$ and $y=8$ into the standard parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-8=2pt \\ 8=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{4}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8 & =p{(-\frac{4}{p})}^{2} \\ 8 & =p\cdot \frac{16}{{p}^{2}} \\ 8 & =\frac{16}{p} \\ p & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x=2(2)t,\,y=(2){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x=4t,\,y=2{t}^{2}.
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ generate the horizontal parabola given by the Cartesian equation ${y}^{2}=-10x?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola ${y}^{2}=4px$ that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x=p{t}^{2},\,y=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Comparing the given Cartesian equation with the general case ${y}^{2}=4px$ and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4px & =-10x \\ 4p & =-10 \\ p & =-\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x=(-\frac{5}{2}){t}^{2},\,y=2(-\frac{5}{2})t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x=-\frac{5}{2}{t}^{2},\,y=-5t.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222477/assets/d8e4aa88acf2a0d69d4c4208dc4951a33cc92e59e177395ec74be3ae0f9a8c7f.png)

Determine a set of parametric equations, defined for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),$ that generate the parabola shown above. Express your answer in the form $x=p{t}^{2},y=2pt,$ where $p$ is a constant.

$x=$
{{field-1}},
$\,y=$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola is horizontal, has its vertex at $(0,0),$ and passes through the point $(-5,-4).$

The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ are

$$
x=p{t}^{2},\,y=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

Since the parabola passes through $(-5,-4),$ we can substitute $x=-5$ and $y=-4$ into the standard parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-5=p{t}^{2} \\ -4=2pt.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the second equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-4 & =2pt \\ t & =-\frac{2}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the first equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-5 & =p{(-\frac{2}{p})}^{2} \\ -5 & =p\cdot \frac{4}{{p}^{2}} \\ p & =-\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x=(-\frac{4}{5}){t}^{2},\,y=2(-\frac{4}{5})t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x=-\frac{4}{5}{t}^{2},\,y=-\frac{8}{5}t.
$$

$$
x=-2{t}^{2},\,y=-4t.

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem:
Consider the following parabola:

$$
x=15{t}^{2},\,y=3t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

The Cartesian equation of the parabola is

${y}^{2}=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =\frac{x}{15},\,t=\frac{y}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=\frac{x}{15}$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & =\frac{x}{15} \\ {y}^{2} & =\frac{3}{5}x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian equation of the parabola is ${y}^{2}=\frac{3}{5}x.$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the parabola defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2},\,y=-t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =-2x,\,t=-y.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & ={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=-2x$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =-2x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian equation of the parabola is ${y}^{2}=-2x.$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the parabola defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2},\,y=\frac{1}{2}t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =4x,\,t=2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =4{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=4x$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{y}^{2} & =4x \\ {y}^{2} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian equation of the parabola is ${y}^{2}=x.$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the parabola defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2},\,y=-\frac{1}{6}t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make $t$ the subject of the parametric equations. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =-4x,\,t=-6y.\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =36{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now eliminate the parameter $t$ by substituting the above into the equation ${t}^{2}=-4x$ and rearranging to find the Cartesian equation of the parabola, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}36{y}^{2} & =-4x \\ {y}^{2} & =-\frac{1}{9}x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian equation of the parabola is ${y}^{2}=-\frac{1}{9}x.$

\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{2}}{36} & =\frac{x}{3} \\ {y}^{2} & =12x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian equation of the parabola is ${y}^{2}=12x.$
