{{field-1}}
feedback.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by  
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line
{{field-2}}
by integrating both sides from $0$ to 
{{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by  
{{field-4}}.
question.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-At}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Integrating ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$ from $0$ to $t$ in $\text{L3}$ yields

$$
y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

So, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by integrating both sides from $0$ to $t.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L5}.$ Evaluating $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ at $t=0$ gives

$$
y(0)={e}^{-A\cdot 0}x(0)=Ix(0)=x(0).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{evaluating at }t=0.$

Question 3
?
Consider the inhomogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(0) is presented below.

L1: Let y(t)=e−Atx(t)

L2: y′(t)=−Ae−Atx(t)+e−Atx′(t)

L3: y′(t)=e−Atg(t)

L4: y(t)−y(0)=∫0te−Asg(s)ds

L5: y(0)=x(0)

L6: y(t)=x(0)+∫0te−Asg(s)ds

L7: eAty(t)=eAtx(0)+∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

L8: eAty(t)=x(t)

L9: x(t)=eAtx(0)+∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

EXPLANATION

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines L2 and L3. Starting from y′(t)=−Ae−Atx(t)+e−Atx′(t) in L2 and substituting x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t) from the original system gives
    y′(t)=−Ae−Atx(t)+e−At(Ax(t)+g(t))=−Ae−Atx(t)+Ae−Atx(t)+e−Atg(t)=e−Atg(t). Thus, L3 follows from L2 by substituting x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).

  • Next, we consider lines L3 and L4. Integrating y′(t)=e−Atg(t) from 0 to t in L3 yields
    y(t)−y(0)=∫0te−Asg(s)ds.
    So, L4 follows from L3 by integrating both sides from 0 to t.

  • Finally, we consider lines L1 and L5. Evaluating y(t)=e−Atx(t) at t=0 gives
    y(0)=e−A⋅0x(0)=Ix(0)=x(0). Therefore, L5 follows from L1 by evaluating at t=0.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-At}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Integrating ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$ from $0$ to $t$ in $\text{L3}$ yields

$$
y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

So, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by integrating both sides from $0$ to $t.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L5}.$ Evaluating $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ at $t=0$ gives

$$
y(0)={e}^{-A\cdot 0}x(0)=Ix(0)=x(0).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{evaluating at }t=0.$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-At}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Integrating ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$ from $0$ to $t$ in $\text{L3}$ yields

$$
y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

So, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by integrating both sides from $0$ to $t.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L5}.$ Evaluating $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ at $t=0$ gives

$$
y(0)={e}^{-A\cdot 0}x(0)=Ix(0)=x(0).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{evaluating at }t=0.$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by  
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by  
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by  
{{field-3}}.
question.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Differentiating $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ and applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-At})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-A){e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{differentiating and using the product rule}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L5}.$ Evaluating $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ at $t=0$ gives

$$
y(0)={e}^{-A\cdot 0}x(0)=Ix(0)=x(0).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{evaluating at }t=0.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,ds
$$

from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{e}^{At}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{At}.$

last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Differentiating $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ and applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-At})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-A){e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{differentiating and using the product rule}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L5}.$ Evaluating $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ at $t=0$ gives

$$
y(0)={e}^{-A\cdot 0}x(0)=Ix(0)=x(0).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{evaluating at }t=0.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,ds
$$

from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{e}^{At}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{At}.$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by  
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by  
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by  
{{field-3}}.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L5}.$ Evaluating $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ at $t=0$ gives

$$
y(0)={e}^{-A\cdot 0}x(0)=Ix(0)=x(0).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{evaluating at }t=0.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,ds
$$

from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{e}^{At}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}

  • We first consider lines L1 and L2. Differentiating y(t)=e−Atx(t) and applying the product rule gives
    y′(t)=(e−At)′x(t)+e−Atx′(t)=(−A)e−Atx(t)+e−Atx′(t)=−Ae−Atx(t)+e−Atx′(t). Thus, L2 follows from L1 by differentiating and using the product rule.

  • Next, we consider lines L1 and L5. Evaluating y(t)=e−Atx(t) at t=0 gives
    y(0)=e−A⋅0x(0)=Ix(0)=x(0). Therefore, L5 follows from L1 by evaluating at t=0.

    eAty(t)=eAtx(0)+eAt∫0te−Asg(s)ds=eAtx(0)+∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds. Therefore, L7 follows from L6 by multiplying both sides by eAt.

Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

feedback.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Differentiating $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ and applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-At})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-A){e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{differentiating and using the product rule}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L5}.$ Evaluating $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ at $t=0$ gives

$$
y(0)={e}^{-A\cdot 0}x(0)=Ix(0)=x(0).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{evaluating at }t=0.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,ds
$$

from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{e}^{At}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{At}.$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by  
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line
{{field-2}}
by substituting 
{{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L9}$ follows from line $\text{L7}$ by  
{{field-4}}.
question.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Differentiating $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ and applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-At})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-A){e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{differentiating and using the product rule}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$, $\text{L5}$, and $\text{L6}.$ From $\text{L4}$ we have

$$
y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Using $y(0)=x(0)$ from $\text{L5}$, this becomes

$$
y(t)-x(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s,
$$

so

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substituting $y(0)=x(0).$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$, $\text{L8}$, and $\text{L9}.$ From $\text{L8}$ we know that

$$
{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).
$$

Substituting ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$ into

$$
{e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s
$$

from $\text{L7}$ gives

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Therefore, $\text{L9}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by $\text{substituting }{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).$

question.html:
Question 5
?
Consider the inhomogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(0) is presented below.

L1: Let y(t)=e−Atx(t)

L2: y′(t)=−Ae−Atx(t)+e−Atx′(t)

L3: y′(t)=e−Atg(t)

L4: y(t)−y(0)=∫0te−Asg(s)ds

L5: y(0)=x(0)

L6: y(t)=x(0)+∫0te−Asg(s)ds

L7: eAty(t)=eAtx(0)+∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

L8: eAty(t)=x(t)

L9: x(t)=eAtx(0)+∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

Line L2 follows from L1 by
differentiating and using the product rule
differentiating and using the product rule
evaluating at t=0
applying a change of variables
substituting x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)
.

Line L6 follows from line
L4
L4
L1
L3
by substituting
y(0)=x(0)
y(0)=x(0)
x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)
eAty(t)=x(t)
y(t)=e−Atx(t)
.

Line L9 follows from line L7 by
substituting eAty(t)=x(t)
multiplying both sides by eAt
applying a change of variables
evaluating at t=0
substituting eAty(t)=x(t)
.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines L1 and L2. Differentiating y(t)=e−Atx(t) and applying the product rule gives
    y′(t)=(e−At)′x(t)+e−Atx′(t)=(−A)e−Atx(t)+e−Atx′(t)=−Ae−Atx(t)+e−Atx′(t). Thus, L2 follows from L1 by differentiating and using the product rule.

  • Next, we consider lines L4, L5, and L6. From L4 we have y(t)−y(0)=∫0te−Asg(s)ds. Using y(0)=x(0) from L5, this becomes
    y(t)−x(0)=∫0te−Asg(s)ds, so y(t)=x(0)+∫0te−Asg(s)ds. Thus, L6 follows from L4 by substituting y(0)=x(0).

  • Finally, we consider lines L7, L8, and L9. From L8 we know that eAty(t)=x(t). Substituting eAty(t)=x(t) into eAty(t)=eAtx(0)+∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds from L7 gives
    x(t)=eAtx(0)+∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds. Therefore, L9 follows from L7 by substituting eAty(t)=x(t).

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Differentiating $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ and applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-At})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-A){e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{differentiating and using the product rule}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$, $\text{L5}$, and $\text{L6}.$ From $\text{L4}$ we have

$$
y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Using $y(0)=x(0)$ from $\text{L5}$, this becomes

$$
y(t)-x(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s,
$$

so

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substituting $y(0)=x(0).$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$, $\text{L8}$, and $\text{L9}.$ From $\text{L8}$ we know that

$$
{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).
$$

Substituting ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$ into

$$
{e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s
$$

from $\text{L7}$ gives

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Therefore, $\text{L9}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by $\text{substituting }{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$, $\text{L8}$, and $\text{L9}.$ From $\text{L8}$ we know that

$$
{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).
$$

Substituting ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$ into

$$
{e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s
$$

from $\text{L7}$ gives

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Therefore, $\text{L9}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by $\text{substituting }{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).$

Consider the inhomogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(0) is presented below.

L1: Let y(t)=e−Atx(t)

L2: y′(t)=−Ae−Atx(t)+e−Atx′(t)

L3: y′(t)=e−Atg(t)

L4: y(t)−y(0)=∫0te−Asg(s)ds

L5: y(0)=x(0)

L6: y(t)=x(0)+∫0te−Asg(s)ds

L7: eAty(t)=eAtx(0)+∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

L8: eAty(t)=x(t)

L9: x(t)=eAtx(0)+∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

EXPLANATION

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines L1 and L2. Differentiating y(t)=e−Atx(t) and applying the product rule gives
    y′(t)=(e−At)′x(t)+e−Atx′(t)=(−A)e−Atx(t)+e−Atx′(t)=−Ae−Atx(t)+e−Atx′(t). Thus, L2 follows from L1 by differentiating and using the product rule.

  • Next, we consider lines L4, L5, and L6. From L4 we have y(t)−y(0)=∫0te−Asg(s)ds. Using y(0)=x(0) from L5, this becomes
    y(t)−x(0)=∫0te−Asg(s)ds, so y(t)=x(0)+∫0te−Asg(s)ds. Thus, L6 follows from L4 by substituting y(0)=x(0).

  • Finally, we consider lines L7, L8, and L9. From L8 we know that eAty(t)=x(t). Substituting eAty(t)=x(t) into eAty(t)=eAtx(0)+∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds from L7 gives
    x(t)=eAtx(0)+∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds. Therefore, L9 follows from L7 by substituting eAty(t)=x(t).

feedback.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Differentiating $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ and applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-At})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-A){e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{differentiating and using the product rule}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$, $\text{L5}$, and $\text{L6}.$ From $\text{L4}$ we have

$$
y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Using $y(0)=x(0)$ from $\text{L5}$, this becomes

$$
y(t)-x(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s,
$$

so

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substituting $y(0)=x(0).$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$, $\text{L8}$, and $\text{L9}.$ From $\text{L8}$ we know that

$$
{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).
$$

Substituting ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$ into

$$
{e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s
$$

from $\text{L7}$ gives

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Therefore, $\text{L9}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by $\text{substituting }{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).$

5.Proving the Matrix Exponential Formula for IVP Solution of an Inhomogeneous System?

Consider the inhomogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(0) is presented below.

L1: Let y(t)=e−Atx(t)

L2: y′(t)=−Ae−Atx(t)+e−Atx′(t)

L3: y′(t)=e−Atg(t)

L4: y(t)−y(0)=∫0te−Asg(s)ds

L5: y(0)=x(0)

L6: y(t)=x(0)+∫0te−Asg(s)ds

L7: eAty(t)=eAtx(0)+∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

L8: eAty(t)=x(t)

L9: x(t)=eAtx(0)+∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

Which of the following is the image of the point $(8,-4)$ under the action of a dilation with center $O$ and scale factor $\frac{1}{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
A dilation with center at the origin and a scale factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ can be represented by the function  

$$
(x,y)↦(\frac{1}{2}x,\frac{1}{2}y).
$$

Applying this function to the point $(8,-4),$ we have

$$
(8,-4)↦(\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8,\,\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-4))=(4,-2).
$$

Therefore, the resulting point is $(4,-2).$

questions.worked_solution:
The dilation with center at the origin and a scale factor of $-\frac{2}{3}$ can be represented by the function

$$
(x,y)↦(-\frac{2}{3}x,-\frac{2}{3}y).
$$

Applying this function to the vertices $(-3,-3),$ $(0,0),$  and $(-3,3),$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3,-3) & ↦(-\frac{2}{3}\cdot (-3),\,-\frac{2}{3}\cdot (-3))=(2,2) \\ (0,0) & ↦(-\frac{2}{3}\cdot 0,\,-\frac{2}{3}\cdot 0)=(0,0) \\ (-3,3) & ↦(-\frac{2}{3}\cdot (-3),\,-\frac{2}{3}\cdot 3)=(2,-2)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
A dilation with center at the origin and a scale factor of $\frac{1}{3}$ can be represented by the function

Applying this function to the endpoints $A(-6,-3)$ and $B(3,6),$ we have the following:

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/14ca2d4167ff6950d5a9d7bb41cc856ecbc211a033518b8b366ac977953700b1.png)

The point ${P}^{′}(3,1.5)$ is the image of the point $P(-4,-2)$ under a dilation with the center at the origin, as shown above. What is the scale factor of the transformation?
questions.worked_solution:
A dilation with center at the origin and a factor of $k$ can be represented by the function

$$
(x,y)↦(kx,ky)\,.
$$

Applying this function to the point $P$ and equating the result to ${P}^{′},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(k\cdot (-4),k\cdot (-2)=(3,1.5)\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}-4k=3 \\ -2k=1.5.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=\frac{3}{-4}=\frac{1.5}{-2}=-\frac{3}{4}.$   

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/d3b818151bcfddd3fd4f642463ba4e06ba1844d4b772652dadde0d3049e441ee.png)

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/bfcd52f31f825e6445700e8495f7acbfce46139144f8bb61e977b2971e01d877.png)

The larger polygon shown above is the image of the smaller one under the action of a dilation. Find the center of the dilation and its scale factor $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
The center of a dilation lies on any line which passes through a point and its image.

Therefore, we can find the center of our dilation as, for example, the point of intersection of the lines $\overset{⟷}{B{B}^{′}}$ and $\overset{⟷}{C{C}^{′}},$ as shown below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/d7215165822a95ce9689e3666ff6ea9454048a936c372b07a6224d199b8d0ed7.png)

From the diagram above, where we have that 

$$
\frac{{B}^{′}{C}^{′}}{BC}=\frac{6}{2}=3,
$$

and the same proportion holds for the other corresponding sides too. As a result, the absolute value of the scale factor is 

$$
|k|=3.
$$

 

Finally, notice that our figures have different orientations, which means that the scale factor of the dilation is negative.

Therefore, the scale factor is $k=-3.$

Example: 
                    Dilating Points in the Coordinate Plane
canonical_examples.problem: Find the image of the point $(-5,2)$ under the action of a dilation with center $O$ and scale factor $-3?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A dilation with center at the origin and a scale factor of $-3$ can be represented by the function

$$
(x,y) \mapsto (-3x,-3y).
$$

Applying this function to the point $(-5,2),$ we have

$$
(-5,2) \mapsto \big((-3) \cdot (-5), \: (-3) \cdot 2 \big) = (15,-6).
$$

Therefore, the resulting point is $(15,-6).$

The point $P'(-2,-4)$ is the image of the point $P(1,2)$ under a dilation with the center at the origin, as shown above. What is the scale factor of the transformation?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A dilation with center at the origin and a factor of $k$ can be represented by the function 

$$
(x,y) \mapsto (kx,ky)\,.
$$

Applying this function to the point $P$ and equating the result to $P',$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(k\cdot 1,k\cdot 2)=(-2,-4)\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}k=-2 \\ 2k=-4.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=\dfrac{(-4)}{2}=-2.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
In the coordinate plane, dilations are typically centered at the origin. When a dilation is centered at the origin, it can be represented by a function

$$
(x,y) \mapsto (kx, ky)
$$

where $k$ is the scale factor of the dilation.

For example, let's compute the image of the point $(3,2)$ (shown below) under the action of a dilation with center $O$ and scale factor $3.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/2da731925da5705e15cb58abd632e52c04139e8052772eeaa3ca2862fd6d3d02.png)

A dilation with center at the origin and a scale factor of $3$ can be represented by the function

$$
(x,y) \mapsto \left(3x,3y\right).
$$

Applying this function to the point $(3,2),$ we have

$$
(3,2) \mapsto \left(3\cdot 3, \:3 \cdot 2 \right) = (9,6).
$$

Therefore, the resulting point is $(9,6).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/9410030b5b309d512c937741e9fdb85abad0aacdd712f81ee0b50897523952cc.png)

tutorials.name: Finding a Center of Dilation
tutorials.problem:
Let's discuss how to find a center of a dilation

The center of a dilation lies on any line that passes through corresponding points on a figure and its image. Therefore, we can find a center of dilation as the intersection of any two of these lines. 

Let's look at some examples:

- Consider the rectangle $ABCD$ and its image $A'B'C'D'$ under the action of a dilation, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/9115c6a43d20f58e8c2e4b9a77337edd18688dd831168405062c6e0fbe207bb0.png)

We can find the center of dilation $O$ by connecting two corresponding points with a straight line and finding their intersection. 

For example, if we draw the lines $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AA'}$ and $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{BB'}$ and find their intersection, we get the center of dilation $O$ shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/4a3b1ac04e7d549aafdcf50ea55e172f385fbb7a71bd061c74581ca50f94535a.png)

- Sometimes, a figure and its image lie on opposite sides of the center of dilation. 

For example, consider the rectangle $ABCD$ and its image $A'B'C'D'$ shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/a8918779d1b5152e7071bdb7ba7d349978b166ff613ec2c8b918f9c2ea5b0b92.png)

If we draw the lines $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AA'}$ and $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{BB'},$ we find that the center of dilation $O$ lies between the two shapes.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/14c6bc0bd148d2ac61c42d4e1636c4301a7af77e773338358e51e4a297f40a48.png)

tutorials.name: The Image of a Line Under a Dilation
tutorials.problem:
If $l$ is a line passing through the center of dilation, then the image $l'$ under the dilation is the same as the original line. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/eb208ea1b492a1d471e0ffb6b3f23fa80a4747f3b5f6da1ad126c30716e52743.png)

If $l$ is a line passing through the center of dilation, then the image $l'$ under the dilation is the same as the original line. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/eb208ea1b492a1d471e0ffb6b3f23fa80a4747f3b5f6da1ad126c30716e52743.png)

However, if $k$ is a line that does not pass through the center of dilation, then the image $k'$ is parallel to the original line.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/09a11211bde36f85dfe48e4a769314d084edc99c523b869ed3f9a518784fb9a6.png)

tutorial.name: Introduction
tutorial.problem:
In the coordinate plane, dilations are typically centered at the origin. When a dilation is centered at the origin, it can be represented by a function

$$
(x,y) \mapsto (kx, ky)
$$

where $k$ is the scale factor of the dilation.

For example, let's compute the image of the point $(3,2)$ (shown below) under the action of a dilation with center $O$ and scale factor $3.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/2da731925da5705e15cb58abd632e52c04139e8052772eeaa3ca2862fd6d3d02.png)

A dilation with center at the origin and a scale factor of $3$ can be represented by the function

$$
(x,y) \mapsto \left(3x,3y\right).
$$

Applying this function to the point $(3,2),$ we have

$$
(3,2) \mapsto \left(3\cdot 3, \:3 \cdot 2 \right) = (9,6).
$$

Therefore, the resulting point is $(9,6).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/9410030b5b309d512c937741e9fdb85abad0aacdd712f81ee0b50897523952cc.png)

tutorial.name: Finding a Center of Dilation
tutorial.problem:
Let's discuss how to find a center of a dilation

The center of a dilation lies on any line that passes through corresponding points on a figure and its image. Therefore, we can find a center of dilation as the intersection of any two of these lines. 

Let's look at some examples:

- Consider the rectangle $ABCD$ and its image $A'B'C'D'$ under the action of a dilation, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/9115c6a43d20f58e8c2e4b9a77337edd18688dd831168405062c6e0fbe207bb0.png)

We can find the center of dilation $O$ by connecting two corresponding points with a straight line and finding their intersection. 

For example, if we draw the lines $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AA'}$ and $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{BB'}$ and find their intersection, we get the center of dilation $O$ shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/4a3b1ac04e7d549aafdcf50ea55e172f385fbb7a71bd061c74581ca50f94535a.png)

- Sometimes, a figure and its image lie on opposite sides of the center of dilation. 

For example, consider the rectangle $ABCD$ and its image $A'B'C'D'$ shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/a8918779d1b5152e7071bdb7ba7d349978b166ff613ec2c8b918f9c2ea5b0b92.png)

If we draw the lines $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AA'}$ and $\overset{\longleftrightarrow}{BB'},$ we find that the center of dilation $O$ lies between the two shapes.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/14c6bc0bd148d2ac61c42d4e1636c4301a7af77e773338358e51e4a297f40a48.png)

A dilation with center at the origin and a factor of $k$ can be represented by the function 

$$
(x,y) \mapsto (kx,ky)\,.
$$

Applying this function to the point $P$ and equating the result to $P',$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(k\cdot 1,k\cdot 2)=(-2,-4)\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}k=-2 \\ 2k=-4.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=\dfrac{(-4)}{2}=-2.$

A dilation with center at the origin and a factor of $k$ can be represented by the function 

$$
(x,y) \mapsto (kx,ky)\,.
$$

Applying this function to the point $P$ and equating the result to $P',$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(k\cdot 1,k\cdot 2)=(-2,-4)\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}k=-2 \\ 2k=-4.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=\dfrac{(-4)}{2}=-2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/219980e6dee08094db21c153f37b107d6fd85709aa50cf8c546a5ba050aac567.png)

observed_steps.worked_solution:
A dilation with center at the origin and a factor of $k$ can be represented by the function

$$
(x,y)↦(kx,ky)\,.
$$

Applying this function to the point $P$ and equating the result to ${P}^{′},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(k\cdot (-4),k\cdot (-2)=(3,1.5)\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}-4k=3 \\ -2k=1.5.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=\frac{3}{-4}=\frac{1.5}{-2}=-\frac{3}{4}.$

The point ${P}^{′}(3,1.5)$ is the image of the point $P(-4,-2)$ under a dilation with the center at the origin, as shown above. What is the scale factor of the transformation?
question.worked_solution:
A dilation with center at the origin and a factor of $k$ can be represented by the function

$$
(x,y)↦(kx,ky)\,.
$$

Applying this function to the point $P$ and equating the result to ${P}^{′},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(k\cdot (-4),k\cdot (-2)=(3,1.5)\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}-4k=3 \\ -2k=1.5.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=\frac{3}{-4}=\frac{1.5}{-2}=-\frac{3}{4}.$   

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/d3b818151bcfddd3fd4f642463ba4e06ba1844d4b772652dadde0d3049e441ee.png)

Question 5
?

The point P′(3,1.5) is the image of the point P(−4,−2) under a dilation with the center at the origin, as shown above. What is the scale factor of the transformation?

a
−12
b
14
c
−23
d
23
e
−34
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A dilation with center at the origin and a factor of k can be represented by the function

(x,y)↦(kx,ky).

Applying this function to the point P and equating the result to P′, we get

(k⋅(−4),k⋅(−2)=(3,1.5)⟹{−4k=3−2k=1.5.

Therefore, k=3−4=1.5−2=−34.

observed_steps.name: Question 6
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Scale Factor of a Dilation in the Coordinate Plane
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The center of a dilation lies on any line which passes through a point and its image.

Therefore, we can find the center of our dilation as, for example, the point of intersection of the lines $\overset{⟷}{B{B}^{′}}$ and $\overset{⟷}{C{C}^{′}},$ as shown below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/d7215165822a95ce9689e3666ff6ea9454048a936c372b07a6224d199b8d0ed7.png)

From the diagram above, where we have that 

$$
\frac{{B}^{′}{C}^{′}}{BC}=\frac{6}{2}=3,
$$

and the same proportion holds for the other corresponding sides too. As a result, the absolute value of the scale factor is 

$$
|k|=3.
$$

 

Finally, notice that our figures have different orientations, which means that the scale factor of the dilation is negative.

Therefore, the scale factor is $k=-3.$

observed_steps.name: Example: The Image of a Line Under a Dilation
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Scale Factor of a Dilation in the Coordinate Plane
observed_steps.worked_solution:
A dilation maps a line $l$ not passing through the center of the dilation onto a parallel line $l'.$ 

To find the image of the line, we proceed as follows: 

- Take a point $B \in l.$

- Find the image $B'$ of $B$ under the dilation.

- Find $l'$ as the line that passes through $B'$ and is parallel to $l.$

Notice that $B(-3,0)$ lies on $l,$ as shown below. The image of this point under the dilation is

$$
\begin{aligned}(\frac{5}{3}\cdot (-3),\frac{5}{3}\cdot 0) & =(-5,0).\end{aligned}

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/b8730b1936d1ff9f0c8d3845a70327e351b23c7085f248bcb6e99e73f0cb8c9e.png)

Which of the following is the image of the point $(8,-4)$ under the action of a dilation with center $O$ and scale factor $\frac{1}{2}?$
question.worked_solution:
A dilation with center at the origin and a scale factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ can be represented by the function  

$$
(x,y)↦(\frac{1}{2}x,\frac{1}{2}y).
$$

Applying this function to the point $(8,-4),$ we have

$$
(8,-4)↦(\frac{1}{2}\cdot 8,\,\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-4))=(4,-2).
$$

Therefore, the resulting point is $(4,-2).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/fb4e4de8278d7791351ee6256f80037345eea30151ade4ff3c28ee16407ffb99.png)

(8,−4)↦(12⋅8,12⋅(−4))=(4,−2).

Therefore, the resulting point is (4,−2).

Applying this function to the vertices $(-3,-3),$ $(0,0),$  and $(-3,3),$ we have the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/98e64a245737736bfc987fe9230b1ee3fc81eef4aedfea8c2e5e9bcf949f8203.png)

What is the image of the polygon shown above under a dilation that is centered at the origin and has a scale factor of $-\frac{2}{3}?$
question.worked_solution:
The dilation with center at the origin and a scale factor of $-\frac{2}{3}$ can be represented by the function

$$
(x,y)↦(-\frac{2}{3}x,-\frac{2}{3}y).
$$

Applying this function to the vertices $(-3,-3),$ $(0,0),$  and $(-3,3),$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3,-3) & ↦(-\frac{2}{3}\cdot (-3),\,-\frac{2}{3}\cdot (-3))=(2,2) \\ (0,0) & ↦(-\frac{2}{3}\cdot 0,\,-\frac{2}{3}\cdot 0)=(0,0) \\ (-3,3) & ↦(-\frac{2}{3}\cdot (-3),\,-\frac{2}{3}\cdot 3)=(2,-2)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the following polygon.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/2921272ffd1c38c082bf2123086d8c7b19a910c91d132810042b86728b820f8d.png)

(x,y)↦(−23x,−23y).

Applying this function to the vertices (−3,−3), (0,0), and (−3,3), we have the following:

(−3,−3)↦(−23⋅(−3),−23⋅(−3))=(2,2)(0,0)↦(−23⋅0,−23⋅0)=(0,0)(−3,3)↦(−23⋅(−3),−23⋅3)=(2,−2)

Therefore, we get the following polygon.

What is the image of the segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ under a dilation that is centered at the origin and has a scale factor of $\frac{1}{3}?$
question.worked_solution:
A dilation with center at the origin and a scale factor of $\frac{1}{3}$ can be represented by the function

$$
(x,y)↦(\frac{1}{3}x,\frac{1}{3}y).
$$

Applying this function to the endpoints $A(-6,-3)$ and $B(3,6),$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-6,-3) & ↦(\frac{1}{3}\cdot (-6),\frac{1}{3}\cdot -3)=(-2,-1) \\ (3,6) & ↦(\frac{1}{3}\cdot (3),\frac{1}{3}\cdot 6)=(1,2)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resulting points are ${A}^{′}(-2,-1)$ and ${B}^{′}(1,2).$

Finally, we connect ${A}^{′}$ and ${B}^{′}$ using a segment, as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/ba27f325ca104397544c7b5d19078d59cf63209a83d89de73cdeb752f5c0fc84.png)

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/14ca2d4167ff6950d5a9d7bb41cc856ecbc211a033518b8b366ac977953700b1.png)

The point ${P}^{′}(3,1.5)$ is the image of the point $P(-4,-2)$ under a dilation with the center at the origin, as shown above. What is the scale factor of the transformation?
question.worked_solution:
A dilation with center at the origin and a factor of $k$ can be represented by the function

$$
(x,y)↦(kx,ky)\,.
$$

Applying this function to the point $P$ and equating the result to ${P}^{′},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(k\cdot (-4),k\cdot (-2)=(3,1.5)\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}-4k=3 \\ -2k=1.5.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=\frac{3}{-4}=\frac{1.5}{-2}=-\frac{3}{4}.$   

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/d3b818151bcfddd3fd4f642463ba4e06ba1844d4b772652dadde0d3049e441ee.png)

Question 5
?

The point P′(3,1.5) is the image of the point P(−4,−2) under a dilation with the center at the origin, as shown above. What is the scale factor of the transformation?

a
−12
b
14
c
−23
d
23
e
−34
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A dilation with center at the origin and a factor of k can be represented by the function

(x,y)↦(kx,ky).

Applying this function to the point P and equating the result to P′, we get

(k⋅(−4),k⋅(−2)=(3,1.5)⟹{−4k=3−2k=1.5.

Therefore, k=3−4=1.5−2=−34.

last_observation.worked_solution:
A dilation with center at the origin and a factor of $k$ can be represented by the function

$$
(x,y)↦(kx,ky)\,.
$$

Applying this function to the point $P$ and equating the result to ${P}^{′},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(k\cdot (-4),k\cdot (-2)=(3,1.5)\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}-4k=3 \\ -2k=1.5.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=\frac{3}{-4}=\frac{1.5}{-2}=-\frac{3}{4}.$

Question 5
?

The point P′(3,1.5) is the image of the point P(−4,−2) under a dilation with the center at the origin, as shown above. What is the scale factor of the transformation?

a
−12
b
14
c
−23
d
23
e
−34
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A dilation with center at the origin and a factor of k can be represented by the function

(x,y)↦(kx,ky).

Applying this function to the point P and equating the result to P′, we get

(k⋅(−4),k⋅(−2)=(3,1.5)⟹{−4k=3−2k=1.5.

Therefore, k=3−4=1.5−2=−34.

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/bfcd52f31f825e6445700e8495f7acbfce46139144f8bb61e977b2971e01d877.png)

The larger polygon shown above is the image of the smaller one under the action of a dilation. Find the center of the dilation and its scale factor $k.$
question.worked_solution:
The center of a dilation lies on any line which passes through a point and its image.

Therefore, we can find the center of our dilation as, for example, the point of intersection of the lines $\overset{⟷}{B{B}^{′}}$ and $\overset{⟷}{C{C}^{′}},$ as shown below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/d7215165822a95ce9689e3666ff6ea9454048a936c372b07a6224d199b8d0ed7.png)

From the diagram above, where we have that 

$$
\frac{{B}^{′}{C}^{′}}{BC}=\frac{6}{2}=3,
$$

and the same proportion holds for the other corresponding sides too. As a result, the absolute value of the scale factor is 

$$
|k|=3.
$$

 

Finally, notice that our figures have different orientations, which means that the scale factor of the dilation is negative.

Therefore, the scale factor is $k=-3.$

question.html:
Question 6
?

The larger polygon shown above is the image of the smaller one under the action of a dilation. Find the center of the dilation and its scale factor k.

a
(0,0),k=23
b
(−1,0),k=−13
c
(0,1),k=−2
d
(−1,2),k=−2
e
(0,2),k=−3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The center of a dilation lies on any line which passes through a point and its image.

Therefore, we can find the center of our dilation as, for example, the point of intersection of the lines BB′⟷ and CC′⟷, as shown below.

From the diagram above, where we have that B′C′BC=62=3, and the same proportion holds for the other corresponding sides too. As a result, the absolute value of the scale factor is |k|=3.

Finally, notice that our figures have different orientations, which means that the scale factor of the dilation is negative.

Therefore, the scale factor is k=−3.

The center of a dilation lies on any line which passes through a point and its image.

Therefore, we can find the center of our dilation as, for example, the point of intersection of the lines $\overset{⟷}{B{B}^{′}}$ and $\overset{⟷}{C{C}^{′}},$ as shown below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221848/assets/d7215165822a95ce9689e3666ff6ea9454048a936c372b07a6224d199b8d0ed7.png)

From the diagram above, where we have that 

$$
\frac{{B}^{′}{C}^{′}}{BC}=\frac{6}{2}=3,
$$

and the same proportion holds for the other corresponding sides too. As a result, the absolute value of the scale factor is 

$$
|k|=3.
$$

 

Finally, notice that our figures have different orientations, which means that the scale factor of the dilation is negative.

Therefore, the scale factor is $k=-3.$

question.html:
Question 6
?

The larger polygon shown above is the image of the smaller one under the action of a dilation. Find the center of the dilation and its scale factor k.

a
(0,0),k=23
b
(−1,0),k=−13
c
(0,1),k=−2
d
(−1,2),k=−2
e
(0,2),k=−3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The center of a dilation lies on any line which passes through a point and its image.

Therefore, we can find the center of our dilation as, for example, the point of intersection of the lines BB′⟷ and CC′⟷, as shown below.

From the diagram above, where we have that B′C′BC=62=3, and the same proportion holds for the other corresponding sides too. As a result, the absolute value of the scale factor is |k|=3.

Finally, notice that our figures have different orientations, which means that the scale factor of the dilation is negative.

Therefore, the scale factor is k=−3.
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Scale Factor of a Dilation in the Coordinate Plane

solution.reasoning: The smaller triangle has leg lengths 2; the larger has leg lengths 6 and lies in the opposite direction from the center, so k=-3. Using corresponding right-angle vertices (3,4) and (-9,-4), C=(P'-kP)/(1-k)=(0,2). This is option e. No Math Academy answer key or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.html:
Question 6
?

The larger polygon shown above is the image of the smaller one under the action of a dilation. Find the center of the dilation and its scale factor k.

a
(0,0),k=23
b
(−1,0),k=−13
c
(0,1),k=−2
d
(−1,2),k=−2
e
(0,2),k=−3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The center of a dilation lies on any line which passes through a point and its image.

Therefore, we can find the center of our dilation as, for example, the point of intersection of the lines BB′⟷ and CC′⟷, as shown below.

From the diagram above, where we have that B′C′BC=62=3, and the same proportion holds for the other corresponding sides too. As a result, the absolute value of the scale factor is |k|=3.

Finally, notice that our figures have different orientations, which means that the scale factor of the dilation is negative.

Therefore, the scale factor is k=−3.
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Scale Factor of a Dilation in the Coordinate Plane

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Let $(x,y)$ be the solution of the following system. What is the value of $x-y?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.04x-0.08y-4=0 \\ 2x-3y=4\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply the top equation by $100,$ as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.04x-0.08y-4=0 & |\,\times 100 \\ 2x-3y=4 & \end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}4x-8y-400=0 \\ 2x-3y=4\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that if we multiply the second equation by $-2,$ we will get a $-4x$ term in the second equation that can cancel with the $4x$ term in the first equation:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4x-8y-400=0 &  \\ 2x-3y=4 & |\,\times (-2)\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}4x-8y-400=0 \\ -4x+6y=-8\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $x$-variable and allows us to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\cancel{4x}-8y-400 & =0 \\ -\cancel{4x}+6y & =-8 \\ (-8y+6y)-400 & =-8 \\ -2y & =392 \\ y & =-196\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $y=-196$ into the equation $2x-3y=4$ to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-3y & =4 \\ 2x-3(-196) & =4 \\ 2x+588 & =4 \\ 2x & =-584 \\ x & =-292\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-292$ and $y=-196.$ So, 

$$
x-y=-292-(-196)=-292+196=-96.
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Let $(x,y)$ be the solution of the following system. What is the value of $x-y?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2.3x+4.6y=69 \\ 10x-20y=100\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply the top equation by $10,$ as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2.3x+4.6y=69 & |\,\times 10 \\ 10x-20y=100 & \end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}23x+46y=690 \\ 10x-20y=100\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that if we divide the first equation by $23$ and the second equation by $10,$ we will get a $2y$ term in the first equation that can cancel with the $-2y$ term in the second equation:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}23x+46y=690 & |\,÷23 \\ 10x-20y=100 & |\,÷10\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}x+2y=30 \\ x-2y=10\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable and allows us to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\cancel{2y} & =30 \\ x-\cancel{2y} & =10 \\ (x+x) & =(30+10) \\ 2x & =40 \\ x & =20\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=20$ into the equation $x+2y=30$ to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2y & =30 \\ (20)+2y & =30 \\ 2y & =30-20 \\ 2y & =10 \\ y & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is $x=20$ and $y=5.$ So, 

$$
x-y=20-(5)=15.
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Find the solution of the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.2p+0.3q=0.6 \\ 0.2p-0.1q=0.4\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply both equations by $10,$ as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.2p+0.3q=0.6 & |\times 10 \\ 0.2p-0.1q=0.4 & |\times 10\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}2p+3q=6 \\ 2p-q=4\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the elimination method to solve the system. Notice that if we multiply the second equation by $-1,$ then we will get a $-2p$ term that can cancel with the $2p$ term in the first equation:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2p+3q=6 &  \\ 2p-q=4 & |\,\times (-1)\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}2p+3q=6 \\ -2p+q=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $p$-variable and allows us to solve for $q:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\cancel{2p}+3q & =6 \\ -\cancel{2p}+q & =-4 \\ (3q+q) & =(6-4) \\ 4q & =2 \\ q & =\frac{2}{4} \\ q & =0.5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $q=0.5$ into the equation $2p-q=4$ to solve for $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2p-q & =4 \\ 2p-0.5 & =4 \\ 2p & =4.5 \\ p & =\frac{4.5}{2} \\ p & =2.25\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $p=2.25,\,q=0.5.$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Let $(x,y)$ be the solution of the following system. What is the value of $x+y?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.05x-0.03y=0.04 \\ 0.4x+0.2y=0.1\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply the first equations by $100$ and the second equation by $10,$ as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.05x-0.03y=0.04 & |\times 100 \\ 0.4x+0.2y=0.1 & |\times 10\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}5x-3y=4 \\ 4x+2y=1\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $2$ and the second equation by $3,$ we will get a $-6y$ term in the first equation that can cancel with the $6y$ term in the second equation:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5x-3y=4 & |\,\times (2) \\ 4x+2y=1 & |\,\times (3)\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}10x-6y=8 \\ 12x+6y=3\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable and allows us to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}10x-\cancel{6y} & =8 \\ 12x+\cancel{6y} & =3 \\ (10x+12x) & =(8+3) \\ 22x & =11 \\ x & =\frac{11}{22} \\ x & =0.5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=0.5$ into the equation $4x+2y=1$ to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+2y & =1 \\ 4(0.5)+2y & =1 \\ 2+2y & =1 \\ 2y & =-1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{2} \\ y & =-0.5\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is $x=0.5$ and $y=-0.5.$ So, 

$$
x+y=0.5+(-0.5)=0.
$$

                    Solving a System Containing Decimals in One Equation
canonical_examples.problem:
Solve the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.5x+3y+4=0 \\ 4x=-20y-20\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply the first equation by $10,$ as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221949/assets/917f575dd4a88faa1976da566d45a5bddb689a06cd5297cdde8afb17042a5cdb.svg)

We also notice that each equation can be simplified by dividing by a common factor. In the first equation, the common factor is $5,$ while in the second equation, the common factor is $4.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221949/assets/49f2e36b7f95d51d584008af9f79f28fe6c6a729d774537cb326d551e7e3b708.svg)

Notice that the second equation is already solved for $x.$ So, we can substitute $x = -5y-5$ into the first equation and then solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+6y+8 & =0 \\ (-5y-5)+6y+8 & =0 \\ y+3 & =0 \\ y & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the value of $x,$ we substitute $y=-3$ back into $x=-5y-5,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-5y-5 \\  & =-5(-3)-5 \\  & =15-5 \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x = 10$ and $y = -3,$ which can be expressed as $(10, -3).$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Solving a System Containing Decimals in Both Equations
canonical_examples.problem:
Solve the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}1.4x+2.8y=1.4 \\ 0.02x+0.01y=0.05\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply the first equation by $10$ and the second equation by $100,$ as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221949/assets/5e8fbe9a6109fb1b4046645e38993449229ff9ea0d4634a22d98e65a38786c2f.svg)

To simplify the first equation, we divide by $14\mathbin{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221949/assets/f673f4aa7086390409fef5d20ae5d9da38d480a501f5b563e2ae0d915c8a00a5.svg)

We will use the substitution method to solve the system. Notice that the first equation can easily be solved for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2y & =1 \\ x & =1-2y\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can substitute $x=1-2y$ into the second equation and then solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+y & =5 \\ 2(1-2y)+y & =5 \\ 2-4y+y & =5 \\ 2-3y & =5 \\ -3y & =3 \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the value of $x,$ we substitute $y=-1$ back into $x=1-2y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =1-2y \\  & =1-2(-1) \\  & =1+2 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x =3$ and $y =-1$, which can be expressed as $(3, -1).$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving a System Containing Decimals in Both Equations

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Sometimes, we might have a system of equations with decimal coefficients, such as the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.2x+y=1 \\ 0.15x-0.04y=0.2\end{aligned}
$$

To make the system easier to solve, we turn it into a system involving integer coefficients only.

In general, we multiply each equation by $10,$ or $100,$ or $1000,$ etc. depending on how many decimal places we need to eliminate. In this particular instance:

- We need to eliminate one decimal place in the top equation, so we multiply by $10.$

- We need to eliminate two decimal places in the bottom equation, so we multiply by $100.$

So, we multiply the first equation by $10$ and the second equation by $100,$ as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221949/assets/1de5984af7b8bde9abed0d10214c8dab9e954d40576971b5f79505dc4e2f6e71.svg)

From here, we can solve the system of equations using either substitution or elimination.

tutorials.content:
Sometimes, we might have a system of equations with decimal coefficients, such as the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.2x+y=1 \\ 0.15x-0.04y=0.2\end{aligned}
$$

To make the system easier to solve, we turn it into a system involving integer coefficients only.

In general, we multiply each equation by $10,$ or $100,$ or $1000,$ etc. depending on how many decimal places we need to eliminate. In this particular instance:

- We need to eliminate one decimal place in the top equation, so we multiply by $10.$

- We need to eliminate two decimal places in the bottom equation, so we multiply by $100.$

So, we multiply the first equation by $10$ and the second equation by $100,$ as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221949/assets/1de5984af7b8bde9abed0d10214c8dab9e954d40576971b5f79505dc4e2f6e71.svg)

From here, we can solve the system of equations using either substitution or elimination.

tutorial.content:
Sometimes, we might have a system of equations with decimal coefficients, such as the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.2x+y=1 \\ 0.15x-0.04y=0.2\end{aligned}
$$

To make the system easier to solve, we turn it into a system involving integer coefficients only.

In general, we multiply each equation by $10,$ or $100,$ or $1000,$ etc. depending on how many decimal places we need to eliminate. In this particular instance:

- We need to eliminate one decimal place in the top equation, so we multiply by $10.$

- We need to eliminate two decimal places in the bottom equation, so we multiply by $100.$

So, we multiply the first equation by $10$ and the second equation by $100,$ as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221949/assets/fd049a94e6c6e528655fb8c917cf6d0618cc629730af9f6f4f756d04ef58d5a9.svg)

From here, we can solve the system of equations using either substitution or elimination.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply the first equation by $10,$ as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221949/assets/bd66381a33549833fb95186407ee49bfbd233bf078a400c6bac98c59fdcb25d7.svg)

We also notice that each equation can be simplified by dividing by a common factor. In the first equation, the common factor is $5,$ while in the second equation, the common factor is $4.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14221949/assets/57f83da0a4064ec00a15edf9009a65e08ac3f1b8314eb0b1959a68c160a2253d.svg)

Notice that the second equation is already solved for $x.$ So, we can substitute $x = -5y-5$ into the first equation and then solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+6y+8 & =0 \\ (-5y-5)+6y+8 & =0 \\ y+3 & =0 \\ y & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the value of $x,$ we substitute $y=-3$ back into $x=-5y-5,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-5y-5 \\  & =-5(-3)-5 \\  & =15-5 \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x = 10$ and $y = -3,$ which can be expressed as $(10, -3).$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply the top equation by $100,$ as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.04x-0.08y-4=0 & |\,\times 100 \\ 2x-3y=4 & \end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}4x-8y-400=0 \\ 2x-3y=4\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that if we multiply the second equation by $-2,$ we will get a $-4x$ term in the second equation that can cancel with the $4x$ term in the first equation:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4x-8y-400=0 &  \\ 2x-3y=4 & |\,\times (-2)\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}4x-8y-400=0 \\ -4x+6y=-8\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $x$-variable and allows us to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\cancel{4x}-8y-400 & =0 \\ -\cancel{4x}+6y & =-8 \\ (-8y+6y)-400 & =-8 \\ -2y & =392 \\ y & =-196\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $y=-196$ into the equation $2x-3y=4$ to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-3y & =4 \\ 2x-3(-196) & =4 \\ 2x+588 & =4 \\ 2x & =-584 \\ x & =-292\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-292$ and $y=-196.$ So, 

$$
x-y=-292-(-196)=-292+196=-96.
$$

To get rid of the decimals, we multiply the top equation by $10,$ as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2.3x+4.6y=69 & |\,\times 10 \\ 10x-20y=100 & \end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}23x+46y=690 \\ 10x-20y=100\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that if we divide the first equation by $23$ and the second equation by $10,$ we will get a $2y$ term in the first equation that can cancel with the $-2y$ term in the second equation:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}23x+46y=690 & |\,÷23 \\ 10x-20y=100 & |\,÷10\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}x+2y=30 \\ x-2y=10\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable and allows us to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\cancel{2y} & =30 \\ x-\cancel{2y} & =10 \\ (x+x) & =(30+10) \\ 2x & =40 \\ x & =20\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=20$ into the equation $x+2y=30$ to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2y & =30 \\ (20)+2y & =30 \\ 2y & =30-20 \\ 2y & =10 \\ y & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is $x=20$ and $y=5.$ So, 

$$
x-y=20-(5)=15.
$$

$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=20$ into the equation $x+2y=30$ to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2y & =30 \\ (20)+2y & =30 \\ 2y & =30-20 \\ 2y & =10 \\ y & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is $x=20$ and $y=5.$ So, 

$$
x-y=20-(5)=15.
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Solving a System Containing Decimals in Both Equations

observed_steps.worked_solution:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply both equations by $10,$ as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.2p+0.3q=0.6 & |\times 10 \\ 0.2p-0.1q=0.4 & |\times 10\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}2p+3q=6 \\ 2p-q=4\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the elimination method to solve the system. Notice that if we multiply the second equation by $-1,$ then we will get a $-2p$ term that can cancel with the $2p$ term in the first equation:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2p+3q=6 &  \\ 2p-q=4 & |\,\times (-1)\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}2p+3q=6 \\ -2p+q=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $p$-variable and allows us to solve for $q:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\cancel{2p}+3q & =6 \\ -\cancel{2p}+q & =-4 \\ (3q+q) & =(6-4) \\ 4q & =2 \\ q & =\frac{2}{4} \\ q & =0.5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $q=0.5$ into the equation $2p-q=4$ to solve for $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2p-q & =4 \\ 2p-0.5 & =4 \\ 2p & =4.5 \\ p & =\frac{4.5}{2} \\ p & =2.25\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $p=2.25,\,q=0.5.$

$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the p-variable and allows us to solve for q:

Finally, we can substitute q=0.5 into the equation 2p−q=4 to solve for p:

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Let $(x,y)$ be the solution of the following system. What is the value of $x-y?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.04x-0.08y-4=0 \\ 2x-3y=4\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply the top equation by $100,$ as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.04x-0.08y-4=0 & |\,\times 100 \\ 2x-3y=4 & \end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}4x-8y-400=0 \\ 2x-3y=4\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that if we multiply the second equation by $-2,$ we will get a $-4x$ term in the second equation that can cancel with the $4x$ term in the first equation:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4x-8y-400=0 &  \\ 2x-3y=4 & |\,\times (-2)\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}4x-8y-400=0 \\ -4x+6y=-8\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $x$-variable and allows us to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\cancel{4x}-8y-400 & =0 \\ -\cancel{4x}+6y & =-8 \\ (-8y+6y)-400 & =-8 \\ -2y & =392 \\ y & =-196\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $y=-196$ into the equation $2x-3y=4$ to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-3y & =4 \\ 2x-3(-196) & =4 \\ 2x+588 & =4 \\ 2x & =-584 \\ x & =-292\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-292$ and $y=-196.$ So, 

$$
x-y=-292-(-196)=-292+196=-96.
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Let $(x,y)$ be the solution of the following system. What is the value of $x-y?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2.3x+4.6y=69 \\ 10x-20y=100\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply the top equation by $10,$ as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2.3x+4.6y=69 & |\,\times 10 \\ 10x-20y=100 & \end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}23x+46y=690 \\ 10x-20y=100\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that if we divide the first equation by $23$ and the second equation by $10,$ we will get a $2y$ term in the first equation that can cancel with the $-2y$ term in the second equation:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}23x+46y=690 & |\,÷23 \\ 10x-20y=100 & |\,÷10\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}x+2y=30 \\ x-2y=10\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable and allows us to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\cancel{2y} & =30 \\ x-\cancel{2y} & =10 \\ (x+x) & =(30+10) \\ 2x & =40 \\ x & =20\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=20$ into the equation $x+2y=30$ to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2y & =30 \\ (20)+2y & =30 \\ 2y & =30-20 \\ 2y & =10 \\ y & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is $x=20$ and $y=5.$ So, 

$$
x-y=20-(5)=15.
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply the top equation by $10,$ as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2.3x+4.6y=69 & |\,\times 10 \\ 10x-20y=100 & \end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}23x+46y=690 \\ 10x-20y=100\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that if we divide the first equation by $23$ and the second equation by $10,$ we will get a $2y$ term in the first equation that can cancel with the $-2y$ term in the second equation:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}23x+46y=690 & |\,÷23 \\ 10x-20y=100 & |\,÷10\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}x+2y=30 \\ x-2y=10\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable and allows us to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\cancel{2y} & =30 \\ x-\cancel{2y} & =10 \\ (x+x) & =(30+10) \\ 2x & =40 \\ x & =20\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=20$ into the equation $x+2y=30$ to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2y & =30 \\ (20)+2y & =30 \\ 2y & =30-20 \\ 2y & =10 \\ y & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is $x=20$ and $y=5.$ So, 

$$
x-y=20-(5)=15.
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Find the solution of the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.2p+0.3q=0.6 \\ 0.2p-0.1q=0.4\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply both equations by $10,$ as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.2p+0.3q=0.6 & |\times 10 \\ 0.2p-0.1q=0.4 & |\times 10\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}2p+3q=6 \\ 2p-q=4\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the elimination method to solve the system. Notice that if we multiply the second equation by $-1,$ then we will get a $-2p$ term that can cancel with the $2p$ term in the first equation:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2p+3q=6 &  \\ 2p-q=4 & |\,\times (-1)\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}2p+3q=6 \\ -2p+q=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $p$-variable and allows us to solve for $q:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\cancel{2p}+3q & =6 \\ -\cancel{2p}+q & =-4 \\ (3q+q) & =(6-4) \\ 4q & =2 \\ q & =\frac{2}{4} \\ q & =0.5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $q=0.5$ into the equation $2p-q=4$ to solve for $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2p-q & =4 \\ 2p-0.5 & =4 \\ 2p & =4.5 \\ p & =\frac{4.5}{2} \\ p & =2.25\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $p=2.25,\,q=0.5.$

Correct

To get rid of the decimals, we multiply both equations by 10, as follows:

{0.2p+0.3q=0.6|×100.2p−0.1q=0.4|×10⟹{2p+3q=62p−q=4

We will use the elimination method to solve the system. Notice that if we multiply the second equation by −1, then we will get a −2p term that can cancel with the 2p term in the first equation:

{2p+3q=62p−q=4|×(−1)⟹{2p+3q=6−2p+q=−4

Adding the two equations eliminates the p-variable and allows us to solve for q:

Question 3
?

Find the solution of the following system:

{0.2p+0.3q=0.60.2p−0.1q=0.4

a
p=6.5,q=9
b
p=1.25,q=−16
c
p=3.5,q=3
d
p=2.25,q=0.5
e
p=4.75,q=5.5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To get rid of the decimals, we multiply both equations by 10, as follows:

{0.2p+0.3q=0.6|×100.2p−0.1q=0.4|×10⟹{2p+3q=62p−q=4

We will use the elimination method to solve the system. Notice that if we multiply the second equation by −1, then we will get a −2p term that can cancel with the 2p term in the first equation:

{2p+3q=62p−q=4|×(−1)⟹{2p+3q=6−2p+q=−4

Adding the two equations eliminates the p-variable and allows us to solve for q:

2p+3q=6−2p+q=−4(3q+q)=(6−4)4q=2q=24q=0.5

Finally, we can substitute q=0.5 into the equation 2p−q=4 to solve for p:

2p−q=42p−0.5=42p=4.5p=4.52p=2.25

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is p=2.25,q=0.5.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem:
Find the solution of the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.2p+0.3q=0.6 \\ 0.2p-0.1q=0.4\end{aligned}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply both equations by $10,$ as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.2p+0.3q=0.6 & |\times 10 \\ 0.2p-0.1q=0.4 & |\times 10\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}2p+3q=6 \\ 2p-q=4\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the elimination method to solve the system. Notice that if we multiply the second equation by $-1,$ then we will get a $-2p$ term that can cancel with the $2p$ term in the first equation:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2p+3q=6 &  \\ 2p-q=4 & |\,\times (-1)\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}2p+3q=6 \\ -2p+q=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $p$-variable and allows us to solve for $q:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\cancel{2p}+3q & =6 \\ -\cancel{2p}+q & =-4 \\ (3q+q) & =(6-4) \\ 4q & =2 \\ q & =\frac{2}{4} \\ q & =0.5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $q=0.5$ into the equation $2p-q=4$ to solve for $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2p-q & =4 \\ 2p-0.5 & =4 \\ 2p & =4.5 \\ p & =\frac{4.5}{2} \\ p & =2.25\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $p=2.25,\,q=0.5.$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Let $(x,y)$ be the solution of the following system. What is the value of $x+y?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.05x-0.03y=0.04 \\ 0.4x+0.2y=0.1\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply the first equations by $100$ and the second equation by $10,$ as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.05x-0.03y=0.04 & |\times 100 \\ 0.4x+0.2y=0.1 & |\times 10\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}5x-3y=4 \\ 4x+2y=1\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $2$ and the second equation by $3,$ we will get a $-6y$ term in the first equation that can cancel with the $6y$ term in the second equation:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5x-3y=4 & |\,\times (2) \\ 4x+2y=1 & |\,\times (3)\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}10x-6y=8 \\ 12x+6y=3\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable and allows us to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}10x-\cancel{6y} & =8 \\ 12x+\cancel{6y} & =3 \\ (10x+12x) & =(8+3) \\ 22x & =11 \\ x & =\frac{11}{22} \\ x & =0.5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=0.5$ into the equation $4x+2y=1$ to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+2y & =1 \\ 4(0.5)+2y & =1 \\ 2+2y & =1 \\ 2y & =-1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{2} \\ y & =-0.5\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is $x=0.5$ and $y=-0.5.$ So, 

$$
x+y=0.5+(-0.5)=0.
$$

Question 4
?

Let (x,y) be the solution of the following system. What is the value of x+y? {0.05x−0.03y=0.040.4x+0.2y=0.1

a
2.5
b
0.5
c
1
d
2
e
0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To get rid of the decimals, we multiply the first equations by 100 and the second equation by 10, as follows:

{0.05x−0.03y=0.04|×1000.4x+0.2y=0.1|×10⟹{5x−3y=44x+2y=1

Notice that if we multiply the first equation by 2 and the second equation by 3, we will get a −6y term in the first equation that can cancel with the 6y term in the second equation:

{5x−3y=4|×(2)4x+2y=1|×(3)⟹{10x−6y=812x+6y=3

Adding the two equations eliminates the y-variable and allows us to solve for x:

10x−6y=812x+6y=3(10x+12x)=(8+3)22x=11x=1122x=0.5

Finally, we can substitute x=0.5 into the equation 4x+2y=1 to solve for y:

4x+2y=14(0.5)+2y=12+2y=12y=−1y=−12y=−0.5

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is x=0.5 and y=−0.5. So, x+y=0.5+(−0.5)=0.

last_observation.worked_solution:
To get rid of the decimals, we multiply the first equations by $100$ and the second equation by $10,$ as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0.05x-0.03y=0.04 & |\times 100 \\ 0.4x+0.2y=0.1 & |\times 10\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}5x-3y=4 \\ 4x+2y=1\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $2$ and the second equation by $3,$ we will get a $-6y$ term in the first equation that can cancel with the $6y$ term in the second equation:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5x-3y=4 & |\,\times (2) \\ 4x+2y=1 & |\,\times (3)\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}10x-6y=8 \\ 12x+6y=3\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable and allows us to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}10x-\cancel{6y} & =8 \\ 12x+\cancel{6y} & =3 \\ (10x+12x) & =(8+3) \\ 22x & =11 \\ x & =\frac{11}{22} \\ x & =0.5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=0.5$ into the equation $4x+2y=1$ to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+2y & =1 \\ 4(0.5)+2y & =1 \\ 2+2y & =1 \\ 2y & =-1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{2} \\ y & =-0.5\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution to the system of equations is $x=0.5$ and $y=-0.5.$ So, 

$$
x+y=0.5+(-0.5)=0.
$$

questions.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{MN}$ traversed from the point $M(1,3)$ to the point $N(3,-1),$ then ${\int }_{C}{e}^{x-y}\,dx+{e}^{x-y}\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i+3\,j$ and $b=3\,i-j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =i+3\,j+t(3\,i-j-(i+3\,j)) \\  & =i+3\,j+t(2\,i-4\,j) \\  & =(2t+1)\,i+(3-4t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=2t+1$ and $y(t)=3-4t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2\,i-4\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x-y}\,dx+{e}^{x-y}\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x-y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+{e}^{x-y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x-y}(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2t+1-(3-4t)}(2+(-4))\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{6t-2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{6t-2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}[{e}^{6(1)-2}-{e}^{6(0)-2}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}[{e}^{4}-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}] \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{6}}{3{e}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{MN}$ traversed from the point $M(1,1)$ to the point $N(3,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}\frac{1}{y}\,dx+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i+j$ and $b=3\,i+3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =i+j+t(3\,i+3\,j-(i+j)) \\  & =i+j+t(2\,i+2\,j) \\  & =(2t+1)\,i+(2t+1)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=2t+1$ and $y(t)=2t+1$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{1}{y}\,dx+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2t+1}\cdot 2+\frac{1}{(2t+1)^{2}}\cdot 2\,dt \\  & ={[\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1)-\frac{1}{2t+1}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot 1+1)-\frac{1}{2\cdot 1+1}]-[\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot 0+1)-\frac{1}{2\cdot 0+1}] \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\frac{1}{3}+1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡3+\frac{2}{3} \\  & =\frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡3+2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
