questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from the point $A(0,1)$ to the point $B(2,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}{e}^{x}\,dx-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=j$ and $b=2\,i+3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =j+t(2\,i+3\,j-j) \\  & =j+t(2\,i+2j) \\  & =2t\,i+(1+2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=2t$ and $y(t)=1+2t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x}\,dx-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{x}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2t}\cdot 2-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi (1+2t)}{2})\cdot 2\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2{e}^{2t}-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi t))dt \\  & ={[{e}^{2t}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi t)]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[{e}^{2(1)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi (1))]-[{e}^{2(0)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi (0))] \\  & =[{e}^{2}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})]-[1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =[{e}^{2}+0]-[1+0] \\  & ={e}^{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{FG}$ traversed from the point $F(1,0)$ to the point $G(2,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}x\,dx-xy\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i$ and $b=2\,i+3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =i+t(2\,i+3\,j-i) \\  & =i+t(i+3\,j) \\  & =(1+t)\,i+3t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=1+t$ and $y(t)=3t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+3\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx-xy\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-xy\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-xy\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1+t)\cdot 1-(1+t)\cdot 3t\cdot 3\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1-8t-9{t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={[t-4{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[1-4(1)^{2}-3(1)^{3}]-[0] \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{MN}$ traversed from the point $M(-1,0)$ to the point $N(2,4),$ then ${\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-i$ and $b=2\,i+4\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =-i+t(2\,i+4\,j-(-i)) \\  & =-i+t(3\,i+4\,j) \\  & =(3t-1)\,i+4t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=3t-1$ and $y(t)=4t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=3\,i+4\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4t(3)-(3t-1)(4)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4\,dt \\  & =4t\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4(1-0) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y=\sqrt{x}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to point $B(1,1),$ then  ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+y)\,dx+(3x+2y)\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=\sqrt{x}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j={t}^{2}\,i+t\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2t\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+y)\,dx+(3x+2y)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(3x+2y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(({x}^{2}+y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(3x+2y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({({t}^{2})}^{2}+t)\cdot 2t+(3{t}^{2}+2t)\cdot 1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{4}+t)\cdot 2t+3{t}^{2}+2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{t}^{5}+5{t}^{2}+2t\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{6}}{3}+\frac{5{t}^{3}}{3}+{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{(1)^{6}}{3}+\frac{5(1)^{3}}{3}+(1)^{2}]-[0] \\  & =[\frac{1}{3}+\frac{5}{3}+1]-[0] \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y={x}^{3}$ traversed from the point $P(1,1)$ to point $Q(2,8),$ then ${\int }_{C}\frac{1}{y}\,dx+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{3}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+{t}^{3}\,j,\,t\in [1,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+3{t}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{1}{y}\,dx+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{t}^{3}}\cdot 1+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\cdot 3{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{t}^{3}}+3\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}}+3t]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2({2}^{2})}+3(2)]-[-\frac{1}{2({1}^{2})}+3(1)] \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}+6+\frac{1}{2}-3 \\  & =\frac{27}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y=(x+1)^{2}$ traversed from the point $P(0,1)$ to point $Q(1,4),$ then ${\int }_{C}\frac{dx+dy}{y}=$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=(x+1)^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+(t+1)^{2}\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2(t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{dx+dy}{y} & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{y}(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{y}(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1+2(t+1)}{(t+1)^{2}}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{(t+1)^{2}}+\frac{2}{t+1}\,dt \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{t+1}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{1+1}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+1)]-[-\frac{1}{0+1}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)] \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡2]-[-1+0] \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y={x}^{2}-1$ traversed from the point $P(1,0)$ to point $Q(2,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{2}-1.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j,\,t\in [1,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}({y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{({t}^{2}-1)}^{2}\cdot 1+t\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{4}-2{t}^{2}+1+2{t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{4}+1\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}+t]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =[\frac{{2}^{5}}{5}+2]-[\frac{{1}^{5}}{5}+1] \\  & =\frac{32}{5}+2-\frac{1}{5}-1 \\  & =\frac{36}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y={x}^{2}-1$ traversed from the point $A(0,-1)$ to point $B(2,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}5{x}^{2}y\,dx+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{2}-1.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j,\,t\in [0,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}5{x}^{2}y\,dx+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{x}^{2}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(5{x}^{2}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{t}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\cdot 1+{t}^{2}({t}^{2}-1+1)\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{t}^{4}-5{t}^{2}+2{t}^{5}\,dt \\  & ={[{t}^{5}-\frac{5}{3}{t}^{3}+\frac{{t}^{6}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[{2}^{5}-\frac{5}{3}(2)^{3}+\frac{{2}^{6}}{3}]-[0] \\  & =32-\frac{40}{3}+\frac{64}{3} \\  & =40\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,dx+xy\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=4$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(2,0)$ to the point $B(0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $1,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,dx+xy\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{x}^{2}\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+xy\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}({x}^{2}\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+xy\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-8{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}dx+\frac{2}{x}\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $(-1,0)$ to the point $(0,-3).$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $3,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [\pi ,\frac{3\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}dx+\frac{2}{x}\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{2}{x}\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+\frac{2}{x}\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{2}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+6\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\operatorname{cos}⁡t+6t]_{\pi }^{3\pi /2} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})+9\pi )-(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +6\pi ) \\  & =(0+9\pi )-(-1+6\pi ) \\  & =3\pi +1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=2$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(\sqrt{2},0)$ to the point $B(0,\sqrt{2}).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the parametrization of the curve $C.$ Since it's a circle if radius $\sqrt{2}$ centered at the origin, the curve $C$ can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,j,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, along the curve we have that $x(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}-x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(-2{sin}^{2}⁡t-2{cos}^{2}⁡t)\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\text{d}t \\  & =-2t{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-2[\frac{\pi }{2}-0] \\  & =-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x-2y)\,dx+2x\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(0,3)$ to the point $B(0,-3).$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $3,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-2y)\,dx+2x\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(x-2y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+2x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}((x-2y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+2x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t))\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+6{sin}^{2}⁡t+6{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}6-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,dx+x\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(2,0)$ to the point $B(-2,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is a circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [0,\pi ]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}\cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-16{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t(1-4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Over Segments
canonical_examples.problem:
If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overline{AB}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to the point $B(1, 1),$ calculate the line integral 

$$
\displaystyle \int\limits_C x^2y\,\mathrm{d}x + xy\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a} = 0\,\mathbf{i} + 0\,\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b} = 1\,\mathbf{i} + 1\,\mathbf{j}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =t\,i+t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \le t \le 1.$ So, we have that $x(t) = t$ and $y(t) = t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,dx+xy\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+xy\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+xy\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\cdot t\cdot 1+t\cdot t\cdot 1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}+\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{7}{12}\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Over Segments

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Cartesian Curves
canonical_examples.problem:
If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y=x^2$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to the point $B(1,1),$ evaluate the line integral 

$$
\displaystyle \int\limits_C (x+y)\,\mathrm{d}x + (x-y)\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y = x^2.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x-y)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x+y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(x-y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((x+y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x-y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t+{t}^{2})\cdot 1+(t-{t}^{2})\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t+3{t}^{2}-2{t}^{3}\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{t}^{3}-\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}+1-\frac{1}{2}]-[0] \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Cartesian Curves

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Computing Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Circles and Ellipses
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14222171/assets/7a6e67435aab40d5bf3630c66f79241008357e1549b1c77b4c0bdfea2b453883.png)

Evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_C \dfrac{y\,\mathrm{d}x - x\,\mathrm{d}y}{x^2+y^2},$ where $C$ is a part of the circle $x^2+y^2=4$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $\left(0,2\right).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, notice that a parametrization for the given path is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & ={x}^{′}(t)\,i+{y}^{′}(t)\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{y\,dx-x\,dy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{y\cdot {x}^{′}-x\cdot {y}^{′}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}},dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{-4{sin}^{2}⁡t-4{cos}^{2}⁡t}{4({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{-4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}{4({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,dt \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\,dt \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Circles and Ellipses

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Let $f(x,y)$ be a function of two variables and $C$ be a path in the $xy$-plane. Recall that the line integral

$$
\int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm dx +  f(x,y)\,\textrm d y
$$

can be evaluated by parameterizing $C$ using the parameter $t\in [a,b]$ and then applying a change of variables, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x+f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+f(x,y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(f(x,y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+f(x,y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

The hardest part is often finding a suitable parameterization for curve $C.$ We'll discuss a number of different cases in this lesson.

\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =t\,i+t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \le t \le 1.$ So, we have that $x(t) = t$ and $y(t) = t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,dx+xy\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+xy\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+xy\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\cdot t\cdot 1+t\cdot t\cdot 1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}+\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{7}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Over Segments
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=j$ and $b=2\,i+3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =j+t(2\,i+3\,j-j) \\  & =j+t(2\,i+2j) \\  & =2t\,i+(1+2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=2t$ and $y(t)=1+2t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x}\,dx-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{x}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2t}\cdot 2-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi (1+2t)}{2})\cdot 2\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2{e}^{2t}-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi t))dt \\  & ={[{e}^{2t}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi t)]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[{e}^{2(1)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi (1))]-[{e}^{2(0)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi (0))] \\  & =[{e}^{2}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})]-[1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =[{e}^{2}+0]-[1+0] \\  & ={e}^{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y = x^2.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x-y)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x+y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(x-y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((x+y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x-y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t+{t}^{2})\cdot 1+(t-{t}^{2})\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t+3{t}^{2}-2{t}^{3}\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{t}^{3}-\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}+1-\frac{1}{2}]-[0] \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}({y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{({t}^{2}-1)}^{2}\cdot 1+t\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{4}-2{t}^{2}+1+2{t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{4}+1\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}+t]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =[\frac{{2}^{5}}{5}+2]-[\frac{{1}^{5}}{5}+1] \\  & =\frac{32}{5}+2-\frac{1}{5}-1 \\  & =\frac{36}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{2}-1.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j,\,t\in [0,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}5{x}^{2}y\,dx+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{x}^{2}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(5{x}^{2}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{t}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\cdot 1+{t}^{2}({t}^{2}-1+1)\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{t}^{4}-5{t}^{2}+2{t}^{5}\,dt \\  & ={[{t}^{5}-\frac{5}{3}{t}^{3}+\frac{{t}^{6}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[{2}^{5}-\frac{5}{3}(2)^{3}+\frac{{2}^{6}}{3}]-[0] \\  & =32-\frac{40}{3}+\frac{64}{3} \\  & =40\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & ={x}^{′}(t)\,i+{y}^{′}(t)\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{y\,dx-x\,dy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{y\cdot {x}^{′}-x\cdot {y}^{′}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}},dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{-4{sin}^{2}⁡t-4{cos}^{2}⁡t}{4({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{-4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}{4({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,dt \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\,dt \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 11
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cx2dx+xydy, where C is part of the ellipse x2+4y2=4 traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point A(2,0) to the point B(0,1).

a
 6∫0π/2cos⁡tsin⁡t(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)dt
b
−6∫0π/2cos2⁡tsin⁡tdt
c
 −2∫0π/2cos2⁡tsin2⁡tdt
d
 3∫0π/2cos⁡tsin2⁡tdt
e
 ∫0π/2cos⁡tsin⁡t(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 2 and 1, respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=2cos⁡ti+sin⁡tj,t∈[0,π2]

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=−2sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows: ∫Cx2dx+xydy=∫0π/2x2dxdtdt+xydydtdt=∫0π/2(x2dxdt+xydydt)dt=∫0π/2(2cos⁡t)2⋅(−2sin⁡t)+(2cos⁡t)⋅sin⁡t⋅cos⁡tdt=∫0π/2−8cos2⁡tsin⁡t+2cos2⁡tsin⁡tdt=−6∫0π/2cos2⁡tsin⁡tdt

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $3,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [\pi ,\frac{3\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$

observed_steps.name: Question 13
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Circles and Ellipses
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the parametrization of the curve $C.$ Since it's a circle if radius $\sqrt{2}$ centered at the origin, the curve $C$ can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,j,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, along the curve we have that $x(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}-x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(-2{sin}^{2}⁡t-2{cos}^{2}⁡t)\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\text{d}t \\  & =-2t{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-2[\frac{\pi }{2}-0] \\  & =-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 14
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x−2y)dx+2xdy, where C is part of the ellipse 9x2+y2=9 traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point A(0,3) to the point B(0,−3).

a
 ∫π/23π/26sin2⁡t−cos⁡tdt
b
 ∫π/23π/23−sin2⁡tcos⁡tdt
c
 ∫π/23π/23sin⁡t+cos⁡tdt
d
∫π/23π/26−sin⁡tcos⁡tdt
e
 2∫π/23π/2sin⁡tcos2⁡tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 1 and 3, respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj,t∈[π2,3π2]

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=−sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows: ∫C(x−2y)dx+2xdy=∫π/23π/2(x−2y)dxdtdt+2xdydtdt=∫π/23π/2((x−2y)dxdt+2xdydt)dt=∫π/23π/2(cos⁡t−2(3sin⁡t))⋅(−sin⁡t)+2(cos⁡t)⋅3cos⁡tdt=∫π/23π/2−sin⁡tcos⁡t+6sin2⁡t+6cos2⁡tdt=∫π/23π/26−sin⁡tcos⁡tdt
question.knowledge_point: Computing Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Circles and Ellipses

observed_steps.name: Question 15
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Circles and Ellipses
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is a circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [0,\pi ]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}\cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-16{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t(1-4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}\cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-16{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t(1-4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cx2ydx+xdy, where C is part of the circle x2+y2=4 traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point A(2,0) to the point B(−2,0).

a
 8∫0πcos2⁡t(1−2cos2⁡t)dt
b
 8∫0πcos2⁡tsin2⁡tdt
c
 2∫0πcos2⁡t(1−2sin2⁡t)dt
d
 4∫0πsin2⁡t(1−4cos2⁡t)dt
e
4∫0πcos2⁡t(1−4sin2⁡t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since C is a circle of radius 2 centered at the origin, it can be parametrized as follows:

r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=2cos⁡ti+2sin⁡tj,t∈[0,π]

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=−2sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows: ∫Cx2ydx+xdy=∫0πx2ydxdtdt+xdydtdt=∫0π(x2ydxdt+xdydt)dt=∫0π(2cos⁡t)2⋅(2sin⁡t)⋅(−2sin⁡t)+(2cos⁡t)⋅2cos⁡tdt=∫0π−16sin2⁡tcos2⁡t+4cos2⁡tdt=4∫0πcos2⁡t(1−4sin2⁡t)dt

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{MN}$ traversed from the point $M(1,3)$ to the point $N(3,-1),$ then ${\int }_{C}{e}^{x-y}\,dx+{e}^{x-y}\,dy=$
question.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i+3\,j$ and $b=3\,i-j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =i+3\,j+t(3\,i-j-(i+3\,j)) \\  & =i+3\,j+t(2\,i-4\,j) \\  & =(2t+1)\,i+(3-4t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=2t+1$ and $y(t)=3-4t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2\,i-4\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x-y}\,dx+{e}^{x-y}\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x-y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+{e}^{x-y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x-y}(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2t+1-(3-4t)}(2+(-4))\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{6t-2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{6t-2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}[{e}^{6(1)-2}-{e}^{6(0)-2}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}[{e}^{4}-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}] \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{6}}{3{e}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Over Segments
last_observation.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i+3\,j$ and $b=3\,i-j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =i+3\,j+t(3\,i-j-(i+3\,j)) \\  & =i+3\,j+t(2\,i-4\,j) \\  & =(2t+1)\,i+(3-4t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=2t+1$ and $y(t)=3-4t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2\,i-4\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x-y}\,dx+{e}^{x-y}\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x-y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+{e}^{x-y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x-y}(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2t+1-(3-4t)}(2+(-4))\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{6t-2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{6t-2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}[{e}^{6(1)-2}-{e}^{6(0)-2}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}[{e}^{4}-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}] \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{6}}{3{e}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =i+3\,j+t(3\,i-j-(i+3\,j)) \\  & =i+3\,j+t(2\,i-4\,j) \\  & =(2t+1)\,i+(3-4t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=2t+1$ and $y(t)=3-4t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2\,i-4\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x-y}\,dx+{e}^{x-y}\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x-y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+{e}^{x-y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x-y}(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2t+1-(3-4t)}(2+(-4))\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{6t-2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{6t-2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}[{e}^{6(1)-2}-{e}^{6(0)-2}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}[{e}^{4}-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}] \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{6}}{3{e}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{MN}$ traversed from the point $M(1,1)$ to the point $N(3,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}\frac{1}{y}\,dx+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,dy=$
question.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i+j$ and $b=3\,i+3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =i+j+t(3\,i+3\,j-(i+j)) \\  & =i+j+t(2\,i+2\,j) \\  & =(2t+1)\,i+(2t+1)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=2t+1$ and $y(t)=2t+1$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{1}{y}\,dx+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2t+1}\cdot 2+\frac{1}{(2t+1)^{2}}\cdot 2\,dt \\  & ={[\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1)-\frac{1}{2t+1}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot 1+1)-\frac{1}{2\cdot 1+1}]-[\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot 0+1)-\frac{1}{2\cdot 0+1}] \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\frac{1}{3}+1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡3+\frac{2}{3} \\  & =\frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡3+2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

If the path C is the line segment MN― traversed from the point M(1,1) to the point N(3,3), then ∫C1ydx+1x2dy=

a
ln⁡3+12
b
2ln⁡2+32
c
ln⁡2+23
d
ln⁡2+34
e
3ln⁡3+23
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are a=i+j and b=3i+3j. So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by r(t)=a+t(b−a)=i+j+t(3i+3j−(i+j))=i+j+t(2i+2j)=(2t+1)i+(2t+1)j, where 0≤t≤1. Thus, we have that x(t)=2t+1 and y(t)=2t+1 along the segment.

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=2i+2j.

We can now evaluate the line integral: ∫C1ydx+1x2dy=∫011ydxdtdt+1x2dydtdt=∫01(1ydxdt+1x2dydt)dt=∫0112t+1⋅2+1(2t+1)2⋅2dt=[ln⁡(2t+1)−12t+1]01=[ln⁡(2⋅1+1)−12⋅1+1]−[ln⁡(2⋅0+1)−12⋅0+1]=ln⁡3−13+1=ln⁡3+23=3ln⁡3+23

last_observation.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i+j$ and $b=3\,i+3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =i+j+t(3\,i+3\,j-(i+j)) \\  & =i+j+t(2\,i+2\,j) \\  & =(2t+1)\,i+(2t+1)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=2t+1$ and $y(t)=2t+1$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{1}{y}\,dx+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2t+1}\cdot 2+\frac{1}{(2t+1)^{2}}\cdot 2\,dt \\  & ={[\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1)-\frac{1}{2t+1}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot 1+1)-\frac{1}{2\cdot 1+1}]-[\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot 0+1)-\frac{1}{2\cdot 0+1}] \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\frac{1}{3}+1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡3+\frac{2}{3} \\  & =\frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡3+2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

If the path C is the line segment MN― traversed from the point M(1,1) to the point N(3,3), then ∫C1ydx+1x2dy=

a
ln⁡3+12
b
2ln⁡2+32
c
ln⁡2+23
d
ln⁡2+34
e
3ln⁡3+23
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are a=i+j and b=3i+3j. So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by r(t)=a+t(b−a)=i+j+t(3i+3j−(i+j))=i+j+t(2i+2j)=(2t+1)i+(2t+1)j, where 0≤t≤1. Thus, we have that x(t)=2t+1 and y(t)=2t+1 along the segment.

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=2i+2j.

We can now evaluate the line integral: ∫C1ydx+1x2dy=∫011ydxdtdt+1x2dydtdt=∫01(1ydxdt+1x2dydt)dt=∫0112t+1⋅2+1(2t+1)2⋅2dt=[ln⁡(2t+1)−12t+1]01=[ln⁡(2⋅1+1)−12⋅1+1]−[ln⁡(2⋅0+1)−12⋅0+1]=ln⁡3−13+1=ln⁡3+23=3ln⁡3+23
question.knowledge_point: Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Over Segments

solution.reasoning: Along the segment, y=x and dy=dx, with x increasing from 1 to 3. Thus the integral is \int_1^3(1/x+1/x^2)\,dx=[\ln x-1/x]_1^3=\ln 3+2/3=(3\ln 3+2)/3, choice e. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key for this question.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{MN}$ traversed from the point $M(1,1)$ to the point $N(3,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}\frac{1}{y}\,dx+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,dy=$
feedback.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i+j$ and $b=3\,i+3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =i+j+t(3\,i+3\,j-(i+j)) \\  & =i+j+t(2\,i+2\,j) \\  & =(2t+1)\,i+(2t+1)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=2t+1$ and $y(t)=2t+1$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{1}{y}\,dx+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2t+1}\cdot 2+\frac{1}{(2t+1)^{2}}\cdot 2\,dt \\  & ={[\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1)-\frac{1}{2t+1}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot 1+1)-\frac{1}{2\cdot 1+1}]-[\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot 0+1)-\frac{1}{2\cdot 0+1}] \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\frac{1}{3}+1 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡3+\frac{2}{3} \\  & =\frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡3+2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from the point $A(0,1)$ to the point $B(2,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}{e}^{x}\,dx-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})\,dy=$
question.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=j$ and $b=2\,i+3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =j+t(2\,i+3\,j-j) \\  & =j+t(2\,i+2j) \\  & =2t\,i+(1+2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=2t$ and $y(t)=1+2t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x}\,dx-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{x}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2t}\cdot 2-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi (1+2t)}{2})\cdot 2\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2{e}^{2t}-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi t))dt \\  & ={[{e}^{2t}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi t)]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[{e}^{2(1)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi (1))]-[{e}^{2(0)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi (0))] \\  & =[{e}^{2}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})]-[1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =[{e}^{2}+0]-[1+0] \\  & ={e}^{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from the point $A(0,1)$ to the point $B(2,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}{e}^{x}\,dx-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})\,dy=$
feedback.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=j$ and $b=2\,i+3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =j+t(2\,i+3\,j-j) \\  & =j+t(2\,i+2j) \\  & =2t\,i+(1+2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=2t$ and $y(t)=1+2t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x}\,dx-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{x}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{x}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2t}\cdot 2-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi (1+2t)}{2})\cdot 2\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2{e}^{2t}-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi t))dt \\  & ={[{e}^{2t}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi t)]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[{e}^{2(1)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi (1))]-[{e}^{2(0)}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi (0))] \\  & =[{e}^{2}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})]-[1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =[{e}^{2}+0]-[1+0] \\  & ={e}^{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{FG}$ traversed from the point $F(1,0)$ to the point $G(2,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}x\,dx-xy\,dy=$
question.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i$ and $b=2\,i+3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =i+t(2\,i+3\,j-i) \\  & =i+t(i+3\,j) \\  & =(1+t)\,i+3t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=1+t$ and $y(t)=3t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+3\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx-xy\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-xy\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-xy\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1+t)\cdot 1-(1+t)\cdot 3t\cdot 3\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1-8t-9{t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={[t-4{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[1-4(1)^{2}-3(1)^{3}]-[0] \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{MN}$ traversed from the point $M(-1,0)$ to the point $N(2,4),$ then ${\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy=$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-i$ and $b=2\,i+4\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =-i+t(2\,i+4\,j-(-i)) \\  & =-i+t(3\,i+4\,j) \\  & =(3t-1)\,i+4t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=3t-1$ and $y(t)=4t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=3\,i+4\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4t(3)-(3t-1)(4)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4\,dt \\  & =4t\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4(1-0) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 6
question.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y=\sqrt{x}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to point $B(1,1),$ then  ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+y)\,dx+(3x+2y)\,dy=$
question.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=\sqrt{x}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j={t}^{2}\,i+t\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2t\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+y)\,dx+(3x+2y)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(3x+2y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(({x}^{2}+y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(3x+2y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({({t}^{2})}^{2}+t)\cdot 2t+(3{t}^{2}+2t)\cdot 1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{4}+t)\cdot 2t+3{t}^{2}+2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{t}^{5}+5{t}^{2}+2t\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{6}}{3}+\frac{5{t}^{3}}{3}+{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{(1)^{6}}{3}+\frac{5(1)^{3}}{3}+(1)^{2}]-[0] \\  & =[\frac{1}{3}+\frac{5}{3}+1]-[0] \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 7
question.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y={x}^{3}$ traversed from the point $P(1,1)$ to point $Q(2,8),$ then ${\int }_{C}\frac{1}{y}\,dx+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,dy=$
question.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{3}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+{t}^{3}\,j,\,t\in [1,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+3{t}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{1}{y}\,dx+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{t}^{3}}\cdot 1+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\cdot 3{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{t}^{3}}+3\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}}+3t]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2({2}^{2})}+3(2)]-[-\frac{1}{2({1}^{2})}+3(1)] \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}+6+\frac{1}{2}-3 \\  & =\frac{27}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y={x}^{3}$ traversed from the point $P(1,1)$ to point $Q(2,8),$ then ${\int }_{C}\frac{1}{y}\,dx+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,dy=$
question.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{3}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+{t}^{3}\,j,\,t\in [1,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+3{t}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{1}{y}\,dx+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{t}^{3}}\cdot 1+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\cdot 3{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{t}^{3}}+3\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}}+3t]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2({2}^{2})}+3(2)]-[-\frac{1}{2({1}^{2})}+3(1)] \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}+6+\frac{1}{2}-3 \\  & =\frac{27}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y=(x+1)^{2}$ traversed from the point $P(0,1)$ to point $Q(1,4),$ then ${\int }_{C}\frac{dx+dy}{y}=$
question.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=(x+1)^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+(t+1)^{2}\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2(t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{dx+dy}{y} & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{y}(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{y}(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1+2(t+1)}{(t+1)^{2}}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{(t+1)^{2}}+\frac{2}{t+1}\,dt \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{t+1}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{1+1}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+1)]-[-\frac{1}{0+1}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)] \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡2]-[-1+0] \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 8
?

If the path C is a part of the parabola y=(x+1)2 traversed from the point P(0,1) to point Q(1,4), then ∫Cdx+dyy=

a
3ln⁡2−12
b
ln⁡3+1
c
2ln⁡3−1
d
ln⁡2−12
e
2ln⁡2+12
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation y=(x+1)2. As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=ti+(t+1)2j,t∈[0,1]

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=i+2(t+1)j.

We can now evaluate the line integral: ∫Cdx+dyy=∫011y(dxdtdt+dydtdt)=∫011y(dxdt+dydt)dt=∫011+2(t+1)(t+1)2dt=∫011(t+1)2+2t+1dt=[−1t+1+2ln⁡(t+1)]01=[−11+1+2ln⁡(1+1)]−[−10+1+2ln⁡(0+1)]=[−12+2ln⁡2]−[−1+0]=2ln⁡2+12

last_observation.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=(x+1)^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+(t+1)^{2}\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2(t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{dx+dy}{y} & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{y}(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{y}(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1+2(t+1)}{(t+1)^{2}}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{(t+1)^{2}}+\frac{2}{t+1}\,dt \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{t+1}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{1+1}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+1)]-[-\frac{1}{0+1}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)] \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡2]-[-1+0] \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 8
?

If the path C is a part of the parabola y=(x+1)2 traversed from the point P(0,1) to point Q(1,4), then ∫Cdx+dyy=

a
3ln⁡2−12
b
ln⁡3+1
c
2ln⁡3−1
d
ln⁡2−12
e
2ln⁡2+12
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation y=(x+1)2. As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=ti+(t+1)2j,t∈[0,1]

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=i+2(t+1)j.

We can now evaluate the line integral: ∫Cdx+dyy=∫011y(dxdtdt+dydtdt)=∫011y(dxdt+dydt)dt=∫011+2(t+1)(t+1)2dt=∫011(t+1)2+2t+1dt=[−1t+1+2ln⁡(t+1)]01=[−11+1+2ln⁡(1+1)]−[−10+1+2ln⁡(0+1)]=[−12+2ln⁡2]−[−1+0]=2ln⁡2+12
question.knowledge_point: Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Cartesian Curves

solution.reasoning: Along y=(x+1)^2, dy=2(x+1) dx, with 0≤x≤1. Thus the integral is \int_0^1[(x+1)^{-2}+2(x+1)^{-1}]\,dx=[-1/(x+1)+2\ln(x+1)]_0^1=2\ln 2+1/2, choice e. No Math Academy answer or grade is captured for this question.

feedback.name: Question 8
feedback.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y=(x+1)^{2}$ traversed from the point $P(0,1)$ to point $Q(1,4),$ then ${\int }_{C}\frac{dx+dy}{y}=$
feedback.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=(x+1)^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+(t+1)^{2}\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2(t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{dx+dy}{y} & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{y}(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{y}(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1+2(t+1)}{(t+1)^{2}}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{(t+1)^{2}}+\frac{2}{t+1}\,dt \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{t+1}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{1+1}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+1)]-[-\frac{1}{0+1}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)] \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡2]-[-1+0] \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 9
question.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y={x}^{2}-1$ traversed from the point $P(1,0)$ to point $Q(2,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy=$
question.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{2}-1.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j,\,t\in [1,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}({y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{({t}^{2}-1)}^{2}\cdot 1+t\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{4}-2{t}^{2}+1+2{t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{4}+1\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}+t]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =[\frac{{2}^{5}}{5}+2]-[\frac{{1}^{5}}{5}+1] \\  & =\frac{32}{5}+2-\frac{1}{5}-1 \\  & =\frac{36}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation y=x2−1. As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve: r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=ti+(t2−1)j,t∈[1,2]

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=i+2tj.

We can now evaluate the line integral: ∫Cy2dx+xdy=∫12y2dxdtdt+xdydtdt=∫12(y2dxdt+xdydt)dt=∫12(t2−1)2⋅1+t⋅2tdt=∫12t4−2t2+1+2t2dt=∫12t4+1dt=[t55+t]12=[255+2]−[155+1]=325+2−15−1=365

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Cartesian Curves
last_observation.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{2}-1.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j,\,t\in [1,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}({y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{({t}^{2}-1)}^{2}\cdot 1+t\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{4}-2{t}^{2}+1+2{t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{4}+1\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}+t]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =[\frac{{2}^{5}}{5}+2]-[\frac{{1}^{5}}{5}+1] \\  & =\frac{32}{5}+2-\frac{1}{5}-1 \\  & =\frac{36}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 10
question.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y={x}^{2}-1$ traversed from the point $A(0,-1)$ to point $B(2,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}5{x}^{2}y\,dx+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,dy=$
question.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{2}-1.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j,\,t\in [0,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}5{x}^{2}y\,dx+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{x}^{2}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(5{x}^{2}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{t}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\cdot 1+{t}^{2}({t}^{2}-1+1)\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{t}^{4}-5{t}^{2}+2{t}^{5}\,dt \\  & ={[{t}^{5}-\frac{5}{3}{t}^{3}+\frac{{t}^{6}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[{2}^{5}-\frac{5}{3}(2)^{3}+\frac{{2}^{6}}{3}]-[0] \\  & =32-\frac{40}{3}+\frac{64}{3} \\  & =40\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

If the path C is a part of the parabola y=x2−1 traversed from the point A(0,−1) to point B(2,3), then ∫C5x2ydx+x2(y+1)dy=

a
32
b
60
c
40
d
43
e
403
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation y=x2−1. As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve: r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=ti+(t2−1)j,t∈[0,2]

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=i+2tj.

We can now evaluate the line integral: ∫C5x2ydx+x2(y+1)dy=∫025x2ydxdtdt+x2(y+1)dydtdt=∫02(5x2ydxdt+x2(y+1)dydt)dt=∫025t2(t2−1)⋅1+t2(t2−1+1)⋅2tdt=∫025t4−5t2+2t5dt=[t5−53t3+t63]02=[25−53(2)3+263]−[0]=32−403+643=40

solution.reasoning: Along y=x^2-1, dy=2x dx and y+1=x^2, with 0≤x≤2. The integral becomes \int_0^2(5x^4-5x^2+2x^5)\,dx=[x^5-5x^3/3+x^6/3]_0^2=32-40/3+64/3=40, choice c. No Math Academy answer or grade is captured for this question.

feedback.name: Question 10
feedback.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y={x}^{2}-1$ traversed from the point $A(0,-1)$ to point $B(2,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}5{x}^{2}y\,dx+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,dy=$
feedback.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{2}-1.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j,\,t\in [0,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}5{x}^{2}y\,dx+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{x}^{2}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(5{x}^{2}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{t}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\cdot 1+{t}^{2}({t}^{2}-1+1)\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{t}^{4}-5{t}^{2}+2{t}^{5}\,dt \\  & ={[{t}^{5}-\frac{5}{3}{t}^{3}+\frac{{t}^{6}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[{2}^{5}-\frac{5}{3}(2)^{3}+\frac{{2}^{6}}{3}]-[0] \\  & =32-\frac{40}{3}+\frac{64}{3} \\  & =40\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 11
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,dx+xy\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=4$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(2,0)$ to the point $B(0,1).$
question.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $1,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,dx+xy\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{x}^{2}\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+xy\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}({x}^{2}\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+xy\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-8{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 11
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cx2dx+xydy, where C is part of the ellipse x2+4y2=4 traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point A(2,0) to the point B(0,1).

a
 6∫0π/2cos⁡tsin⁡t(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)dt
b
−6∫0π/2cos2⁡tsin⁡tdt
c
 −2∫0π/2cos2⁡tsin2⁡tdt
d
 3∫0π/2cos⁡tsin2⁡tdt
e
 ∫0π/2cos⁡tsin⁡t(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 2 and 1, respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=2cos⁡ti+sin⁡tj,t∈[0,π2]

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=−2sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows: ∫Cx2dx+xydy=∫0π/2x2dxdtdt+xydydtdt=∫0π/2(x2dxdt+xydydt)dt=∫0π/2(2cos⁡t)2⋅(−2sin⁡t)+(2cos⁡t)⋅sin⁡t⋅cos⁡tdt=∫0π/2−8cos2⁡tsin⁡t+2cos2⁡tsin⁡tdt=−6∫0π/2cos2⁡tsin⁡tdt

last_observation.name: Question 11
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Computing Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Circles and Ellipses
last_observation.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $1,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,dx+xy\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{x}^{2}\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+xy\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}({x}^{2}\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+xy\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-8{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 11
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cx2dx+xydy, where C is part of the ellipse x2+4y2=4 traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point A(2,0) to the point B(0,1).

a
 6∫0π/2cos⁡tsin⁡t(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)dt
b
−6∫0π/2cos2⁡tsin⁡tdt
c
 −2∫0π/2cos2⁡tsin2⁡tdt
d
 3∫0π/2cos⁡tsin2⁡tdt
e
 ∫0π/2cos⁡tsin⁡t(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 2 and 1, respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=2cos⁡ti+sin⁡tj,t∈[0,π2]

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=−2sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows: ∫Cx2dx+xydy=∫0π/2x2dxdtdt+xydydtdt=∫0π/2(x2dxdt+xydydt)dt=∫0π/2(2cos⁡t)2⋅(−2sin⁡t)+(2cos⁡t)⋅sin⁡t⋅cos⁡tdt=∫0π/2−8cos2⁡tsin⁡t+2cos2⁡tsin⁡tdt=−6∫0π/2cos2⁡tsin⁡tdt
question.knowledge_point: Computing Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Circles and Ellipses

solution.reasoning: Parametrize the ellipse by x=2\cos t and y=\sin t for 0≤t≤\pi/2. Then dx=-2\sin t dt and dy=\cos t dt, so x^2 dx+xy dy=(-8\cos^2 t\sin t+2\cos^2 t\sin t)dt=-6\cos^2 t\sin t dt. This gives choice b. No Math Academy answer or grade is captured for this question.

feedback.name: Question 11
feedback.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,dx+xy\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=4$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(2,0)$ to the point $B(0,1).$
feedback.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $1,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,dx+xy\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{x}^{2}\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+xy\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}({x}^{2}\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+xy\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-8{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cx2dx+xydy, where C is part of the ellipse x2+4y2=4 traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point A(2,0) to the point B(0,1).

a
 6∫0π/2cos⁡tsin⁡t(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)dt
b
−6∫0π/2cos2⁡tsin⁡tdt
c
 −2∫0π/2cos2⁡tsin2⁡tdt
d
 3∫0π/2cos⁡tsin2⁡tdt
e
 ∫0π/2cos⁡tsin⁡t(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 2 and 1, respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=2cos⁡ti+sin⁡tj,t∈[0,π2]

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=−2sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows: ∫Cx2dx+xydy=∫0π/2x2dxdtdt+xydydtdt=∫0π/2(x2dxdt+xydydt)dt=∫0π/2(2cos⁡t)2⋅(−2sin⁡t)+(2cos⁡t)⋅sin⁡t⋅cos⁡tdt=∫0π/2−8cos2⁡tsin⁡t+2cos2⁡tsin⁡tdt=−6∫0π/2cos2⁡tsin⁡tdt

question.name: Question 12
question.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}dx+\frac{2}{x}\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $(-1,0)$ to the point $(0,-3).$
question.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $3,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [\pi ,\frac{3\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}dx+\frac{2}{x}\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{2}{x}\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+\frac{2}{x}\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{2}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+6\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\operatorname{cos}⁡t+6t]_{\pi }^{3\pi /2} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})+9\pi )-(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +6\pi ) \\  & =(0+9\pi )-(-1+6\pi ) \\  & =3\pi +1\end{aligned}
$$

Question 12
?

Evaluate ∫Cdx+2xdy, where C is part of the ellipse 9x2+y2=9 traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point (−1,0) to the point (0,−3).

a
2π−1
b
3π−4
c
 4π
d
3π+1
e
 3π+12
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 1 and 3, respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj,t∈[π,3π2]

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=−sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj.

We can now evaluate the line integral:

∫Cdx+2xdy=∫π3π/2dxdtdt+2xdydtdt=∫π3π/2(dxdt+2xdydt)dt=∫π3π/2(−sin⁡t)+2cos⁡t⋅3cos⁡tdt=∫π3π/2−sin⁡t+6dt=[cos⁡t+6t]π3π/2=(cos⁡(3π2)+9π)−(cos⁡π+6π)=(0+9π)−(−1+6π)=3π+1

last_observation.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $3,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [\pi ,\frac{3\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}dx+\frac{2}{x}\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{2}{x}\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+\frac{2}{x}\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{2}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+6\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\operatorname{cos}⁡t+6t]_{\pi }^{3\pi /2} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})+9\pi )-(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +6\pi ) \\  & =(0+9\pi )-(-1+6\pi ) \\  & =3\pi +1\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Computing Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Circles and Ellipses

solution.reasoning: Parametrize C by x=\cos t and y=3\sin t, with \pi≤t≤3\pi/2. Then dx=-\sin t dt and (2/x)dy=6 dt. Hence the integral is [-\cos t+6t]_{\pi}^{3\pi/2}=1+3\pi, choice d. Although 2/x is undefined at the final endpoint, the improper integral converges because the parametrized integrand extends continuously there. Evaluate ∫Cdx+2xdy, where C is part of the ellipse 9x2+y2=9 traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point (−1,0) to the point (0,−3).

a
2π−1
b
3π−4
c
 4π
d
3π+1
e
 3π+12
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 1 and 3, respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj,t∈[π,3π2]

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=−sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj.

We can now evaluate the line integral:

∫Cdx+2xdy=∫π3π/2dxdtdt+2xdydtdt=∫π3π/2(dxdt+2xdydt)dt=∫π3π/2(−sin⁡t)+2cos⁡t⋅3cos⁡tdt=∫π3π/2−sin⁡t+6dt=[cos⁡t+6t]π3π/2=(cos⁡(3π2)+9π)−(cos⁡π+6π)=(0+9π)−(−1+6π)=3π+1

question.name: Question 13
question.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=2$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(\sqrt{2},0)$ to the point $B(0,\sqrt{2}).$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the parametrization of the curve $C.$ Since it's a circle if radius $\sqrt{2}$ centered at the origin, the curve $C$ can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,j,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, along the curve we have that $x(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}-x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(-2{sin}^{2}⁡t-2{cos}^{2}⁡t)\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\text{d}t \\  & =-2t{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-2[\frac{\pi }{2}-0] \\  & =-\pi \end{aligned}
$$
