Question 13
?

Evaluate ∫Cydx−xdy, where C is part of the circle x2+y2=2 traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point A(2,0) to the point B(0,2).

a
0
b
−π3
c
π3
d
−π
e
π
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find the parametrization of the curve C. Since it's a circle if radius 2 centered at the origin, the curve C can be parametrized as follows:

r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=2cos⁡(t)i+2sin⁡(t)j,t∈[0,π2].

So, along the curve we have that x(t)=2cos⁡t and y(t)=2sin⁡t.

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=−2sin⁡(t)i+2cos⁡(t)j.

Therefore, we can calculate the line integral as follows: ∫Cydx−xdy=∫0π/2ydxdtdt−xdydtdt=∫0π/2(ydxdt−xdydt)dt=∫0π/2(2sin⁡t⋅(−2sin⁡t)−2cos⁡t⋅2cos⁡t)dt=∫0π/2(−2sin2⁡t−2cos2⁡t)dt=−2∫0π/2dt=−2t|0π/2=−2[π2−0]=−π

feedback.name: Question 13
feedback.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=2$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(\sqrt{2},0)$ to the point $B(0,\sqrt{2}).$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the parametrization of the curve $C.$ Since it's a circle if radius $\sqrt{2}$ centered at the origin, the curve $C$ can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,j,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, along the curve we have that $x(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}-x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(-2{sin}^{2}⁡t-2{cos}^{2}⁡t)\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\text{d}t \\  & =-2t{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-2[\frac{\pi }{2}-0] \\  & =-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 14
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x-2y)\,dx+2x\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(0,3)$ to the point $B(0,-3).$
question.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $3,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-2y)\,dx+2x\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(x-2y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+2x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}((x-2y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+2x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t))\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+6{sin}^{2}⁡t+6{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}6-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x−2y)dx+2xdy, where C is part of the ellipse 9x2+y2=9 traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point A(0,3) to the point B(0,−3).

a
 ∫π/23π/26sin2⁡t−cos⁡tdt
b
 ∫π/23π/23−sin2⁡tcos⁡tdt
c
 ∫π/23π/23sin⁡t+cos⁡tdt
d
∫π/23π/26−sin⁡tcos⁡tdt
e
 2∫π/23π/2sin⁡tcos2⁡tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 1 and 3, respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj,t∈[π2,3π2]

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=−sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows: ∫C(x−2y)dx+2xdy=∫π/23π/2(x−2y)dxdtdt+2xdydtdt=∫π/23π/2((x−2y)dxdt+2xdydt)dt=∫π/23π/2(cos⁡t−2(3sin⁡t))⋅(−sin⁡t)+2(cos⁡t)⋅3cos⁡tdt=∫π/23π/2−sin⁡tcos⁡t+6sin2⁡t+6cos2⁡tdt=∫π/23π/26−sin⁡tcos⁡tdt

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Computing Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Circles and Ellipses
last_observation.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $3,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-2y)\,dx+2x\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(x-2y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+2x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}((x-2y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+2x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t))\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+6{sin}^{2}⁡t+6{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}6-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 14
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x−2y)dx+2xdy, where C is part of the ellipse 9x2+y2=9 traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point A(0,3) to the point B(0,−3).

a
 ∫π/23π/26sin2⁡t−cos⁡tdt
b
 ∫π/23π/23−sin2⁡tcos⁡tdt
c
 ∫π/23π/23sin⁡t+cos⁡tdt
d
∫π/23π/26−sin⁡tcos⁡tdt
e
 2∫π/23π/2sin⁡tcos2⁡tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 1 and 3, respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj,t∈[π2,3π2]

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=−sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows: ∫C(x−2y)dx+2xdy=∫π/23π/2(x−2y)dxdtdt+2xdydtdt=∫π/23π/2((x−2y)dxdt+2xdydt)dt=∫π/23π/2(cos⁡t−2(3sin⁡t))⋅(−sin⁡t)+2(cos⁡t)⋅3cos⁡tdt=∫π/23π/2−sin⁡tcos⁡t+6sin2⁡t+6cos2⁡tdt=∫π/23π/26−sin⁡tcos⁡tdt
question.knowledge_point: Computing Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Circles and Ellipses

solution.reasoning: Parametrize C by x=\cos t and y=3\sin t for \pi/2≤t≤3\pi/2. Then (x-2y)dx+2x dy=[-\sin t\cos t+6\sin^2 t+6\cos^2 t]dt=(6-\sin t\cos t)dt, giving choice d. No Math Academy answer or grade is captured for this question.

feedback.name: Question 14
feedback.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x-2y)\,dx+2x\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(0,3)$ to the point $B(0,-3).$
feedback.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $3,$ respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-2y)\,dx+2x\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(x-2y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+2x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}((x-2y)\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+2x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t))\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+6{sin}^{2}⁡t+6{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}6-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x−2y)dx+2xdy, where C is part of the ellipse 9x2+y2=9 traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point A(0,3) to the point B(0,−3).

a
 ∫π/23π/26sin2⁡t−cos⁡tdt
b
 ∫π/23π/23−sin2⁡tcos⁡tdt
c
 ∫π/23π/23sin⁡t+cos⁡tdt
d
∫π/23π/26−sin⁡tcos⁡tdt
e
 2∫π/23π/2sin⁡tcos2⁡tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 1 and 3, respectively, it can be parametrized as follows:

r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj,t∈[π2,3π2]

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=−sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows: ∫C(x−2y)dx+2xdy=∫π/23π/2(x−2y)dxdtdt+2xdydtdt=∫π/23π/2((x−2y)dxdt+2xdydt)dt=∫π/23π/2(cos⁡t−2(3sin⁡t))⋅(−sin⁡t)+2(cos⁡t)⋅3cos⁡tdt=∫π/23π/2−sin⁡tcos⁡t+6sin2⁡t+6cos2⁡tdt=∫π/23π/26−sin⁡tcos⁡tdt

question.name: Question 15
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,dx+x\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(2,0)$ to the point $B(-2,0).$
question.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is a circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [0,\pi ]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}\cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-16{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t(1-4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cx2ydx+xdy, where C is part of the circle x2+y2=4 traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point A(2,0) to the point B(−2,0).

a
 8∫0πcos2⁡t(1−2cos2⁡t)dt
b
 8∫0πcos2⁡tsin2⁡tdt
c
 2∫0πcos2⁡t(1−2sin2⁡t)dt
d
 4∫0πsin2⁡t(1−4cos2⁡t)dt
e
4∫0πcos2⁡t(1−4sin2⁡t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since C is a circle of radius 2 centered at the origin, it can be parametrized as follows:

r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=2cos⁡ti+2sin⁡tj,t∈[0,π]

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=−2sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows: ∫Cx2ydx+xdy=∫0πx2ydxdtdt+xdydtdt=∫0π(x2ydxdt+xdydt)dt=∫0π(2cos⁡t)2⋅(2sin⁡t)⋅(−2sin⁡t)+(2cos⁡t)⋅2cos⁡tdt=∫0π−16sin2⁡tcos2⁡t+4cos2⁡tdt=4∫0πcos2⁡t(1−4sin2⁡t)dt

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Computing Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Circles and Ellipses
last_observation.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is a circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [0,\pi ]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}\cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-16{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t(1-4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cx2ydx+xdy, where C is part of the circle x2+y2=4 traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point A(2,0) to the point B(−2,0).

a
 8∫0πcos2⁡t(1−2cos2⁡t)dt
b
 8∫0πcos2⁡tsin2⁡tdt
c
 2∫0πcos2⁡t(1−2sin2⁡t)dt
d
 4∫0πsin2⁡t(1−4cos2⁡t)dt
e
4∫0πcos2⁡t(1−4sin2⁡t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since C is a circle of radius 2 centered at the origin, it can be parametrized as follows:

r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=2cos⁡ti+2sin⁡tj,t∈[0,π]

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=−2sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows: ∫Cx2ydx+xdy=∫0πx2ydxdtdt+xdydtdt=∫0π(x2ydxdt+xdydt)dt=∫0π(2cos⁡t)2⋅(2sin⁡t)⋅(−2sin⁡t)+(2cos⁡t)⋅2cos⁡tdt=∫0π−16sin2⁡tcos2⁡t+4cos2⁡tdt=4∫0πcos2⁡t(1−4sin2⁡t)dt
question.knowledge_point: Computing Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Circles and Ellipses

solution.reasoning: Set x=2\cos t and y=2\sin t, 0≤t≤\pi. Then x^2y dx+x dy=(-16\cos^2 t\sin^2 t+4\cos^2 t)dt, giving choice e directly. Its integral is 0. Choice d also integrates to 0, so both d and e are equivalent in value; e is the best supported intended parametrization. No Math Academy key or grade is captured.

feedback.name: Question 15
feedback.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,dx+x\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(2,0)$ to the point $B(-2,0).$
feedback.worked_solution:
Since $C$ is a circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin, it can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [0,\pi ]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}\cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-16{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t(1-4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.html:
Question 15
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cx2ydx+xdy, where C is part of the circle x2+y2=4 traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point A(2,0) to the point B(−2,0).

a
 8∫0πcos2⁡t(1−2cos2⁡t)dt
b
 8∫0πcos2⁡tsin2⁡tdt
c
 2∫0πcos2⁡t(1−2sin2⁡t)dt
d
 4∫0πsin2⁡t(1−4cos2⁡t)dt
e
4∫0πcos2⁡t(1−4sin2⁡t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since C is a circle of radius 2 centered at the origin, it can be parametrized as follows:

r(t)=x(t)i+y(t)j=2cos⁡ti+2sin⁡tj,t∈[0,π]

The derivative of r(t) is given by r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=−2sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows: ∫Cx2ydx+xdy=∫0πx2ydxdtdt+xdydtdt=∫0π(x2ydxdt+xdydt)dt=∫0π(2cos⁡t)2⋅(2sin⁡t)⋅(−2sin⁡t)+(2cos⁡t)⋅2cos⁡tdt=∫0π−16sin2⁡tcos2⁡t+4cos2⁡tdt=4∫0πcos2⁡t(1−4sin2⁡t)dt

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
The following table shows the fuel consumption rate, $F(t),$ of a generator (in liters per hour) over a period of $8$ hours.

| $t\,\text{(hours)}$ | $0$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ | $8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $F\,\text{(liters/hour)}$ | $4$ | $3$ | $5$ | $2$ | $6$ |

Use the right Riemann sum for $F(t)$ over the interval $[0,8]$ with four subintervals to approximate the total amount of fuel used.

The total amount of fuel is 
{{field-1}} liters.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's compute the step size $Δt,$ which is just the width of each rectangle. In this case, the endpoints of our interval are $a=0$ and $b=8,$ and there are $n=4$ rectangles, so the step size is

$$
Δt=\frac{b-a}{n}=\frac{8-0}{4}=2.
$$

The area $A$ under the graph can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{F(2)+F(4)+F(6)+F(8)}})\cdot {{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $F(t)$ at each point:

| $t$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ | $8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $F(t)$ | $3$ | $5$ | $2$ | $6$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(3+5+2+6)\cdot 2 \\  & =16\cdot 2 \\  & =32\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total amount of fuel used over a period of $8$ hours. So, the total amount of fuel is $32$ liters.

The following table shows the rate $r(t)$, in flour bags per minute, at which a machine makes flour over a period of $75$ minutes.

| $t\,\text{(minutes)}$ | $0$ | $15$ | $30$ | $45$ | $60$ | $75$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $r\,\text{(flour bags/minute)}$ | $30$ | $25$ | $35$ | $40$ | $35$ | $25$ |

Use the right Riemann sum for $r(t)$ over the interval $[0,75]$, with five subintervals, to approximate the number of flour bags made by the machine in $75$ minutes.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's compute the step size $Δt,$ which is just the width of each rectangle. In this case, the endpoints of our interval are $a=0$ and $b=75,$ and there are $n=5$ rectangles, so the step size is

$$
Δt=\frac{b-a}{n}=\frac{75-0}{5}=15.
$$

The area $A$ under the graph can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{r(15)+r(30)+r(45)+r(60)+r(75)}})\cdot {{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $r(t)$ at each point:

| $t$ | $15$ | $30$ | $45$ | $60$ | $75$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $r(t)$ | $25$ | $35$ | $40$ | $35$ | $25$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(25+35+40+35+25)\cdot 15 \\  & =160\cdot 15 \\  & =2\,400\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total number of flour bags made by the machine in $75$ minutes.  So, the number of flour bags is approximately $2\,400.$

$$

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{R(10)+R(20)+R(30)+R(40)}})\cdot {{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.

$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Estimate the area under the curve $y=-{x}^{2}+2x$ over the interval $[0,2]$ using a right Riemann sum with step size $Δx=0.5.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's sketch our situation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222967/assets/0b9dd2388a7b60866eb15d336d51d181853fe5ac0e52dcd3e02f53fdd4848532.png)

The area $A$ under the graph can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0.5)+f(1)+f(1.5)+f(2)}})\cdot {{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $0.5$ | $1$ | $1.5$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $0.75$ | $1$ | $0.75$ | $0$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(0.75+1+0.75+0)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =2.5\cdot 0.5 \\  & =1.25\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
The following table gives the speed of a minivan measured during a $4$-second interval.

| $t\,(\text{seconds})$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $v(t)\,(\text{meters/second})$ | $17$ | $18$ | $k$ | $25$ | $27$ |

 If the right Riemann sum approximation of the total distance that the minivan traveled during the $4$-second interval has a value of $85$ meters, what is the value of $k?$

*Hint: The distance traveled is given by the area under the speed-time graph.*
questions.worked_solution:
The area $A$ under the curve $y=v(t)$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{v(1)+v(2)+v(3)+v(4)}})\cdot {{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $v(t)$ at each point:

| $t$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $v(t)$ | $18$ | $k$ | $25$ | $27$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(18+k+25+27)\cdot 1 \\  & =70+k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total distance that the minivan traveled. Since we are given that the right Riemann sum approximation of the total distance is $85$ meters,  we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}70+k & =85 \\ k & =15.\end{aligned}
$$

The following table shows the cooling rate of a walk-in freezer over a period of $10$ hours, starting at $9\,\text{a.m}.$

| $t\,(\text{hours})$ | $9$ | $11$ | $13$ | $15$ | $17$ | $19$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $R(t)\,(\text{kilojoules/hour})$ | $5$ | $4$ | $3$ | $2$ | $4$ | $k$ |

 If the right Riemann sum approximation of the total energy removed from $9\,\text{a.m}$ to $7\,\text{p.m.}$ has a value of $40$ kilojoules, then what is the value of $k?$ 

$k=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area $A$ under the curve (rate vs. time) can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{R(11)+R(13)+R(15)+R(17)+R(19)}})\cdot {{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of the rate at each point:

| $t$ | $11$ | $13$ | $15$ | $17$ | $19$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $R(t)$ | $4$ | $3$ | $2$ | $4$ | $k$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(4+3+2+4+k)\cdot 2 \\  & =2(k+13) \\  & =2k+26\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total energy removed from $9\,\text{a.m}$ to $7\,\text{p.m}.$ Since we are given that the right Riemann sum approximation of the total energy removed is $40$ kilojoules, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2k+26 & =40 \\ 2k & =40-26 \\ k & =\frac{14}{2} \\ k & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The table below gives some values of a continuous function $f(t)$ on the closed interval $[10,40].$ The right Riemann sum approximation to the area under the curve $y=f(t)$ with $3$ equal subintervals has a value of $480.$ What must be the value of $k?$

| $t$ | $10$ | $20$ | $30$ | $40$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(t)$ | $18$ | $12$ | $k$ | $16$ |
questions.worked_solution:
The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f(20)+f(30)+f(40)}})\cdot {{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(t)$ at each point:

| $t$ | $20$ | $30$ | $40$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(t)$ | $12$ | $k$ | $16$ |

So, we obtain the following approximation to the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(12+k+16)\cdot 10 \\  & =(28+k)\cdot 10\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are given that $A$ must be $480$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(28+k)\cdot 10 & =480 \\ 28+k & =48 \\ k & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

The table below gives the values of a continuous function $f(x)$ on the closed interval $[0,15]$ with a regular step size. If the right Riemann sum approximation to the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ with $3$ subintervals defined by the given points has a value of $60$, then what must be the value of $k?$

| $x$ | $0$ | $5$ | $10$ | $15$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $k$ |
questions.worked_solution:
The area $A$ under the graph can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f(5)+f(10)+f(15)}})\cdot {{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $5$ | $10$ | $15$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $3$ | $4$ | $k$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(3+4+k)\cdot 5 \\  & =(7+k)\cdot 5 \\  & =5k+35\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are given that $A$ must be  $60,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}5k+35 & =60 \\ 5k & =60-35 \\ k & =\frac{25}{5} \\ k & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem: Estimate the area under the curve $y=4-{x}^{2}$ over the interval $[0,2]$ using a right Riemann sum with step size $Δx=0.5.$ Is this an overestimate or an underestimate?
questions.worked_solution:
Let's sketch our situation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222967/assets/5c52bbe248df0e5a595298d978276023bcb681daa904f37e2818013687aab52e.png)

The area $A$ under the graph can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0.5)+f(1)+f(1.5)+f(2)}})\cdot {{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $0.5$ | $1$ | $1.5$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $3.75$ | $3$ | $1.75$ | $0$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(3.75+3+1.75+0)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =8.50\cdot 0.5 \\  & =4.25\end{aligned}
$$

Because the function is *strictly decreasing* over the interval $[0,2],$ the rectangles reach *below* the function, which means our approximation is an *underestimate* of the correct area.

$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(2+3+4+5)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =14\cdot 0.5 \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Because the function is *strictly increasing* over the interval $[-1,1],$ the rectangles reach *above* the function, which means our approximation is an *overestimate* of the correct area.

questions.name: Question 16
questions.problem:
A drone has positive velocity $v(t)$ after being flown upward from an initial height of $0$ feet at time  $t=0$ seconds. The velocity of the drone is recorded for selected values of $t$ over the interval $0\le t\le 40$ seconds, as shown in the table below. 

| $t\,\text{(seconds)}$ | $0$ | $7$ | $15$ | $25$ | $32$ | $40$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $v\,\text{(feet/second)}$ | $3$ | $10$ | $25$ | $40$ | $46$ | $49$ |

Use the right Riemann sum over $[0,40]$ with five subintervals to approximate the total distance covered by the drone.

*Hint: The distance traveled is given by the area under the velocity-time graph.*
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A$ denote the area under the curve $y=v(t)$ over $[0,40].$ 
In this case, we have $n=3$ rectangles. Using the right Riemann sum, the total distance can be approximated as 

$$
A≈v(7)Δ{t}_{1}+v(15)Δ{t}_{2}+v(25)Δ{t}_{3}+v(32)Δ{t}_{4}+v(40)Δ{t}_{5},
$$

where each $Δ{t}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $t$-value and the previous one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{t}_{i}={t}_{i}-{t}_{i-1}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δt$'s.

| $t$ | $0$ | $7$ | $15$ | $25$ | $32$ | $40$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δt$ | $-$ | $7$ | $8$ | $10$ | $7$ | $8$ |
| $v(t)$ | $-$ | $10$ | $25$ | $40$ | $46$ | $49$ |

We plug in the numbers to approximate the number of liters and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈10\cdot 7+25\cdot 8+40\cdot 10+46\cdot 7+49\cdot 8 \\  & =70+200+400+322+392 \\  & =1\,384.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total distance covered by the drone. So, the distance is approximately $1\,384$ feet.

questions.problem:
The following table shows the values of a continuous function $f(x)$ over the interval $[4,9].$

| $x$ | $4$ | $5.5$ | $8$ | $9$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $4$ | $6$ | $9.5$ |

Use the right Riemann sum, with the three subintervals indicated by the data, to approximate the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ over the interval $[4,9].$
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we have $n=3$ rectangles. Using the right Riemann sum, the area is approximated as 

$$
A≈f(5.5)Δ{x}_{1}+f(8)Δ{x}_{2}+f(9)Δ{x}_{3},
$$

where each $Δ{x}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $x$-value and the previous one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i}-{x}_{i-1}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δx$'s.

| $x$ | $4$ | $5.5$ | $8$ | $9$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δx$ | $-$ | $1.5$ | $2.5$ | $1$ |
| $f(x)$ | $-$ | $4$ | $6$ | $9.5$ |

Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈4\cdot 1.5+6\cdot 2.5+9.5\cdot 1 \\  & =6+15+9.5 \\  & =30.5.\end{aligned}
$$

| $x$ | $1$ | $2.5$ | $5$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $3$ | $5$ | $8.5$ | $9$ |

Use the right Riemann sum, with the three subintervals indicated by the data, to approximate the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ over the interval $[1,7].$
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we have $n=3$ rectangles. Using the right Riemann sum, the area is approximated as 

$$
A≈f(2.5)Δ{x}_{1}+f(5)Δ{x}_{2}+f(7)Δ{x}_{3},
$$

where each $Δ{x}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $x$-value and the previous one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i}-{x}_{i-1}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δx$'s.

| $x$ | $1$ | $2.5$ | $5$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δx$ | $-$ | $1.5$ | $2.5$ | $2$ |
| $f(x)$ | $-$ | $5$ | $8.5$ | $9$ |

Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈5\cdot 1.5+8.5\cdot 2.5+9\cdot 2 \\  & =7.5+21.25+18 \\  & =46.75.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 20
questions.problem:
The table below gives the medication infusion rate $r(t)$, in milligrams per minute, for a patient.

| $t\,\text{(minutes)}$ | $0$ | $4$ | $7$ | $10$ | $13$ | $18$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $r(t)\,\text{(mg/min)}$ | $6$ | $5$ | $3$ | $4$ | $2$ | $1$ |

Use the right Riemann sum over $[0,18]$ with five subintervals to approximate the total medication delivered (in milligrams).

The total medication delivered is
{{field-1}} milligrams.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A$ denote the area under the curve $y=r(t)$ over $[0,18].$ In this case, we have $n=5$ rectangles. Using the right Riemann sum, the area is computed as 

$$
A≈r(4)Δ{t}_{1}+r(7)Δ{t}_{2}+r(10)Δ{t}_{3}+r(13)Δ{t}_{4}+r(18)Δ{t}_{5},
$$

where each $Δ{t}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $t$-value and the previous one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{t}_{i}={t}_{i}-{t}_{i-1}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δt$'s.

| $t$ | $0$ | $4$ | $7$ | $10$ | $13$ | $18$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δt$ | $-$ | $4$ | $3$ | $3$ | $3$ | $5$ |
| $r(t)$ | $-$ | $5$ | $3$ | $4$ | $2$ | $1$ |

We plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈5\cdot 4+3\cdot 3+4\cdot 3+2\cdot 3+1\cdot 5 \\  & =20+9+12+6+5 \\  & =52.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total accumulation of medication. So, the total medication delivered is $52$ milligrams.

canonical_examples.problem: Estimate the area under the curve $y=(2x-4)^2+2$ over the interval $[0,2]$ using a right Riemann sum with step size $\Delta x=0.5.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's sketch our situation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222967/assets/94618262fb303035cd03ccf0274694d7083d9cd3a23d4231e3a8fccde8ac4fe1.png)

$$
\mathcal A\approx(\overbrace{{\color{red}{f(0.5)}}+{\color{red}{f(1)}}+{\color{red}{f(1.5)}}+{\color{red}{f(2)}}}^{\color{red}{\large\text{heights}}})\cdot \underbrace{\color{blue}\Delta x}_{\color{blue}{\large\text{width}}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $0.5$ | $1$ | $1.5$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $11$ | $6$ | $3$ | $2$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(11+6+3+2)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =22\cdot 0.5 \\  & =11\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Solving for an Unknown Given the Value of a Right Riemann Sum With Regular Step Size
canonical_examples.problem:
The table below gives some values of a continuous function $f(x)$ on the closed interval $[-4,2].$ The right Riemann sum approximation to the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ with $3$ equal subintervals has a value of $12.$ What must be the value of $k?$

| $x$ | $-4$ | $-2$ | $0$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $5$ | $3$ | $k$ | $2$ |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The area $\mathcal{A}$ under the graph can be approximated using the formula for the right Riemann sum:

$$
\mathcal A\approx(\overbrace{{\color{red}{f(-2)}}+{\color{red}{f(0)}}+{\color{red}{f(2)}}}^{\color{red}{\large\text{heights}}})\cdot \underbrace{\color{blue}\Delta x}_{\color{blue}{\large\text{width}}}
$$

So, we set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $-2$ | $0$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $3$ | $k$ | $2$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(3+k+2)\cdot 2 \\  & =(k+5)\cdot 2 \\  & =2k+10\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are given that $\mathcal A$ must be $12,$ we obtain

$$
\eqalign{
2k+10 & =12\[5pt]
      2k &= 12-10\[5pt]
        k &= \dfrac{2}{2}\[5pt]
         k  &= 1.
}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Determining Whether a Right Riemann Sum is an Overestimate or Underestimate
canonical_examples.problem: Estimate the area under the curve $y=(2x-4)^2+2$ over the interval $[0,2]$ using a right Riemann sum with step size $\Delta x=0.5.$ Is this an overestimate or an underestimate?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's sketch our situation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222967/assets/94618262fb303035cd03ccf0274694d7083d9cd3a23d4231e3a8fccde8ac4fe1.png)

 

The area $\mathcal{A}$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\mathcal A\approx(\overbrace{{\color{red}{f(0.5)}}+{\color{red}{f(1)}}+{\color{red}{f(1.5)}}+{\color{red}{f(2)}}}^{\color{red}{\large\text{heights}}})\cdot \underbrace{\color{blue}\Delta x}_{\color{blue}{\large\text{width}}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $0.5$ | $1$ | $1.5$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $11$ | $6$ | $3$ | $2$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(11+6+3+2)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =22\cdot 0.5 \\  & =11\end{aligned}
$$

Because the function is *strictly decreasing* over the interval $[0,2],$ the rectangles reach *below* the function, which means our approximation is an *underestimate* of the correct area.

$$
\mathcal{A}	\approx	f(2)\Delta x_1+f(3)\Delta x_2+f(3.5)\Delta x_3+f(4)\Delta x_4,
$$

where each $\Delta x_i$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $x$-value and the previous one, i.e.,

$$
\Delta x_i = x_{i}-x_{i-1}.
$$

We set up a table of values that include the $\Delta x$'s.

| $f(x)$ | $-$ | $4$ | $8.5$ | $10$ | $8$ |

Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈4\cdot 1+8.5\cdot 1+10\cdot 0.5+8\cdot 0.5 \\  & =4+8.5+5+4 \\  & =21.5.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose that we wish to find the area $\mathcal{A}$ under the curve $y=x^2$ between the $x$-values $x=1$ and $x=4,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222967/assets/3538fb94de9aac062e7ed65b9496085d478be911e5da2bf8480b260cec70ae4f.png)

 

We can approximate the area using, for instance, the area of three rectangles, each with a width equal to $1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222967/assets/cbb7b5af27aa5ebd3b5bbb51026017454999682dcf7e172411df79278564a5ae.png)

So, we find the area of each rectangle and then add them all together.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈\overset{\text{[math]1[/math]st rectangle}}{\overset{⏞}{[\,\overset{\text{height}}{\overset{⏞}{f(2)}}\,\cdot \,{{1}_{⏟}}_{\text{base}}\,]}}+\overset{\text{[math]2[/math]nd rectangle}}{\overset{⏞}{[\,\overset{\text{height}}{\overset{⏞}{f(3)}}\,\cdot \,{{1}_{⏟}}_{\text{base}}\,]}}+\overset{\text{[math]3[/math]rd rectangle}}{\overset{⏞}{[\,\overset{\text{height}}{\overset{⏞}{f(4)}}\,\cdot \,{{1}_{⏟}}_{\text{base}}\,]}} \\  & =[{2}^{2}\cdot 1]+[{3}^{2}\cdot 1]+[{4}^{2}\cdot 1] \\  & =4+9+16 \\  & =29\end{aligned}
$$

 

Here, we approximated the area using a **right Riemann sum**, which means that the top-*right* corner of each rectangle touches the curve.

Because the function is *strictly increasing* over the interval $[1,4],$ the rectangles reach *above* the function, which means our approximation is an *overestimate* of the actual area (see the picture above).

tutorials.name: A General Formula for the Right Riemann Sum
tutorials.problem:
In general, the area $\mathcal{A}$ under the curve $y=f(x)$ over the interval $[a,b]$ can be approximated using a right Riemann sum by calculating the area of each rectangle and adding them together. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222967/assets/6aa3fd6dca84719aa7d34fdf75586a33005dd34c416d4456662f9d1876679f61.png)

In the image, we assume that $x_0=a$ and $x_n=b.$  

The resulting area can be calculated as

$$
\mathcal{A}	\approx f(x_1)\Delta x+f(x_2)\Delta x+f(x_3)\Delta x+ \cdots + f(x_n) \Delta x,
$$

where $n$ is the number of rectangles and the step size $\Delta x$ is given by

$$
\Delta x=\dfrac{b-a}{n}.
$$

We can simplify by factoring out the $\Delta x,$ which gives the following general formula:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222967/assets/8570545c3437ee862deba766b58f5746629452459505488a4c59ca17869aa95c.svg)

tutorials.name: Overestimates and Underestimates
tutorials.problem:
Whether the right Riemann sum underestimates or overestimates the actual area under a function depends on whether the function is increasing or decreasing.

- If the function $f(x)$ is increasing, then the rectangles reach *above* the function, which means the right Riemann sum gives an *overestimate* of the actual area under the curve $y=f(x).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222967/assets/71bc3147a2d7ee5867740e67f55d2a257065f0f225b62b4af3b5f5990c0d4ffc.png)

- If the function $f(x)$ is decreasing, then  the rectangles fall *below* the function, which means the right Riemann sum gives an *underestimate* of the actual area under the curve $y=f(x).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222967/assets/0bc5bc2d5daa2b42e640d31b998707af503b4c4489531ef7ddd41f4374405ef7.png)

tutorials.name: Right Riemann Sums with Irregular Step Size
tutorials.problem:
In the last few examples, the step size $\Delta{x}$ was the same for each of the rectangles. In these cases, we say that the step size is **regular**.

There are situations where the step size can vary, which we call an **irregular step size**. But we can still use a right Riemann sum to approximate the area.

For example, let's use a right Riemann sum to approximate the area under the curve of the continuous function $y=f(x)$ whose data is given in the table below.

| $x$ | $1$ | $1.5$ | $2.5$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $2$ | $6$ | $8$ |

The first thing we note is that the domain of the function $y=f(x)$ is *partitioned* as 

$$
\eqalign{
 [1,4] &= [1, 1.5] \cup [1.5, 2.5] \cup [2.5, 4].
}
$$

There are situations where the step size can vary, which we call an **irregular step size**. But we can still use a right Riemann sum to approximate the area.

tutorial.problem:
Suppose that we wish to find the area $\mathcal{A}$ under the curve $y=x^2$ between the $x$-values $x=1$ and $x=4,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222967/assets/3538fb94de9aac062e7ed65b9496085d478be911e5da2bf8480b260cec70ae4f.png)

 

We can approximate the area using, for instance, the area of three rectangles, each with a width equal to $1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222967/assets/cbb7b5af27aa5ebd3b5bbb51026017454999682dcf7e172411df79278564a5ae.png)

So, we find the area of each rectangle and then add them all together.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈\overset{\text{[math]1[/math]st rectangle}}{\overset{⏞}{[\,\overset{\text{height}}{\overset{⏞}{f(2)}}\,\cdot \,{{1}_{⏟}}_{\text{base}}\,]}}+\overset{\text{[math]2[/math]nd rectangle}}{\overset{⏞}{[\,\overset{\text{height}}{\overset{⏞}{f(3)}}\,\cdot \,{{1}_{⏟}}_{\text{base}}\,]}}+\overset{\text{[math]3[/math]rd rectangle}}{\overset{⏞}{[\,\overset{\text{height}}{\overset{⏞}{f(4)}}\,\cdot \,{{1}_{⏟}}_{\text{base}}\,]}} \\  & =[{2}^{2}\cdot 1]+[{3}^{2}\cdot 1]+[{4}^{2}\cdot 1] \\  & =4+9+16 \\  & =29\end{aligned}
$$

 

Here, we approximated the area using a **right Riemann sum**, which means that the top-*right* corner of each rectangle touches the curve.

Because the function is *strictly increasing* over the interval $[1,4],$ the rectangles reach *above* the function, which means our approximation is an *overestimate* of the actual area (see the picture above).

tutorial.name: A General Formula for the Right Riemann Sum
tutorial.problem:
In general, the area $\mathcal{A}$ under the curve $y=f(x)$ over the interval $[a,b]$ can be approximated using a right Riemann sum by calculating the area of each rectangle and adding them together. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222967/assets/6aa3fd6dca84719aa7d34fdf75586a33005dd34c416d4456662f9d1876679f61.png)

In the image, we assume that $x_0=a$ and $x_n=b.$  

The resulting area can be calculated as

$$
\mathcal{A}	\approx f(x_1)\Delta x+f(x_2)\Delta x+f(x_3)\Delta x+ \cdots + f(x_n) \Delta x,
$$

where $n$ is the number of rectangles and the step size $\Delta x$ is given by

$$
\Delta x=\dfrac{b-a}{n}.
$$

We can simplify by factoring out the $\Delta x,$ which gives the following general formula:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222967/assets/2ac927829d869b3018d4534a7536b49de0207a98a21826b2915a50fe9e89f1dc.svg)

First, let's compute the step size $Δt,$ which is just the width of each rectangle. In this case, the endpoints of our interval are $a=0$ and $b=8,$ and there are $n=4$ rectangles, so the step size is

$$
Δt=\frac{b-a}{n}=\frac{8-0}{4}=2.
$$

The area $A$ under the graph can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{F(2)+F(4)+F(6)+F(8)}})\cdot {{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.

So, we now set up a table with the values of $F(t)$ at each point:

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(3+5+2+6)\cdot 2 \\  & =16\cdot 2 \\  & =32\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total amount of fuel used over a period of $8$ hours. So, the total amount of fuel is $32$ liters.

question.html:
Question 6
?

The following table gives the speed of a minivan measured during a 4-second interval.

t(seconds) 0 1 2 3 4
v(t)(meters/second) 17 18 k 25 27
If the right Riemann sum approximation of the total distance that the minivan traveled during the 4-second interval has a value of 85 meters, what is the value of k?

Hint: The distance traveled is given by the area under the speed-time graph.

a
25
b
15
c
22
d
23
e
20
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area A under the curve y=v(t) can be approximated using the formula

A≈(v(1)+v(2)+v(3)+v(4)⏞heights)⋅Δt⏟width.

So, we now set up a table with the values of v(t) at each point:

t 1 2 3 4
v(t) 18 k 25 27

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

A≈(18+k+25+27)⋅1=70+k

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total distance that the minivan traveled. Since we are given that the right Riemann sum approximation of the total distance is 85 meters, we obtain 70+k=85k=15.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The area $A$ under the curve (rate vs. time) can be approximated using the formula

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $R(t)$ | $4$ | $3$ | $2$ | $4$ | $k$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(4+3+2+4+k)\cdot 2 \\  & =2(k+13) \\  & =2k+26\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total energy removed from $9\,\text{a.m}$ to $7\,\text{p.m}.$ Since we are given that the right Riemann sum approximation of the total energy removed is $40$ kilojoules, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2k+26 & =40 \\ 2k & =40-26 \\ k & =\frac{14}{2} \\ k & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorial.name: Overestimates and Underestimates
tutorial.problem:
Whether the right Riemann sum underestimates or overestimates the actual area under a function depends on whether the function is increasing or decreasing.

- If the function $f(x)$ is increasing, then the rectangles reach *above* the function, which means the right Riemann sum gives an *overestimate* of the actual area under the curve $y=f(x).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222967/assets/71bc3147a2d7ee5867740e67f55d2a257065f0f225b62b4af3b5f5990c0d4ffc.png)

- If the function $f(x)$ is decreasing, then  the rectangles fall *below* the function, which means the right Riemann sum gives an *underestimate* of the actual area under the curve $y=f(x).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222967/assets/0bc5bc2d5daa2b42e640d31b998707af503b4c4489531ef7ddd41f4374405ef7.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222967/assets/71bc3147a2d7ee5867740e67f55d2a257065f0f225b62b4af3b5f5990c0d4ffc.png)

- If the function $f(x)$ is decreasing, then  the rectangles fall *below* the function, which means the right Riemann sum gives an *underestimate* of the actual area under the curve $y=f(x).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222967/assets/0bc5bc2d5daa2b42e640d31b998707af503b4c4489531ef7ddd41f4374405ef7.png)

tutorial.name: Right Riemann Sums with Irregular Step Size
tutorial.problem:
In the last few examples, the step size $\Delta{x}$ was the same for each of the rectangles. In these cases, we say that the step size is **regular**.

There are situations where the step size can vary, which we call an **irregular step size**. But we can still use a right Riemann sum to approximate the area.

For example, let's use a right Riemann sum to approximate the area under the curve of the continuous function $y=f(x)$ whose data is given in the table below.

| $x$ | $1$ | $1.5$ | $2.5$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $2$ | $6$ | $8$ |

The first thing we note is that the domain of the function $y=f(x)$ is *partitioned* as 

$$
\eqalign{

In the last few examples, the step size $\Delta{x}$ was the same for each of the rectangles. In these cases, we say that the step size is **regular**.

There are situations where the step size can vary, which we call an **irregular step size**. But we can still use a right Riemann sum to approximate the area.

For example, let's use a right Riemann sum to approximate the area under the curve of the continuous function $y=f(x)$ whose data is given in the table below.

| $x$ | $1$ | $1.5$ | $2.5$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $2$ | $6$ | $8$ |

The first thing we note is that the domain of the function $y=f(x)$ is *partitioned* as 

$$
\eqalign{
 [1,4] &= [1, 1.5] \cup [1.5, 2.5] \cup [2.5, 4].
}
$$

By calculating the area of each rectangle, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

Plugging our numbers into the above, we find

$$
\eqalign{
\mathcal{A}	&\approx	{\color{red}2} \cdot ({\color{blue}1.5-1})
						+ {\color{red}6} \cdot ({\color{blue}2.5-1.5})
						+ {\color{red}8} \cdot ({\color{blue}4-2.5}) \ 
			&= {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}0.5} +{\color{red}6} \cdot {\color{blue}1}+ {\color{red}8} \cdot {\color{blue}1.5}  \

Let $A$ denote the area under the curve $y=r(t)$ over $[0,18].$ In this case, we have $n=5$ rectangles. Using the right Riemann sum, the area is computed as 

$$
A≈r(4)Δ{t}_{1}+r(7)Δ{t}_{2}+r(10)Δ{t}_{3}+r(13)Δ{t}_{4}+r(18)Δ{t}_{5},
$$

where each $Δ{t}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $t$-value and the previous one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{t}_{i}={t}_{i}-{t}_{i-1}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δt$'s.

| $t$ | $0$ | $4$ | $7$ | $10$ | $13$ | $18$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δt$ | $-$ | $4$ | $3$ | $3$ | $3$ | $5$ |
| $r(t)$ | $-$ | $5$ | $3$ | $4$ | $2$ | $1$ |

We plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈5\cdot 4+3\cdot 3+4\cdot 3+2\cdot 3+1\cdot 5 \\  & =20+9+12+6+5 \\  & =52.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total accumulation of medication. So, the total medication delivered is $52$ milligrams.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
The following table shows the fuel consumption rate, $F(t),$ of a generator (in liters per hour) over a period of $8$ hours.

| $t\,\text{(hours)}$ | $0$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ | $8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $F\,\text{(liters/hour)}$ | $4$ | $3$ | $5$ | $2$ | $6$ |

Use the right Riemann sum for $F(t)$ over the interval $[0,8]$ with four subintervals to approximate the total amount of fuel used.

The total amount of fuel is 
{{field-1}} liters.
question.worked_solution:
First, let's compute the step size $Δt,$ which is just the width of each rectangle. In this case, the endpoints of our interval are $a=0$ and $b=8,$ and there are $n=4$ rectangles, so the step size is

$$
Δt=\frac{b-a}{n}=\frac{8-0}{4}=2.
$$

The area $A$ under the graph can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{F(2)+F(4)+F(6)+F(8)}})\cdot {{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $F(t)$ at each point:

| $t$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ | $8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $F(t)$ | $3$ | $5$ | $2$ | $6$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(3+5+2+6)\cdot 2 \\  & =16\cdot 2 \\  & =32\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total amount of fuel used over a period of $8$ hours. So, the total amount of fuel is $32$ liters.

question.problem:
The following table shows the rate $r(t)$, in flour bags per minute, at which a machine makes flour over a period of $75$ minutes.

| $t\,\text{(minutes)}$ | $0$ | $15$ | $30$ | $45$ | $60$ | $75$ |

| $r\,\text{(flour bags/minute)}$ | $30$ | $25$ | $35$ | $40$ | $35$ | $25$ |

Use the right Riemann sum for $r(t)$ over the interval $[0,75]$, with five subintervals, to approximate the number of flour bags made by the machine in $75$ minutes.
question.worked_solution:
First, let's compute the step size $Δt,$ which is just the width of each rectangle. In this case, the endpoints of our interval are $a=0$ and $b=75,$ and there are $n=5$ rectangles, so the step size is

$$
Δt=\frac{b-a}{n}=\frac{75-0}{5}=15.
$$

The area $A$ under the graph can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{r(15)+r(30)+r(45)+r(60)+r(75)}})\cdot {{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $r(t)$ at each point:

| $t$ | $15$ | $30$ | $45$ | $60$ | $75$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $r(t)$ | $25$ | $35$ | $40$ | $35$ | $25$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(25+35+40+35+25)\cdot 15 \\  & =160\cdot 15 \\  & =2\,400\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total number of flour bags made by the machine in $75$ minutes.  So, the number of flour bags is approximately $2\,400.$

question.problem:
The following table shows the water flow rate, $R(t),$ through a pipe (in liters per minute) over a period of $40$ minutes.

| $t\,\text{(minutes)}$ | $0$ | $10$ | $20$ | $30$ | $40$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $R\,\text{(liters/minute)}$ | $12$ | $15$ | $17$ | $16$ | $14$ |

Use the right Riemann sum for $R(t)$ over the interval $[0,40]$ with four subintervals to approximate the total volume of water pumped.

The total volume is 
{{field-1}} liters.
question.worked_solution:
First, let's compute the step size $Δt,$ which is just the width of each rectangle. In this case, the endpoints of our interval are $a=0$ and $b=40,$ and there are $n=4$ rectangles, so the step size is

$$
Δt=\frac{b-a}{n}=\frac{40-0}{4}=10.
$$

The area $A$ under the graph can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{R(10)+R(20)+R(30)+R(40)}})\cdot {{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $R(t)$ at each point:

| $t$ | $10$ | $20$ | $30$ | $40$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $R(t)$ | $15$ | $17$ | $16$ | $14$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(15+17+16+14)\cdot 10 \\  & =62\cdot 10 \\  & =620\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total volume of water pumped over a period of $40$ minutes. So, the total volume is $620$ liters.

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
The following table gives the speed of a minivan measured during a $4$-second interval.

| $t\,(\text{seconds})$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $v(t)\,(\text{meters/second})$ | $17$ | $18$ | $k$ | $25$ | $27$ |

 If the right Riemann sum approximation of the total distance that the minivan traveled during the $4$-second interval has a value of $85$ meters, what is the value of $k?$

*Hint: The distance traveled is given by the area under the speed-time graph.*
question.worked_solution:
The area $A$ under the curve $y=v(t)$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{v(1)+v(2)+v(3)+v(4)}})\cdot {{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $v(t)$ at each point:

| $t$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $v(t)$ | $18$ | $k$ | $25$ | $27$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(18+k+25+27)\cdot 1 \\  & =70+k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total distance that the minivan traveled. Since we are given that the right Riemann sum approximation of the total distance is $85$ meters,  we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}70+k & =85 \\ k & =15.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
The area $A$ under the curve $y=v(t)$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{v(1)+v(2)+v(3)+v(4)}})\cdot {{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $v(t)$ at each point:

| $t$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $v(t)$ | $18$ | $k$ | $25$ | $27$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(18+k+25+27)\cdot 1 \\  & =70+k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total distance that the minivan traveled. Since we are given that the right Riemann sum approximation of the total distance is $85$ meters,  we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}70+k & =85 \\ k & =15.\end{aligned}
$$

t(seconds) 0 1 2 3 4
v(t)(meters/second) 17 18 k 25 27
If the right Riemann sum approximation of the total distance that the minivan traveled during the 4-second interval has a value of 85 meters, what is the value of k?

Hint: The distance traveled is given by the area under the speed-time graph.

a
25
b
15
c
22
d
23
e
20
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area A under the curve y=v(t) can be approximated using the formula

A≈(v(1)+v(2)+v(3)+v(4)⏞heights)⋅Δt⏟width.

So, we now set up a table with the values of v(t) at each point:

t 1 2 3 4
v(t) 18 k 25 27

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

A≈(18+k+25+27)⋅1=70+k

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total distance that the minivan traveled. Since we are given that the right Riemann sum approximation of the total distance is 85 meters, we obtain 70+k=85k=15.

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
The following table shows the cooling rate of a walk-in freezer over a period of $10$ hours, starting at $9\,\text{a.m}.$

| $t\,(\text{hours})$ | $9$ | $11$ | $13$ | $15$ | $17$ | $19$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $R(t)\,(\text{kilojoules/hour})$ | $5$ | $4$ | $3$ | $2$ | $4$ | $k$ |

 If the right Riemann sum approximation of the total energy removed from $9\,\text{a.m}$ to $7\,\text{p.m.}$ has a value of $40$ kilojoules, then what is the value of $k?$ 

$k=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
The area $A$ under the curve (rate vs. time) can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{R(11)+R(13)+R(15)+R(17)+R(19)}})\cdot {{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of the rate at each point:

| $t$ | $11$ | $13$ | $15$ | $17$ | $19$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $R(t)$ | $4$ | $3$ | $2$ | $4$ | $k$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(4+3+2+4+k)\cdot 2 \\  & =2(k+13) \\  & =2k+26\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total energy removed from $9\,\text{a.m}$ to $7\,\text{p.m}.$ Since we are given that the right Riemann sum approximation of the total energy removed is $40$ kilojoules, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2k+26 & =40 \\ 2k & =40-26 \\ k & =\frac{14}{2} \\ k & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
The following table shows the water drainage rate of a reservoir over a period of $8$ hours, starting at $2\,\text{p.m}.$

| $t\,(\text{hours})$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ | $8$ | $10$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $R(t)\,(\text{gallons/hour})$ | $2$ | $k$ | $5$ | $4$ | $3$ |

If the right Riemann sum approximation of the total water drained from $2\,\text{p.m}$ to $10\,\text{p.m.}$ has a value of $30$ gallons, then what is the value of $k?$ 

$k=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
The area $A$ under the curve (rate vs. time) can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{R(4)+R(6)+R(8)+R(10)}})\cdot {{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of the rate at each point:

| $t$ | $4$ | $6$ | $8$ | $10$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $R(t)$ | $k$ | $5$ | $4$ | $3$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(k+5+4+3)\cdot 2 \\  & =2(k+12) \\  & =2k+24\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total water drained from $2\,\text{p.m}$ to $10\,\text{p.m}.$ Since we are given that the right Riemann sum approximation of the total drainage is $30$ gallons, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2k+24 & =30 \\ 2k & =30-24 \\ k & =\frac{6}{2} \\ k & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 10
question.problem:
The table below gives the values of a continuous function $f(x)$ on the closed interval $[0,15]$ with a regular step size. If the right Riemann sum approximation to the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ with $3$ subintervals defined by the given points has a value of $60$, then what must be the value of $k?$

| $x$ | $0$ | $5$ | $10$ | $15$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $k$ |
question.worked_solution:
The area $A$ under the graph can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f(5)+f(10)+f(15)}})\cdot {{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $5$ | $10$ | $15$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $3$ | $4$ | $k$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(3+4+k)\cdot 5 \\  & =(7+k)\cdot 5 \\  & =5k+35\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are given that $A$ must be  $60,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}5k+35 & =60 \\ 5k & =60-35 \\ k & =\frac{25}{5} \\ k & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 13
question.problem: Estimate the area under the curve $y=4-{x}^{2}$ over the interval $[0,2]$ using a right Riemann sum with step size $Δx=0.5.$ Is this an overestimate or an underestimate?
question.worked_solution:
Let's sketch our situation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14222967/assets/5c52bbe248df0e5a595298d978276023bcb681daa904f37e2818013687aab52e.png)

The area $A$ under the graph can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0.5)+f(1)+f(1.5)+f(2)}})\cdot {{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $0.5$ | $1$ | $1.5$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $3.75$ | $3$ | $1.75$ | $0$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(3.75+3+1.75+0)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =8.50\cdot 0.5 \\  & =4.25\end{aligned}
$$

Because the function is *strictly decreasing* over the interval $[0,2],$ the rectangles reach *below* the function, which means our approximation is an *underestimate* of the correct area.

question.name: Question 16
question.problem:
A drone has positive velocity $v(t)$ after being flown upward from an initial height of $0$ feet at time  $t=0$ seconds. The velocity of the drone is recorded for selected values of $t$ over the interval $0\le t\le 40$ seconds, as shown in the table below. 

| $t\,\text{(seconds)}$ | $0$ | $7$ | $15$ | $25$ | $32$ | $40$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $v\,\text{(feet/second)}$ | $3$ | $10$ | $25$ | $40$ | $46$ | $49$ |

Use the right Riemann sum over $[0,40]$ with five subintervals to approximate the total distance covered by the drone.

*Hint: The distance traveled is given by the area under the velocity-time graph.*
question.worked_solution:
Let $A$ denote the area under the curve $y=v(t)$ over $[0,40].$ 
In this case, we have $n=3$ rectangles. Using the right Riemann sum, the total distance can be approximated as 

$$
A≈v(7)Δ{t}_{1}+v(15)Δ{t}_{2}+v(25)Δ{t}_{3}+v(32)Δ{t}_{4}+v(40)Δ{t}_{5},
$$

where each $Δ{t}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $t$-value and the previous one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{t}_{i}={t}_{i}-{t}_{i-1}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δt$'s.

| $t$ | $0$ | $7$ | $15$ | $25$ | $32$ | $40$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δt$ | $-$ | $7$ | $8$ | $10$ | $7$ | $8$ |
| $v(t)$ | $-$ | $10$ | $25$ | $40$ | $46$ | $49$ |

We plug in the numbers to approximate the number of liters and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈10\cdot 7+25\cdot 8+40\cdot 10+46\cdot 7+49\cdot 8 \\  & =70+200+400+322+392 \\  & =1\,384.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total distance covered by the drone. So, the distance is approximately $1\,384$ feet.

Question 16
?

A drone has positive velocity v(t) after being flown upward from an initial height of 0 feet at time t=0 seconds. The velocity of the drone is recorded for selected values of t over the interval 0≤t≤40 seconds, as shown in the table below.

t(seconds) 0 7 15 25 32 40
v(feet/second) 3 10 25 40 46 49
Use the right Riemann sum over [0,40] with five subintervals to approximate the total distance covered by the drone.

Hint: The distance traveled is given by the area under the velocity-time graph.

a
1254 feet
b
1184 feet
c
1384 feet
d
1442 feet
e
1314 feet
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let A denote the area under the curve y=v(t) over [0,40]. In this case, we have n=3 rectangles. Using the right Riemann sum, the total distance can be approximated as A≈v(7)Δt1+v(15)Δt2+v(25)Δt3+v(32)Δt4+v(40)Δt5, where each Δti is calculated by considering the step between a particular t-value and the previous one, i.e.,

Δti=ti−ti−1.

We set up a value table that includes the Δt's.

t 0 7 15 25 32 40
Δt − 7 8 10 7 8
v(t) − 10 25 40 46 49

We plug in the numbers to approximate the number of liters and get A≈10⋅7+25⋅8+40⋅10+46⋅7+49⋅8=70+200+400+322+392=1384.

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total distance covered by the drone. So, the distance is approximately 1384 feet.

question.html:
Question 19
?

The following table shows the values of a continuous function f(x) over the interval [1,7].

x 1 2.5 5 7
f(x) 3 5 8.5 9

Use the right Riemann sum, with the three subintervals indicated by the data, to approximate the area under the curve y=f(x) over the interval [1,7].

a
49.25
b
45.5
c
50.5
d
39.75
e
46.75
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

In this case, we have n=3 rectangles. Using the right Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

A≈f(2.5)Δx1+f(5)Δx2+f(7)Δx3,

where each Δxi is calculated by considering the step between a particular x-value and the previous one, i.e.,

Δxi=xi−xi−1.

We set up a value table that includes the Δx's.

x 1 2.5 5 7
Δx − 1.5 2.5 2
f(x) − 5 8.5 9
Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

A≈5⋅1.5+8.5⋅2.5+9⋅2=7.5+21.25+18=46.75.

question.name: Question 20
question.problem:
The table below gives the medication infusion rate $r(t)$, in milligrams per minute, for a patient.

| $t\,\text{(minutes)}$ | $0$ | $4$ | $7$ | $10$ | $13$ | $18$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $r(t)\,\text{(mg/min)}$ | $6$ | $5$ | $3$ | $4$ | $2$ | $1$ |

Use the right Riemann sum over $[0,18]$ with five subintervals to approximate the total medication delivered (in milligrams).

The total medication delivered is
{{field-1}} milligrams.
question.worked_solution:
Let $A$ denote the area under the curve $y=r(t)$ over $[0,18].$ In this case, we have $n=5$ rectangles. Using the right Riemann sum, the area is computed as 

$$
A≈r(4)Δ{t}_{1}+r(7)Δ{t}_{2}+r(10)Δ{t}_{3}+r(13)Δ{t}_{4}+r(18)Δ{t}_{5},
$$

where each $Δ{t}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $t$-value and the previous one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{t}_{i}={t}_{i}-{t}_{i-1}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δt$'s.

| $t$ | $0$ | $4$ | $7$ | $10$ | $13$ | $18$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δt$ | $-$ | $4$ | $3$ | $3$ | $3$ | $5$ |
| $r(t)$ | $-$ | $5$ | $3$ | $4$ | $2$ | $1$ |

We plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈5\cdot 4+3\cdot 3+4\cdot 3+2\cdot 3+1\cdot 5 \\  & =20+9+12+6+5 \\  & =52.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total accumulation of medication. So, the total medication delivered is $52$ milligrams.
